topics.title: APT41
topics.summary: APT41 is a prolific intrusion set that the United States Department of Justice and multiple commercial vendors have publicly linked to China-based activity, with reporting describing a dual mission of state-directed espionage alongside financially motivated intrusions carried out by the same or overlapping personnel. That combination is unusual and is the reason the group appears in both espionage and cybercrime reporting; analysts should treat the dual-mission characterisation as a widely reported assessment rather than something directly observable in telemetry. Reported targeting spans healthcare and pharmaceutical research, telecommunications, technology and software providers, gaming, media, and logistics, with victims identified across North America, Europe, and Asia. Tradecraft described in public reporting includes exploitation of internet-facing applications and web-facing servers for initial access, abuse of valid accounts and credentials obtained from prior compromises, custom malware and loaders that are frequently updated, digital code-signing certificates abused or stolen to sign malicious binaries, and supply-chain compromise of software build and update processes. The group has also been reported to deploy ransomware for impact, which blurs the line between espionage and extortion and makes the affiliate-versus-state distinction operationally less useful for defenders. Practical defensive implications are that certificate trust is not a security control in itself, that software supply chains must be treated as an attack surface with provenance and build integrity controls, and that detection should emphasise anomalous code-signing behaviour, unusual child processes from web server software, and credentials used from unexpected locations. Attribution statements about APT41 are third-party assessments, and overlap between this cluster and other China-nexus tracking names is acknowledged in public reporting.
objectives: Explain why the espionage-and-financial dual-mission model changes how an intrusion is scoped and escalated.
Build detections for web server processes spawning command interpreters and administrative utilities.
Assess code-signing abuse and describe the provenance and build-integrity controls that reduce supply-chain exposure.
Identify anomalous certificate use, including unexpected signers and signing events outside the release pipeline.
Map supply-chain compromise scenarios onto ATT&CK techniques and identify which are detectable at the enterprise layer.
Rank containment options when an intrusion has both intelligence-collection and destructive objectives.
Explain how credential reuse from unrelated prior compromises shortens attacker time to lateral movement.
Write an attribution paragraph that separates observed behaviour from third-party assessment of sponsorship.

topics.title: FIN7
topics.summary: FIN7 is a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by multiple vendors under names including Carbon Spider, Sangria Tempest, ELBRUS, and Navigator Group. Unlike state-sponsored groups, attribution here is largely a criminal-tracking exercise rather than a question of state sponsorship, and several individuals associated with the activity have been publicly charged in the United States, which gives the group an unusually concrete legal dimension compared with most clusters. Reporting describes a long-running campaign against the retail, hospitality, restaurant, and gaming sectors, with additional targeting of banking, insurance, and healthcare organisations, concentrated heavily in the United States with victims also reported in Europe and Australia. The group's best-documented tradecraft is social engineering at scale: telephone calls and email approaches impersonating legitimate service providers, catering suppliers, or IT support, used to persuade employees to open documents or install remote management software. Reporting has described both malicious document delivery exploiting application features and, in later waves, the use of legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling as an initial access vector, which is significant because it makes the intrusion look like normal administrative activity. Post-compromise behaviour in public reporting includes the deployment of custom point-of-sale malware in earlier campaigns, a shift toward ransomware and extortion activity including through affiliates, credential theft, reconnaissance of payment and email systems, and lateral movement using standard administrative protocols. The group has been described as operating with a structured organisational model including separate teams for intrusion and monetisation, and has been reported selling or granting access to other criminal operators. For defenders in retail and hospitality, the practical priority is detecting abuse of remote management software, unusual outbound payment-related traffic, and social engineering that arrives through voice channels that email-focused controls do not cover.
objectives: Explain how abuse of legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling differs from malware-based initial access and how to detect it.
Analyse telephone-oriented social engineering against help desk and finance functions and design verification controls that resist it.
Detect point-of-sale and payment environment reconnaissance using network segmentation and process telemetry.
Explain how criminal access brokers change the threat model for an organisation that may be a secondary rather than primary target.
Build detection coverage for credential theft and lateral movement in a flat retail network and prioritise segmentation work.
Compare the group's documented shift from payment card theft to ransomware and extortion and explain the defensive implications.
Explain how legal and law enforcement reporting can inform but not replace technical threat intelligence.

topics.title: HAFNIUM
topics.summary: HAFNIUM is an intrusion set that Microsoft and other vendors have attributed to a China-based nexus, and the cluster became widely known in early 2021 after reporting described mass exploitation of vulnerabilities in on-premises internet-facing Microsoft Exchange Server deployments. The group is best understood by its initial access method rather than by a distinctive malware family: public reporting describes opportunistic scanning for vulnerable Exchange servers followed by server-side exploitation that allowed attackers to run commands, drop web shells, and reach credentials and mailbox data without needing to phish a user. Victims reported at the time spanned infectious disease researchers, law firms, defence contractors, policy think tanks, and non-governmental organisations, with a concentration in the United States; subsequent reporting described follow-on activity against additional Exchange flaws and against other internet-facing products. Tradecraft attributed to the group includes web shell persistence on compromised servers, credential theft from the host including from memory, lateral movement using remote administration tooling, and the use of compromised infrastructure for further operations. Because the initial access vector is an unpatched or unreachable-to-patch perimeter service, the defender's central problem is inventory and patch velocity for systems that are exposed to the internet but are often not covered by standard endpoint agents and may lack adequate logging. Detection effort should target web server process trees, file-write events in application directories, authentication from unusual sources, and mailbox access patterns inconsistent with user behaviour. Attribution is a third-party assessment and the group's publicly known tooling is not unique to the cluster.
objectives: Explain why on-premises, internet-facing and agentless servers are a persistent blind spot in detection coverage.
Build detections for web server processes spawning command interpreters and for web shell file-write behaviour.
Describe what Exchange server compromise exposes beyond the host itself, including mailbox and credential material.
Design logging and inventory requirements for perimeter services that fall outside standard endpoint tooling.
Prioritise patch and mitigation work using exposure data rather than severity scores alone.
Sequence containment for a compromised perimeter server while preserving volatile evidence for investigation.
Explain how credential theft from an exploited server enables follow-on access to other enterprise systems.

topics.title: Ke3chang
topics.summary: Ke3chang is a long-running espionage intrusion set that multiple commercial vendors assess as China-based and state-aligned, with public reporting tracing activity back more than a decade and describing sustained targeting of government ministries, diplomatic organisations, military-adjacent entities, and, more recently, non-governmental organisations and media outlets. Victim concentrations reported by vendors include the Middle East, Europe, and North America, with a stable interest in diplomatic and governmental communications. The group is most often described in reporting for its malware families rather than for a distinctive initial access trick: researchers have documented layered backdoors and downloaders that have been rewritten and recompiled repeatedly over the years, with components reported under names such as TidePool and RoyalCli, alongside credential theft from browsers and mail clients. Initial access is commonly described as spearphishing with malicious documents or links, sometimes combined with credential phishing pages that mimic legitimate webmail or file-sharing services, and persistence is reported through registry-based autostart mechanisms and scheduled tasks. The defender-relevant characteristic is longevity and iteration: the same intrusion set recurs against similar targets with refreshed tooling, so detections tied to specific file names or hashes decay quickly while behavioural detections remain useful. Detection effort is best spent on document-to-interpreter process chains, unusual autostart registry modification, anomalous outbound sessions from office and mail applications, and credential access patterns on endpoints belonging to diplomatic or executive staff. Attribution statements are third-party assessments and should be presented with their confidence level rather than as established fact.
objectives: Describe how iterative malware rewriting defeats indicator-based detection and what detection strategy survives it.
Build detections for registry autostart persistence and scheduled task creation on managed endpoints.

Explain why vendor naming conventions for this cluster vary and how to reconcile them in reporting.

topics.title: Lazarus Group
topics.summary: Lazarus Group is an umbrella designator applied by vendors and governments to a broad collection of intrusion activity that public reporting attributes, with varying confidence, to North Korean state-sponsored operators. The United States government has formally attributed specific activity and campaigns to North Korean state actors under the HIDDEN COBRA label, while the vendor ecosystem splits the wider cluster into sub-clusters such as Diamond Sleet, Zinc, Labyrinth Chollima, and Guardian of Peace, each with distinct tooling and mission focus. The scope of this grouping is therefore genuinely contested: analysts disagree about which campaigns share operators, infrastructure, and funding lines, and some activity labelled Lazarus in early reporting has since been reassigned. Reporting describes a uniquely wide target set driven by revenue generation as well as espionage, including financial institutions, cryptocurrency exchanges and payment platforms, defence contractors, aerospace and engineering firms, media and entertainment companies, healthcare and pharmaceutical organisations, and government agencies. Geographic reporting concentrates on South Korea, the United States, Japan, India, and Southeast Asia, with cryptocurrency-focused activity reported globally. Described tradecraft spans spearphishing of individuals with credible lures including job offers and social media contact, exploitation of public-facing applications and widely deployed software, supply-chain compromise of trusted update mechanisms, abuse of valid credentials, custom backdoors and loader families, destructive and disruptive operations including ransomware deployment and wiper activity, and monetisation through cryptocurrency theft and the use of front companies. The group's operational diversity means defenders cannot rely on a small set of behavioural rules; the defensible common threads are supply-chain trust, third-party developer tooling, and identity-based access to financial and administrative systems.

Analyse supply-chain compromise of software update and build mechanisms and identify the controls that would detect or prevent it.
Explain how social-engineering lures such as fraudulent job offers are recognised and countered in a recruitment-heavy organisation.
Detect destructive or disruptive activity patterns early by identifying the precursors that precede them in the intrusion lifecycle.
Assess the risk of third-party developer tooling and dependency compromise when defining build pipeline trust boundaries.
Explain how cryptocurrency and payment fraud objectives change the assets a defender must protect and monitor.
Prioritise detection coverage for an organisation that holds both intellectual property and financial transaction capability.
Evaluate the reliability of public reporting when a tracking label spans multiple distinct operational clusters.

topics.title: menuPass
topics.summary: menuPass is a long-running intrusion set that vendors and, in at least one notable case, a national government have linked to Chinese state-sponsored activity, with the United States Department of Justice announcing charges against individuals described as associated with the group. The cluster is tracked under names including APT10, Stone Panda, Red Apollo, Potassium, and Cicada, and the boundaries of those labels vary between publishers, particularly where the group is described as supporting other operators by granting or reselling access. Public reporting describes targeting of managed service providers and information technology outsourcing firms, defence and aerospace contractors, telecommunications operators, healthcare and pharmaceutical organisations, and government agencies, with victims reported across North America, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The most consequential tradecraft described in reporting is abuse of trusted third-party relationships: managed service providers with legitimate remote administrative access to multiple downstream customers became the entry path to those customers, and in some described waves the group is assessed to have obtained and used service provider credentials and tooling for that purpose. Other reported behaviour includes spearphishing with malicious documents, exploitation of public-facing applications, use of custom backdoors and loaders with modular, extensible designs, abuse of legitimate remote administration software, credential harvesting and use of valid accounts, and long-dwell collection of documents and email before exfiltration to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Reporting has also described the group selling or providing network access to other state-interest operators, which complicates attribution because the actor that gains entry is not always the actor that exploits it. For defenders, the central lesson is that outsourced administration is a trust boundary: provider credentials, jump hosts, and remote management tooling deserve the same monitoring rigour as internal privileged access.
objectives: Explain how managed service provider trust is abused and what monitoring must exist on provider-connected administration paths.
Design detection for legitimate remote administration tooling used with stolen provider credentials and separate it from routine support activity.
Analyse the risk that network access is sold or handed to another operator and how that affects incident scoping and attribution.
Detect modular backdoor and loader behaviour through host telemetry when static signatures do not apply.
Explain how credential harvesting from administrator workstations enables downstream victim compromise across an outsourcing relationship.
Evaluate contractual and technical controls for third-party access, including just-in-time provisioning and session recording.
Build a threat hunting plan for long-dwell document and email collection using access-pattern anomalies.

topics.title: Storm-0501
topics.summary: Storm-0501 is a financially motivated intrusion set tracked by Microsoft under its weather-themed naming convention for unattributed or partially attributed clusters, and also reported by other vendors under the Vanilla Tempest and DEV-0501 designations. Public reporting describes the group as a ransomware affiliate and operator that has moved across multiple ransomware ecosystems over time, which is characteristic of the affiliate model where the same intrusion crew rents or switches payloads depending on access to builders and negotiation infrastructure. Reported targeting concentrates on United States organisations across healthcare, education, manufacturing, government, and retail, with a documented emphasis on hybrid cloud environments where an on-premises identity tier is synchronised to a cloud tenant. The tradecraft described in vendor reporting includes exploitation of internet-facing applications and remote access services for initial access, abuse of valid accounts, credential theft and dumping, and lateral movement using native remote administration tooling before impact. A recurring theme in reporting is the abuse of the identity control plane: compromising privileged on-premises accounts, manipulating or creating accounts to establish persistence, and using the hybrid trust relationship to reach cloud subscriptions and storage. For a defender, that pattern argues for treating identity as the primary detection surface, specifically anomalous privileged role assignments, unexpected directory synchronisation changes, and mailbox or storage access from unfamiliar hosts. Attribution of this cluster is less settled than for state-sponsored groups and the naming itself signals that vendor confidence in a durable identity is limited, so behavioural detections transfer better than actor-specific indicators.
objectives: Describe the ransomware affiliate operating model and why the same crew appears under multiple ecosystem names.
Trace how compromise of an on-premises identity tier leads to control of a synchronised cloud tenant.
Construct detections for suspicious privileged role assignment, account creation, and directory synchronisation changes.
Prioritise triage of alerts in hybrid identity environments where on-premises and cloud telemetry must be correlated.
Explain how credential dumping and valid-account abuse shorten the time from initial access to impact.
Draft a containment sequence for a hybrid identity compromise that preserves evidence and limits ransomware staging.
Evaluate why vendor cluster names such as Storm-xxxx carry limited attribution meaning and how to write actor-agnostic detections.

topics.title: Threat Group-3390
topics.summary: Threat Group-3390 is a long-running intrusion set that public reporting, including work published by several vendors and by MITRE ATT&CK, associates with activity widely assessed by third parties as linked to a Chinese state-interest nexus, though no government has formally indicted or sanctioned the activity under this name, so the sponsorship claim rests on vendor analysis rather than official attribution. The cluster is tracked under many overlapping names, including Emissary Panda, Lucky Mouse, Bronze Union, Earth Smilodon, and APT27, and different publishers have drawn the boundaries of those labels differently over time, with some activity reassigned between clusters as new evidence emerged. Reporting describes targeting of government ministries and agencies, defence and aerospace organisations, energy and critical infrastructure operators, gaming and technology companies, and organisations in the Middle East, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Europe, with additional victims reported in North America. The group is notable in open reporting for combining web-facing exploitation with heavy use of publicly available remote access tooling, which lowers the cost of operations and blurs the line between targeted intrusion and commodity compromise. Described tradecraft includes exploitation of public-facing applications for initial access, abuse of external remote services including web shells and remote management interfaces, credential dumping and reuse of valid administrator accounts, lateral movement over standard administrative protocols, scheduled task and service-based persistence, and exfiltration staged to attacker-controlled or legitimate third-party web services. Several reporting streams describe usage of custom downloaders alongside commodity tooling and an interest in harvesting intellectual property and email. Defenders should note that the group's reliance on administration-facing protocols means detection strategies centred on endpoint malware alone will miss significant portions of the intrusion lifecycle, and that the use of legitimate remote services makes allow-listing decisions consequential.

topics.title: Turla
topics.summary: Turla is one of the longest-documented espionage intrusion sets, assessed by multiple governments and vendors as associated with Russian state security services, most commonly linked in public reporting to the Federal Security Service. That association rests on third-party analysis of infrastructure, tooling, and targeting, and although several national authorities have stated it with high confidence, it remains an attribution judgement rather than an observable technical fact. Reporting describes targeting of government and diplomatic entities, military organisations, research and defence-industrial bodies, and, in later campaigns, entities in Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and North America. The group is known in public reporting for technically distinctive tradecraft: satellite-based and hijacked-network command and control paths, including abuse of other actors' infrastructure; the Snake framework, a long-lived modular implant documented extensively in national advisories; DNS-based covert channels; custom rootkit components; and the use of compromised legitimate websites and cloud services to blend with normal traffic. It has also been reported to co-opt and operate implants on networks already compromised by other intrusion sets, which means victim telemetry may show two distinct actors and incident scope must be established carefully. For defenders, the group's emphasis on low-and-slow collection and network-layer concealment makes host-only monitoring insufficient. Detection effort should include DNS anomaly analysis, hunting for long-lived encrypted sessions to unexpected destinations, review of egress paths for unauthorised tunnels, and integrity monitoring of core system components. Attribution of this cluster should be presented with explicit confidence language, and the overlapping vendor naming schemes should be reconciled before comparing campaigns.

topics.title: Volt Typhoon
topics.summary: Volt Typhoon is a state-sponsored intrusion set that multiple Western government agencies have publicly attributed to a People's Republic of China nexus, described in joint advisories as a prepositioning threat aimed at critical infrastructure rather than at espionage for immediate intelligence gain. Reporting consistently characterises the targeting as spanning communications, energy, transportation, water and wastewater, and maritime sectors, with victims identified across the continental United States as well as in Guam and other Indo-Pacific locations. The group's defining tradecraft is living-off-the-land: it relies heavily on native command interpreters, built-in administrative utilities, and legitimate remote access mechanisms rather than deploying bespoke malware, which means much of its activity can look superficially like routine administration. Reporting describes long dwell time, use of compromised small-office and home-office network devices such as routers and edge appliances as operational relay infrastructure, and attempts to obtain credentials and map the target environment. The practical consequence for defenders is that signature-based detection has limited value here. Detection effort is better spent on baselining normal administrative behaviour, alerting on unusual combinations of native tooling invoked from unexpected parent processes, monitoring for authentication from residential or hosting-provider address space, and treating edge-device integrity as a first-class control. Attribution of Volt Typhoon is stated by those governments with high confidence, but it remains a political and analytical judgement rather than a technical fact observable in telemetry, and the group shares tooling overlap with other China-nexus activity, so analysts should separate behaviour from attribution when writing detections.

Identify behavioural indicators in process ancestry and command-line telemetry that distinguish native-tool abuse from legitimate administration.
Describe how compromised edge and small-office network devices are used as operational relay infrastructure and how to hunt for the resulting traffic.
Build a baselining approach for administrative accounts and service accounts so deviations become visible.
Assess the residual risk to operational technology and critical infrastructure environments when credential access succeeds without malware.
Explain the difference between behavioural evidence in telemetry and government attribution statements, and how to represent confidence honestly in reporting.
Prioritise detection engineering effort across identity, endpoint, and network telemetry for a low-signature, long-dwell threat.

topics.title: AES GCM
topics.summary: AES-GCM is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) mode that combines the AES block cipher in counter mode with a GHASH-based universal hash to produce ciphertext plus a 128-bit authentication tag, so confidentiality and integrity are delivered by a single key. The construction takes a 128-bit block cipher key (AES-128, AES-192 or AES-256), a unique nonce of typically 96 bits, the plaintext, and optional associated data that is authenticated but not encrypted. Decryption fails closed: if the tag does not verify, no plaintext is released, which is why GCM is preferred over unauthenticated modes such as CBC in modern protocols like TLS 1.3, IPsec ESP, and 802.11 WPA3. The security proof of GCM depends absolutely on nonce uniqueness per key; reusing a nonce with the same key leaks the XOR of plaintexts and, worse, exposes the GHASH authentication subkey, letting an attacker forge arbitrary messages. Other practical failure modes are truncating the tag too aggressively, ignoring tag verification in application code, reusing keys across contexts, and exhausting the 96-bit counter space on long-lived high-volume keys. Implementations also vary in constant-time behaviour, so side channels during GHASH multiplication matter on embedded and shared hardware. For defenders this means key and nonce lifecycle management, per-message key derivation, envelope encryption patterns, and reliable detection of downgrade or fallback to legacy cipher suites are all first-class operational concerns rather than implementation details.
objectives: Explain how AES-GCM composes counter-mode encryption with GHASH authentication and what the authentication tag guarantees.
Describe exactly what breaks when a nonce is reused with the same key, and how that failure surfaces in captured traffic.
Choose appropriate tag lengths and associated data for a protocol, and justify why tag truncation is a risk decision.
Recognise downgrade and fallback behaviour in TLS or IPsec logs that indicates traffic is no longer protected by an AEAD mode.
Design envelope encryption and per-message key derivation so that high-volume services never exhaust nonce space.
Evaluate a code review finding where a GCM tag is computed but not actually verified before use.
Map cryptographic weakening of transport encryption to adversary techniques for collection and command and control.

topics.title: Alert Fatigue
topics.summary: Alert fatigue is the degradation of analyst attention and judgement caused by a detection pipeline that raises more alerts than a team can meaningfully examine. It is not simply a volume problem. Fatigue sets in when alerts are numerous and individually low-yield, so that the rational response becomes pattern matching on the alert title, batch-closing whole categories, and treating the queue as work to be cleared rather than as evidence to be assessed. The operational consequences are measurable: rising time to acknowledge the alerts that matter, missed true positives hidden inside noisy detections, analyst burnout and turnover, and a dangerous normalisation of anomalous activity. The root causes are structural. Rules built on a single event with no threshold, no entity context and no business weighting will fire on legitimate administrative behaviour. Log sources with poor parsing produce malformed fields that make every alert look identical. Duplicate detections from overlapping content raise the same activity several times. Suppressions are applied permanently instead of with an expiry, so detections quietly die and nobody notices the resulting blind spot. Because fatigue is a measurement and content-quality problem, the treatment is engineering rather than exhortation. Teams track per-rule alert volume against per-rule confirmed-true rate, retire or rewrite rules below a usefulness threshold, add allow-listing with mandatory expiry, enrich alerts with asset and identity context before an analyst ever sees them, and consolidate overlapping detections. Detection content then becomes a maintained product with owners, review dates and a documented reason to exist.
objectives: You will be able to explain how alert volume, low yield and duplicate content interact to produce analyst over-trust in titles and batch closures.
You will be able to measure per-rule alert volume against confirmed-true rate and use it to identify content that should be rewritten or retired.
You will be able to add entity context and thresholds to a noisy rule without destroying its ability to catch the behaviour it targets.
You will be able to design suppressions with mandatory expiry, ownership and a review condition rather than permanent exclusions.
You will be able to evaluate the operational cost of a detection before deploying it, including expected daily volume at current estate scale.
You will be able to argue a defensible case for retiring a detection while documenting the compensating control for the coverage it removes.

topics.title: Alert Triage
topics.summary: Triage is the first analytical pass over an alert or a queue of alerts, in which an analyst decides what the signal means, how urgent it is, and what happens next. It is a bounded activity with a defined output, not open-ended investigation: for each alert the analyst produces a disposition, a confidence statement, the evidence that supports it, and an escalation decision. Good triage follows a fixed sequence. Validate that the alert is real and not a duplicate, a scheduled job or a known test; establish the entities involved, meaning accounts, hosts, source addresses and business context; reconstruct the timeline from raw logs rather than trusting the alert's own summary; look for corroborating or contradicting telemetry from independent sources such as identity, endpoint and network records; and only then decide whether the activity is benign, suspicious or confirmed malicious. The consistent failure modes are well understood. Analysts anchor on the alert title and never open the underlying events. They accept an enrichment field as fact when it is stale or unverified. They close an alert because a similar one was benign last month. They escalate too early and burn responder capacity, or too late and let a foothold mature. Effective SOCs reduce these errors structurally: clear severity and escalation criteria, checklists for the highest-volume alert types, suppression with an expiry date rather than permanent closure, and requirement that the disposition evidence be written down so a reviewer can reproduce the judgement. Triage quality is best measured not by alerts closed but by escalation precision and by whether real incidents were initially triaged as benign.
objectives: You will be able to apply a repeatable triage sequence that validates, contextualises, reconstructs and corroborates an alert before disposition.
You will be able to reconstruct an event timeline from raw telemetry instead of relying on an alert's generated summary.
You will be able to write a disposition that records evidence, confidence and escalation rationale in a form another analyst can reproduce.
You will be able to prioritise a mixed queue using asset criticality, identity privilege and observed adversary behaviour rather than raw severity labels.
You will be able to recognise and correct common triage biases such as title anchoring, stale enrichment trust and precedent-based closure.
You will be able to decide when to suppress rather than close an alert, and specify an expiry and review condition for the suppression.

topics.title: Anti Forensics
topics.summary: Anti-forensics is the set of techniques an adversary uses to frustrate, mislead or delay forensic analysis, either by destroying evidence, by making analysis uneconomic, or by planting artefacts that send investigators down the wrong path. The category spans data destruction such as secure wiping, free-space overwriting and the deletion of logs; artefact manipulation including timestamp alteration, log tampering and the removal of entries from event or audit trails; concealment through encryption, steganography, alternate data streams, hidden partitions and packed or obfuscated binaries; tool subversion, where malicious code interferes with the very utilities a responder would run, including kernel-mode rootkits and the disabling of security logging; and attribution attacks such as the deliberate use of another organisation's naming conventions or living-off-the-land binaries to blend into normal activity. For defenders, anti-forensics matters less as a list of tools than as an interpretive warning: the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and the failure of a standard tool to find something may itself be a finding worth pursuing. Investigations respond by collecting volatile data before artefacts can be altered, corroborating every conclusion across independent sources, validating acquisition and analysis tools against known-good behaviour, and treating inconsistencies in timestamps or log continuity as investigative leads. Reporting anti-forensic indicators, including gaps, tampering and tool anomalies, alongside substantive findings protects the credibility of the case and informs detection engineering, because these techniques often require behaviour that can be detected even when the artefacts themselves cannot be recovered.
objectives: Categorise anti-forensic techniques by whether they destroy, manipulate, conceal or misattribute evidence.
Interpret missing, discontinuous or inconsistent artefacts as investigative findings rather than as proof of innocence.
Adapt collection order and tooling when an environment may contain kernel-level or tool-subverting implants.
Corroborate conclusions across independent evidence sources so they withstand deliberate artefact manipulation.
Map observed anti-forensic behaviour to adversary tactics and identify the detection opportunities it creates.
Document and communicate confidence limits when evidence integrity or completeness is in question.
Brief stakeholders on how anti-forensics affects scope estimates, investigation timelines and legal defensibility.

topics.title: Antimalware Scan Interface
topics.summary: The Antimalware Scan Interface is a Windows interface that lets applications and scripting runtimes hand content to the installed antimalware provider for inspection before that content is executed, interpreted or loaded. Its importance comes from the gap it fills: script engines and dynamic runtimes do not necessarily write a file to disk before running code, so a traditional file scanner sees nothing to inspect. By calling into AMSI, a participating host such as a scripting engine, an office macro runtime, or a dynamic scripting component can submit the script text, the decoded buffer or the module being loaded, and the antimalware provider can return a verdict that causes the host to abort. AMSI is not itself a detection engine; it is a broker, and its effectiveness depends entirely on the provider behind it and on the host actually calling it with useful content. That dependency is the source of its well-known weaknesses. Bypass research concentrates on preventing the scan rather than defeating the signatures: corrupting the in-memory state of the interface so that calls fail open, patching the provider's scanning function inside a process, or structuring code so that the meaningful payload never appears in a single buffer that gets submitted. Because several of these approaches leave distinctive artefacts, AMSI remains valuable to defenders: failures of the interface, unexpected patching of its components, and mismatches between what a script claims to do and what the provider observed are all high-signal events when the relevant logging is enabled, and AMSI output frequently feeds straight into endpoint detection platforms.
objectives: Explain what AMSI is, how a participating host submits content, and why the design closes a scripting visibility gap.
Identify which runtimes and applications call AMSI and what each contributes to endpoint detection.
Describe the classes of AMSI bypass at a conceptual level and the artefacts each tends to leave behind.
Detect tampering with AMSI components by monitoring module integrity and provider load failures.
Assess the limitations of AMSI against encoded, segmented or encrypted content that never reaches it intact.
Integrate AMSI verdicts and errors into endpoint alert triage alongside script block and process telemetry.

topics.title: Attribute-Based Access Control
topics.summary: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) is an access control model that evaluates a policy against attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the environment at the moment of the request, rather than relying solely on a pre-assigned role. Typical subject attributes include department, clearance, employment status, device compliance state and manager, while resource attributes include classification, owner, tenant and data residency, and environment attributes include time, network origin, authentication strength and risk score. Because the decision is computed rather than looked up, ABAC can express rules such as permitting access only when the requesting device is managed, the user is a current employee in the owning department, and the request arrives from a trusted network during business hours. That expressiveness is also the model's principal operational hazard: policies interact, and a rule written to satisfy one business case can silently widen access when combined with another. Policy authoring therefore needs the same rigour as code, including version control, review, automated testing against representative request scenarios, and documentation of the attribute sources that feed each decision. Attribute quality becomes a security dependency, because a stale human resources feed or a device compliance signal that fails open can convert a correct policy into an incorrect decision. Implementing ABAC usually starts alongside existing RBAC, using roles as coarse-grained building blocks and attributes as fine-grained conditions, and this is the pattern most cloud identity platforms and policy engines such as Open Policy Agent and Cedar-family languages support.
objectives: You will be able to define subject, resource, action and environment attributes and map them to real access requirements.
You will be able to write and test an attribute-based policy and reason about how it composes with existing role grants.

topics.title: Attribution
topics.summary: Attribution is the analytic judgement that links a set of observed activity to a responsible actor, and it is one of the most overclaimed products in cyber threat intelligence. Analysts distinguish at least three questions that are routinely conflated: technical attribution of tooling and infrastructure to a cluster of activity, operational attribution of that cluster to a consistent set of people and their tradecraft, and strategic or political attribution of those people to a state, sponsor or criminal organisation. Each step is weaker than the last and requires evidence of a different kind, so confidence should fall as the claim becomes more consequential. The core technical difficulty is that tooling, malware families, infrastructure and even credentials are shared, resold, stolen or deliberately planted. False flags are cheap: strings, language artefacts, time zone artefacts and reused code can all be inserted to mislead. Mature practice therefore relies on corroboration across independent sources, on clustering by infrastructure and capability rather than by a single indicator, and on structured analytic techniques that force the analyst to argue the alternative hypothesis. Naming conventions matter as well. Tracking a cluster with a neutral designator keeps the technical analysis separable from the attribution claim, whereas reusing a named actor label imports assumptions about intent and sponsorship that the evidence may not support. Public attribution also carries legal, diplomatic and operational consequences, so it is normally a leadership decision informed by intelligence rather than a side effect of a technical report. Defensively, attribution rarely changes the immediate response, because containment, eradication and recovery depend on what the adversary can do, not on who they are, though it does shape long-term risk, control investment and intelligence sharing.
objectives: You will be able to separate technical, operational and strategic attribution and state the evidence each requires.
You will be able to argue an alternative hypothesis and identify the false flag opportunities in a given evidence set.
You will be able to cluster activity by infrastructure and capability instead of relying on a single indicator.

topics.title: BGP Hijacking
topics.summary: The Border Gateway Protocol is the routing protocol that exchanges reachability information between autonomous systems on the internet, and it operates on trust: a network announces the address prefixes it can reach, and its neighbours generally believe the announcement. BGP hijacking exploits that trust by announcing a prefix the attacker does not legitimately control, or by announcing a more specific prefix that wins longest-prefix matching, so traffic destined for the real owner is delivered elsewhere. The consequences range from denial of service, because traffic is blackholed or dropped, to interception, because the attacker forwards traffic onward while observing or modifying it. A route leak, where a network accidentally re-announces routes learned from one provider to another, produces similar effects without malicious intent and is a frequent cause of large-scale incidents. Because the protocol has no built-in origin authentication, a bad announcement can propagate globally within minutes and is corrected only after the legitimate operator and its providers respond, which means detection speed matters as much as prevention. Prevention uses cryptographic or registry-based attestation of route origin: a resource public key infrastructure with route origin authorisations lets a network publish which autonomous system may originate which prefix, and BGPsec aims to protect the path itself, although adoption remains uneven. Filtering at the edge, rejecting announcements for prefixes a peer is not authorised to originate and applying maximum prefix limits, prevents a large share of accidental leaks. Detection complements prevention through public route monitoring services, looking-glass queries, and comparison of observed paths against expected paths. For defenders outside routing teams, hijacking matters because it can redirect traffic to an attacker-controlled network, support impersonation of a domain or service, and enable interception of sessions whose protection depends on the endpoints involved.
objectives: You will be able to explain how prefix announcements and longest-prefix matching make hijacking possible.
You will be able to distinguish a malicious hijack from an accidental route leak by evidence.

You will be able to describe how route origin authorisation and BGPsec constrain unauthorised announcements.

topics.title: Business Impact Analysis
topics.summary: A business impact analysis is the structured study that determines how the loss or degradation of each business process, and the resources that process depends on, would affect the organisation over time. It is the analytical foundation of business continuity and disaster recovery planning because it produces the numbers that drive every later decision: the maximum tolerable period of disruption, the recovery time objective, the recovery point objective, the minimum acceptable service level and the priority order for restoration when resources are scarce. A competent analysis works process-first rather than asset-first. It starts from the organisation's products and services, breaks them into business processes, identifies the people, applications, data, facilities, suppliers and infrastructure each process needs, and then models impact across several dimensions: financial, regulatory and legal, operational, customer and reputational, and safety where relevant. Impact is assessed over a time axis because most disruption is tolerable for minutes and intolerable after days, and that curve is what makes a recovery objective defensible rather than arbitrary. Practitioners should insist on named process owners providing input, because a BIA produced solely by the security team will encode technical assumptions that no part of the business has agreed to. The output feeds continuity strategies, dependency mapping, third-party risk assessment, recovery testing scenarios and the risk register, and it should be refreshed when the business changes rather than on a fixed multi-year cycle alone.
objectives: You will be able to derive business processes and their dependencies from products and services rather than from an asset list.
You will be able to model impact across financial, regulatory, operational, customer and safety dimensions.

topics.title: C2 Beacon
topics.summary: A command-and-control beacon is the component of an intrusion that maintains a channel between implanted code on a victim host and infrastructure the operator controls, periodically checking in for instructions or waiting to be activated. The beacon's design goal is reliability under adverse conditions: it must survive intermittent connectivity, survive the loss of individual servers, and remain inconspicuous in network and host telemetry. That produces a recognisable set of behaviours worth studying. Beacons poll on a schedule, frequently with a randomised jitter component so that intervals do not look machine-generated. They blend into permitted traffic by using common application protocols over ports that are rarely blocked, or by tunnelling through domain name resolution, and they frequently use legitimate third-party services as relay points rather than bespoke infrastructure. They also tend to fail in characteristic ways: repeated connections to a hostname that resolves to a documentation-range address or a domain registered very recently, a steady byte-size profile in both directions, TLS sessions with unusual parameters, or a process that talks to the internet at regular intervals with no user interaction. Defenders have two complementary angles. Network analytics and flow metadata can surface beaconing periodicity and long-lived low-volume channels without any payload inspection, which is valuable when traffic is encrypted end to end. Host and identity telemetry can surface which process is making the connection, under which account, and what it did immediately before and after. Because the channel is what makes dwell time possible, disrupting or detecting it early is often the single most consequential intervention available to a defender, and it is also the point at which an adversary's operational security is most exposed.
objectives: Explain what a C2 beacon does on a victim host and why periodic check-in shapes its observable behaviour.

topics.title: Certificate Pinning
topics.summary: Certificate pinning is the practice of restricting which certificates or public keys a client will accept for a given service, instead of trusting every certificate authority in the platform trust store. The client embeds or is configured with an expected leaf certificate, a public key, a hash of either, or the identity of a specific issuing authority, and it rejects any chain that does not match. This closes the gap left by the CA model, where any trusted authority, or anyone who can convince one to issue, can produce a certificate that validates for a hostname the attacker does not control. Pinning is common in mobile applications, thick clients, embedded device firmware, service meshes and internal API calls. It is also one of the more brittle controls in wide deployment, because pins must be updated in lockstep with certificate rotation and clients that cannot be updated will fail closed at renewal time. Common failures are pinning only the leaf certificate with no backup pin, storing pins in a configuration file that is itself updated over the network, pinning by common name rather than key material, implementing pin checks in a layer that can be bypassed by hooking or proxying, and failing to test pin mismatch handling. Defenders care about pinning from both directions, since a sudden wave of pin validation failures across clients may indicate an interception attempt, a misissued certificate, or a botched deployment.
objectives: Distinguish leaf certificate pinning, public key pinning and issuing-authority pinning, and state the tradeoffs of each.
Explain how pinning mitigates CA compromise and misissuance without replacing the rest of chain validation.

Diagnose why a pinning implementation can be bypassed through dynamic instrumentation or a user-installed root.

topics.title: Chain OF Custody
topics.summary: Chain of custody is the documented, unbroken record of who collected a piece of evidence, when and where it was collected, how it was handled and stored, who accessed it afterwards, and how it was transferred between custodians. In digital forensics the evidence is usually a disk image, a memory capture, a mobile extraction, a log export or a set of network captures, and the record takes the form of a custody form supported by artefacts such as write blockers, hash values, sealed storage, signed transfer receipts and case management timestamps. The purpose is to make the evidence defensible: in a disciplinary hearing, a civil dispute, a regulatory investigation or a criminal prosecution, opposing counsel will challenge whether the artefact presented is the same artefact that existed at the scene, and an unbroken chain with matching cryptographic hashes is the standard answer. Chain of custody begins before acquisition with authorisation and scope, continues through the use of validated tools and write blockers, and extends into analysis, where working copies are made and originals remain sealed. Breakpoints - an unexplained gap, a missing signature, an analyst who examined the original without documenting it, storage in an uncontrolled location - do not automatically make evidence inadmissible, but they weaken its weight and can be fatal in the strictest proceedings. Good practice treats custody as a habit rather than as paperwork: hash on acquisition and again on every transfer, log every access, store in access-controlled locations, and never let convenience override the record.

topics.title: Cloud Security Posture Management
topics.summary: Cloud security posture management is the continuous discovery, assessment and remediation of configuration risk across cloud accounts, covering identity grants, network exposure, storage permissions, encryption settings, logging coverage and compliance against a chosen baseline. A CSPM capability connects to provider APIs with read-only credentials, enumerates every resource in scope, evaluates each against policy rules, and reports the drift between intended and actual state with enough context to prioritise. Its output is deliberately different from a vulnerability scanner: rather than finding flaws in code, it finds misconfiguration in deployed infrastructure, which is the dominant cause of cloud incidents. Effective implementations depend on several disciplines. Rules must be mapped to recognised benchmarks so that findings carry external meaning, and they must be tuned so that each alert corresponds to a real risk, because unmanaged volume produces alert fatigue and silent suppression. Ownership has to route to the team able to fix the resource, and the tool must distinguish misconfiguration that is exploitable now from latent risk. Coverage itself is a risk area, since accounts and regions excluded from scanning are invisible, and a new account created outside the pipeline arrives unmonitored. Mature programmes treat posture findings as code defects, feeding them back into templates and guardrails so the same mistake cannot be redeployed.
objectives: You will be able to explain what CSPM evaluates and how it differs from vulnerability scanning, CSPP and cloud infrastructure entitlement work.
You will be able to map posture findings to a recognised benchmark and justify the priority assigned to each.
You will be able to tune noisy rules without suppressing genuine exposure, and identify the tradeoff each suppression introduces.
You will be able to detect coverage gaps such as unscanned accounts, regions and newly created subscriptions.
You will be able to write a posture finding report that a platform team can act on without further triage.

topics.title: Cloud Workload Protection Platform
topics.summary: A cloud workload protection platform protects the running compute layer of a cloud estate, covering virtual machines, containers, serverless functions, and increasingly the orchestration control plane that schedules them. Where posture management examines configuration, workload protection examines behaviour at runtime: process execution, file integrity, network connections, privilege changes, memory anomalies, image contents and package vulnerabilities across the whole lifecycle from build to retirement. Typical capability clusters include agent or agentless vulnerability assessment of images and hosts, file and process integrity monitoring, runtime threat detection with behavioural rules, network microsegmentation and flow visibility, container image scanning with admission control, serverless function analysis, and integration of findings into the same incident pipeline as endpoint detection. The operational challenge is that cloud workloads are ephemeral and horizontally scaled, so host-centric assumptions break: a compromised container may live for minutes, identifiers change on every deploy, and an analyst cannot rely on a single stable hostname. Effective programmes therefore anchor detection on immutable artefacts such as image digests, workload identity, service accounts and deployment metadata, and they connect runtime signal to the pipeline that produced the workload. Without that linkage, teams see unusual activity but cannot attribute it to a build, a team or an image, and remediation becomes guesswork.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish what a workload protection platform covers from what posture management and entitlement analysis cover.

topics.title: Code Signing
topics.summary: Code signing is the use of a digital signature over a software artifact so that a consumer can verify who produced it and whether it has changed since it was signed. The signer hashes the artifact with a cryptographic digest and signs that digest with a private key; the verifier checks the signature with the corresponding public key, validates the certificate chain to a trusted root, and confirms the artifact digest matches. Signing is the mechanism behind operating system and package manager trust decisions, driver and installer approval, browser extension and mobile application distribution, container image trust policies and artifact repository promotion rules. For a practising engineer the interesting part is everything around the cryptography. Which identity signs, how that identity is proven to the certificate authority, where the private key lives, how the signing operation is authorised and logged, and how the trust decision is enforced at the point of installation or deployment all determine whether signing provides real assurance or merely ceremony. Weaknesses that keep recurring are long-lived unprotected private keys, signing services reachable from a compromised build job, verification that checks a signature exists but not whose it is, timestamping omitted so signatures expire with the certificate, and revocation infrastructure that is never consulted. Modern practice moves towards short-lived keys held in hardware or a managed signing service, keyless signing bound to a workload identity, transparency logs that record every signing event, and build provenance that binds an artifact to the exact source revision and build definition that produced it.
objectives: You will be able to explain the signing and verification flow, including certificate chain validation, digest comparison and the role of timestamping.
You will be able to describe how signing trust is consumed by operating systems, package managers, container runtimes and browsers.
You will be able to design a signing key custody model using hardware modules or managed signing services with authorised, logged use.
You will be able to identify common verification failures, such as accepting any valid signature regardless of signer identity or skipping revocation checks.
You will be able to explain build provenance and how it binds an artifact to its source revision and build definition.
You will be able to assess what a signing programme would and would not prevent if a build system were compromised.

topics.title: Conditional Access
topics.summary: Conditional access is a policy engine that evaluates signals about a sign-in attempt and then decides whether to allow it, block it, or allow it only after additional requirements are satisfied such as multi-factor authentication, a compliant device or a trusted network location. The signals typically include user or group membership, application being accessed, device platform, device compliance or join state, client application type, source IP address and named location, and sign-in risk or user risk computed by the identity provider. This is the mechanism that turns identity from a binary decision into a graded one, and it is the practical enforcement point for zero trust principles in most enterprise estates today because it can require stronger evidence for sensitive applications while keeping low-risk access frictionless. The security outcome depends entirely on policy coverage and on how exceptions are managed: a policy that excludes a service account, a legacy protocol client or a break-glass identity creates a path that does not require the control, and adversaries deliberately hunt for those paths by attempting authentication through older client stacks that cannot satisfy modern requirements. Policy design therefore needs both a default posture that blocks what is not explicitly permitted and a deliberate, documented set of exclusions with compensating monitoring. Orchestration between policies matters too, since many platforms combine all applicable policies and require satisfaction of every grant control they contain, so an apparently narrow policy can change behaviour for a large population. Defenders rely on the resulting telemetry, because sign-in logs annotated with policy outcomes allow alerting on repeated policy failures from one identity, on successful sign-ins that bypassed an expected control, and on new or modified policy definitions that quietly weaken posture.
objectives: You will be able to enumerate the signals available to a conditional access policy and select the ones relevant to a stated requirement.
You will be able to distinguish grant controls from session controls and explain how multiple applicable policies combine.

topics.title: Confidence Level
topics.summary: Confidence is the explicit, calibrated expression of how much weight an analytic judgement should carry, and it is distinct from the likelihood that an event will occur. A useful threat intelligence product states both: how reliable the sourcing is, and how strongly the analysis supports the conclusion. It then uses consistent estimative wording so consumers can rank competing claims against each other. Source reliability and information credibility are frequently assessed with a two-axis scheme that rates the source from completely reliable to unreliable and the information from confirmed to improbable, which produces a compact code an analyst can attach to each statement. Analytic confidence is a different judgement. It reflects the quality and quantity of evidence, the coherence of the argument, the soundness of the methods used, and the extent to which alternatives were considered. Established intelligence community standards for analytic writing require that judgements be sourced, that uncertainty be expressed in words with defined meanings, and that probability be distinguished from confidence. In practice, teams define a small vocabulary and keep to it, for example low, moderate and high confidence paired with stated reasons, and they avoid vague hedges such as possibly or could be, which carry no ranking information. Common failure modes include overconfidence driven by a single vivid source, anchoring on an initial vendor attribution, and treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence when collection was never attempted. Calibration improves by recording judgements and later scoring them against outcomes, by peer review that challenges the reasoning rather than the conclusion, and by writing estimative statements a reader can falsify. For defenders, confidence determines action: high-confidence judgements may justify immediate blocking or escalation, while low-confidence reporting should generate hunting, monitoring or collection requirements rather than disruptive change.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish source reliability, information credibility, analytic confidence and likelihood within one product.
You will be able to apply a defined confidence vocabulary consistently and state the reasoning behind each rating.
You will be able to replace vague hedging with ranked estimative wording that a reader can falsify.
You will be able to identify overconfidence, anchoring and absence-of-evidence fallacies in a draft assessment.

topics.title: Container Escape
topics.summary: Container escape is the class of techniques by which a process confined to a container reaches the underlying host, another tenant's container, or the cluster control plane, converting a workload compromise into infrastructure compromise. Containers share the host kernel, so the boundary is enforced by kernel features such as namespaces, control groups, capabilities, mandatory access control profiles and seccomp filters rather than by a hypervisor, and escape generally follows from a configuration or kernel flaw that weakens those controls. Recurring categories include privileged containers that hold effectively all capabilities and device access, containers mounting the host filesystem or the container runtime socket, excessive Linux capabilities combined with writable host paths, host namespace sharing for networking or process identifiers, kernel vulnerabilities reachable from within a container, and misconfigured runtime or orchestration components that trust client input excessively. The consequences of a successful escape are severe because the host usually holds credentials: node identity, cluster service account tokens, cloud instance role credentials reachable through the metadata endpoint, and secrets mounted for other workloads. Defensive practice therefore concentrates on preventing the conditions rather than only detecting the technique: forbid privileged mode and host path mounts, drop capabilities, run read-only root filesystems, apply seccomp and mandatory access control, isolate with user namespaces or sandboxed runtimes, restrict access to the runtime socket, and assume that any workload with host access has already compromised the node.
objectives: You will be able to explain why containers share the host kernel and how namespaces, capabilities and mandatory access control form the boundary.

You will be able to describe what credentials and mounted secrets become reachable after a node is compromised.
You will be able to triage container escape indicators such as host namespace access and unexpected device usage.

topics.title: Containment
topics.summary: Containment is the incident response phase in which a team deliberately limits the spread, impact and persistence of an active intrusion while preserving both the evidence and the business functions needed to recover. It is a risk decision made with incomplete information: the analyst usually knows that at least one host or identity is compromised and does not yet know the full scope, so containment trades some operational disruption for a reduced chance that the adversary moves laterally, exfiltrates data or re-establishes access from a foothold nobody has found. Short-term containment is applied within minutes to hours and is usually blunt - network isolation of an endpoint, disabling an account, blocking a command-and-control destination at the egress proxy or DNS resolver, revoking active sessions and tokens, or rotating exposed credentials. Long-term containment keeps the environment stable while eradication and recovery are planned, often by segmenting affected subnets, applying temporary compensating controls, or standing up clean rebuild infrastructure. Effective containment depends on decisions made long before the incident: who has authority to take production systems offline, how isolation is technically performed without tipping off the adversary, and how forensic images and volatile data are captured before a rebuild destroys them. Containment carries risk of its own, because an attacker who detects isolation may accelerate destructive action, so timing and sequencing matter. Teams document every containment action with a timestamp, an owner and a rationale, because those records support later scoping, legal hold and regulatory reporting.
objectives: Define containment in terms of the spread, impact and evidence tradeoffs it is intended to manage.
Differentiate short-term and long-term containment and select the appropriate approach for a given intrusion stage.
Identify the pre-approved authority, contacts and tooling required to isolate a production system without delay.
Sequence containment actions so that volatile evidence is captured before rebuilds, reboots or log rotation destroy it.
Recognise the operational and adversary-detection risks created by isolation, account revocation and traffic blocking.
Document containment decisions so they support later scoping, legal hold and regulatory notification.
Evaluate whether a proposed containment action is proportionate to the scope of compromise that has actually been confirmed.

topics.title: Control Gap
topics.summary: A control gap is the measurable difference between the protection an organisation believes it has and the protection that is actually implemented, operating and effective. Three distinct failure modes hide inside that single phrase, and separating them is the core skill. A design gap exists when no control addresses the risk at all, for example no privileged access review for a tier-zero identity store. An implementation gap exists when a control is defined but not deployed everywhere it is needed, such as endpoint detection present on workstations but absent on the servers that hold the crown jewels. An operating effectiveness gap exists when the control is deployed but does not function as intended, which covers disabled logging, alert rules that never fire, exceptions that quietly became permanent, and configuration drift after a change. Practitioners find gaps through several converging sources: control testing and walkthroughs, framework crosswalks against a target baseline, attack-path or red-team findings, audit and assessment reports, incident and near-miss analysis, and telemetry coverage checks that compare an asset inventory against the systems actually reporting logs. Ranking gaps requires more than counting, because a missing detection on an identity provider that can reach everything matters more than a missing hardening baseline on an isolated lab. Good gap registers record the evidence, the affected scope, the residual risk, the remediation owner, the acceptance criteria and the verification method that will prove closure, and they distinguish genuine remediation from documentation that merely restates the intent.

topics.title: Cyber Kill Chain
topics.summary: The Cyber Kill Chain is a seven-stage model of an intrusion that describes how an adversary progresses from reconnaissance to mission impact. The stages are reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on objectives. Its purpose is not to describe every intrusion precisely but to give defenders a shared vocabulary and a set of choke points where activity can be detected or disrupted before the adversary reaches the final stage. The model rests on an asymmetry: the adversary must succeed at every stage, while defenders need to break only one link, which reframes defence as cost imposition rather than perfect prevention. In practice the chain is most useful for structuring detection coverage reviews, sequencing incident narratives and choosing controls. Hardening the external attack surface targets reconnaissance. Mail and web filtering target delivery. Patch management and exploit mitigations target exploitation. Application control and endpoint hardening target installation. Network monitoring and egress control target command and control. Data loss prevention, backup integrity and segmentation limit actions on objectives. The model has well-known limitations. It was written with perimeter intrusion in mind, so it maps awkwardly to cloud identity attacks, supply-chain compromises, insider activity and hands-on-keyboard operations that skip or reorder stages. It is also linear, while real intrusions loop, repeat and run stages concurrently. Analysts therefore commonly pair it with ATT&CK for technique-level detail and with the Diamond Model for actor and infrastructure context. Used with those caveats, the kill chain remains a durable briefing tool because non-specialist stakeholders can follow it, and it exposes where an organisation has no detection at all rather than merely where its tools are noisy.
objectives: You will be able to name the seven Cyber Kill Chain stages and place observed activity into the correct stage.
You will be able to identify the choke points where a control or detection can break the chain before impact.

topics.title: Dark Web Monitoring
topics.summary: Dark web monitoring is the systematic collection and analysis of content from sources that mainstream search engines do not index, including criminal forums, illicit marketplaces, paste sites, private messaging channels, ransomware leak sites and credential dumps, in order to detect exposure, fraud enablers and threats to an organisation. For defenders it supports four main use cases: discovering leaked or stolen credentials and session material before it is used, identifying brand impersonation and phishing infrastructure, learning about planned or ongoing campaigns that name the organisation or its suppliers, and gathering adversary tradecraft that can be turned into detection. Collection is harder than it first appears. Sources are ephemeral and hostile, registration often requires vouching or payment, access carries legal, contractual and personal safety risk, and much of the content is recycled, fabricated or seeded by criminals and by researchers themselves. Verification is therefore the core analyst skill: a credential listing proves nothing until a controlled check confirms it is current, and a forum post claiming an intrusion may simply be a sales pitch. Sound programmes use dedicated isolated collection environments, maintain strict separation between collection identities and corporate infrastructure, operate under rules of engagement approved by legal and leadership, and handle material that may contain personal data in line with privacy regulation. Output is only valuable when it reaches a workflow, so mature teams route validated findings into identity remediation, takedown requests, fraud monitoring and intelligence reporting, and they record which sources produced results and which produced noise.

topics.title: Detection as Code
topics.summary: Detection as code is the practice of managing detection content, meaning rules, correlation logic, enrichment mappings and the tests that validate them, with the same engineering discipline applied to application source code. Detection logic lives in a version control repository rather than being clicked into a console. Changes arrive as reviewed pull requests with an author, a reviewer and a written rationale. Every rule carries structured metadata: an identifier, a description, the ATT&CK techniques it addresses, the required log sources, a severity and a documented owner. A continuous integration pipeline validates syntax against the target platform's schema, lints for required fields, checks that referenced log sources exist, executes unit tests against sample events that should and should not fire the rule, and then deploys through environments in a controlled fashion. The benefits are concrete rather than aesthetic. History answers when a detection changed, who changed it and why, which is exactly what an incident review needs. Tests catch the regression where a well-meaning edit to shared logic silently breaks unrelated rules. Portability improves because content expressed in a vendor-neutral format can be translated to several query languages instead of being rewritten by hand. The genuine difficulties are also concrete: keeping the tests' sample telemetry representative of production, handling secrets and environment-specific values without committing them, preventing repository drift from what is actually deployed in the console, and staffing the review process so that it does not simply become an approval rubber stamp. Detection as code therefore succeeds only when the pipeline and the review culture are real, not when a repository is created and left to diverge.

You will be able to author a rule with structured metadata that identifies its owner, required log sources, severity and ATT&CK coverage.

topics.title: Diamond Model
topics.summary: The Diamond Model is an intrusion analysis framework that describes every malicious event as the interaction of four core features: an adversary, a capability, an infrastructure and a victim. The adversary is the actor or group directing activity. The capability is the tool, malware, exploit or credential the actor wields. The infrastructure is the physical or logical channel used to deliver the capability and control it, such as a domain, mail service, virtual private server or compromised host. The victim is the target, whether a person, organisation, account, asset or data set. Each event is drawn as a diamond with those four vertices. The value of the model lies in its edges and the pivots they permit: given any single known vertex, an analyst can reason about the others, and a confirmed link on one edge strengthens hypotheses along the rest. If two events share infrastructure and a capability but differ in victim, that suggests a broader campaign. If two share a victim and a capability but use different infrastructure, that suggests the actor is rotating channels defensively. The model also carries a socio-political meta-feature layer and, in the extended form, a technology meta-feature, acknowledging that adversary motivation and victim characteristics shape activity as much as tools do. Because the Diamond Model is event-centric, it complements rather than replaces kill-chain and ATT&CK views: it answers who did what to whom using what, while ATT&CK answers how. In practice, analysts use it to cluster events, generate collection requirements, prioritise intelligence gaps and document confidence. Its limits are equally important. The model is descriptive, so it imposes no analytic rigour by itself, and pivoting from infrastructure alone is prone to the same false attribution traps as any single-source inference.
objectives: You will be able to label the four Diamond Model vertices and the edges between them for a given intrusion report.
You will be able to pivot from a known infrastructure vertex to defensible hypotheses about capability and adversary.
You will be able to cluster multiple events into a campaign by comparing shared and divergent vertices.
You will be able to explain how the Diamond Model complements ATT&CK and kill-chain analysis instead of replacing them.
You will be able to identify intelligence gaps as missing vertices or unsupported edges and turn them into collection requirements.
