topics.title: Disk Imaging
topics.summary: Disk imaging is the process of creating a bit-for-bit copy of a storage device, or of a defined set of allocated and unallocated regions, so that examination happens on a working copy while the original remains sealed and unmodified. The image captures everything the file system exposes plus what it does not: deleted file remnants, slack space, partition and boot sectors, volume snapshots, swap and hibernation files, and file system metadata such as timestamps and journal records. Because a single capture preserves all of that in one verifiable artefact, imaging is preferable to live file copying whenever the media can be removed or safely quiesced, and it is frequently the only way to recover deleted or partially overwritten material. Acquisition runs through a write blocker, either hardware or a validated software equivalent, and the resulting image is verified with a cryptographic hash computed at acquisition and again after transfer, since a mismatch invalidates the copy. Formats matter for practicality: raw images are simple and widely supported but large, while compressed or segmented formats with embedded metadata suit evidence transport and long-term retention. Logistics are as important as tooling, including capacity estimation, planning downtime for servers that cannot simply be taken offline, documenting the exact device and range captured, labelling media, and storing images in access-controlled locations. Analysis then covers file system parsing, deleted file recovery, artifact extraction and correlation with memory, log and network evidence.
objectives: Explain what a bit-for-bit image captures that a live file copy does not, including unallocated and slack space.
Select an acquisition approach, image format and tool for a given device, downtime window and evidence volume.
Perform a write-blocked acquisition and verify it with cryptographic hashes at acquisition and after transfer.
Document device identity, captured range, tooling, operator and hash values in a defensible acquisition record.
Plan storage, labelling and retention for large images with sensitivity and legal-hold requirements in mind.
Recover deleted and partially overwritten artefacts from an image and explain their evidential limits.
Correlate disk artefacts with memory, identity and network evidence to support a scoped incident narrative.

topics.title: Distributed Denial of Service
topics.summary: A distributed denial of service attack attempts to make a service unavailable by exhausting a resource, using many sources so that no single host can simply be blocked. Volume-based attacks saturate network links with floods of packets or bytes. Protocol attacks consume state on network devices or servers, for example by exhausting connection tables or abusing a handshake so that half-open sessions accumulate. Application-layer attacks send requests that look individually legitimate but are expensive to serve, such as repeated searches, login attempts or interface calls that trigger heavy database work, so modest traffic volumes can still cause outages. Modern campaigns are frequently multi-vector and short, blending floods with application requests to defeat single-layer defences, and they are sometimes paired with extortion, used as distraction from another intrusion, or used as cover for data theft. Mitigation is layered and depends on where capacity actually exists. Upstream scrubbing services and content delivery networks absorb volumetric traffic and filter close to the source, which is essential because local links are usually far smaller than the attack. On-premises appliances handle smaller floods and can act quickly, but they cannot exceed the size of the circuits they protect. Application defences include caching, rate limiting per identity rather than per address, restricting expensive endpoints, and requiring a challenge for suspicious clients. Preparation matters more than any single tool: a written runbook that names who can enable scrubbing, how traffic is rerouted and how providers are contacted turns a panic into a procedure. Monitoring should include baseline traffic profiles, alerts on abnormal connection counts and response latency, and periodic testing of failover and mitigation paths, while post-incident review should separate genuine capacity failures from outages caused by a mitigation that blocked legitimate users.
objectives: You will be able to classify volumetric, protocol and application-layer attacks and the resource each exhausts.
You will be able to baseline normal traffic and recognise the onset of an attack from monitoring data.
You will be able to design layered mitigation across upstream scrubbing, local appliances and application controls.
You will be able to write and rehearse a mitigation runbook with clear decision rights and provider contacts.
You will be able to distinguish a real capacity failure from an outage caused by over-blocking.
You will be able to rank multi-vector attack scenarios by business impact for a given service.

topics.title: DNS Tunnelling
topics.summary: DNS tunnelling is a technique for carrying arbitrary data inside DNS queries and responses, exploiting the fact that name resolution is permitted almost everywhere, including networks where most other outbound traffic is blocked. An adversary who controls an authoritative name server can encode payload in the leftmost labels of a query, for example a long high-entropy subdomain, and receive data back through the response, producing a bidirectional covert channel without ever opening a direct connection to an external host. The same mechanism supports exfiltration, with stolen data chunked across successive queries, and it can carry a command channel, which is why defenders usually treat it as DNS-based command and control or exfiltration over DNS rather than as a standalone intrusion technique. Detection rests on behaviour rather than payload, because the queries themselves are well formed. Useful signals include sustained query volume to a single domain, unusually long or random-looking labels, high randomness in subdomain strings, unusual record types, elevated rates of non-existent domain responses, and low-and-slow patterns designed to stay under rate thresholds. Tuning is difficult because legitimate services share some of those characteristics: content delivery networks, endpoint telemetry agents and software update mechanisms all generate high query volume to a small set of names, and security products themselves use DNS for reputation lookups. Effective detection therefore combines several weak signals, baselines per host and per domain, and enrichment with reputation, registration age and resolution history rather than relying on any single rule. Mitigation is layered: restrict recursive resolvers to internal clients, block direct outbound DNS from endpoints, log and retain query data centrally, monitor authoritative servers for the organisation's own domains, and use response policy zones to block known malicious names.
objectives: You will be able to explain how data is encoded into DNS queries and responses and why the channel bypasses egress filtering.
You will be able to build detection queries using label length, entropy, volume and response-code patterns.
You will be able to baseline legitimate high-volume DNS consumers and reduce false positives.

You will be able to design resolver, egress and response policy controls that constrain tunnelling without breaking resolution.

topics.title: Dynamic Application Security Testing
topics.summary: Dynamic application security testing is the automated assessment of a running application, sending crafted requests or driving a browser and analysing the responses for security weaknesses such as injection, broken authentication, insecure session handling, misconfigured headers, exposed administrative interfaces and unsafe redirects. Because it exercises the deployed artifact, DAST observes the same surfaces an attacker would, which makes it strong at finding configuration, authentication and session problems that static analysis cannot see. The trade-off is coverage and certainty in the other direction: black-box scanning only reaches what it can discover, it cannot reason about code it cannot see, and destructive or stateful techniques risk corrupting test data, so scans are usually run against a dedicated environment seeded with representative content and credentials. Authenticated scanning is the single biggest determinant of value; an unauthenticated scan of a modern single-page application typically crawls a login page and little else. For a practising engineer the operational questions are environment fidelity, credential handling, scan scope, rate limiting, and how findings are de-duplicated across runs so a repeated issue is not rediscovered as new. Pairing DAST with an API specification gives far better coverage than crawl-only scanning, and pairing it with static analysis closes the loop between code-level and runtime evidence. Common failure modes include scanning production during peak hours, scanning an environment with debug features enabled so results do not reflect production, and reporting every informational header finding as if it carried the same weight as a confirmed injection.
objectives: You will be able to explain what running the application adds over static analysis and which defect classes it uniquely exposes.
You will be able to configure an authenticated DAST scan with a safe test account, a scoped target and rate limits that protect the environment.

topics.title: ECDSA
topics.summary: ECDSA is the elliptic curve analogue of the Digital Signature Algorithm, producing signatures whose security depends on the hardness of the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem rather than integer factorisation. A signature is generated from a private scalar, a per-signature secret nonce, and the message hash; verification uses the public point and the curve parameters. Because the security per bit is higher than RSA, ECDSA keys are far smaller for equivalent strength, which is why it dominates TLS certificates, code signing, SSH keys and hardware-backed authentication on mobile devices. The critical operational property is that the nonce must be unique and unpredictable for every signature made with a given private key. Reusing a nonce across two signatures over different messages allows the private key to be recovered algebraically from the two signatures alone, and this is not a theoretical concern: it has happened repeatedly through flawed random number generation and through code paths that derive the nonce deterministically but incorrectly. Other practical hazards include weak or duplicated entropy on embedded devices, curve parameters that are not the standardised NIST or Curve25519 family, malleable signature encodings that break naive transaction or protocol logic, and libraries that accept a public key without validating that it lies on the curve. Defensive practice therefore centres on vetted libraries, deterministic nonce generation, hardware key storage, and inventorying where signatures are produced.
objectives: Explain how ECDSA signing and verification use the curve, the private scalar and the per-signature nonce.
Describe how nonce reuse across two signatures reveals a private key and what evidence of that failure looks like.

Validate curve parameters and public key encoding during a review of a signature verification implementation.

topics.title: EDR
topics.summary: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) is a class of endpoint agent that continuously records process, file, registry, network and identity telemetry from a host, applies behavioural analytics and signature logic to that stream, and gives responders the ability to query, isolate and remediate the endpoint remotely. Unlike legacy antivirus, which largely evaluated files at rest or on execution, EDR treats sequence and context as the primary signal: a signed administrative utility writing to a run key, a shell spawning from an office productivity process, or a credential store being read by an unexpected parent are all interesting regardless of whether any single artefact matches a known bad hash. Modern deployments typically combine a lightweight kernel or platform-level sensor, a local detection engine for offline resilience, and a cloud backend that correlates across the estate, performs retroactive hunting over retained telemetry, and drives automated response actions. Practitioners care about EDR because it is the main source of truth for host-level investigation: it answers who ran what, as whom, from where, and what happened next. Its weaknesses are equally important to understand. Coverage varies by operating system and kernel version, sensor tampering and driver-level evasion can blind the agent, high-volume environments generate alert fatigue that buries real intrusions, and telemetry retention windows constrain how far back an analyst can hunt after a slow-burn compromise is discovered. EDR also raises its own governance questions around data residency, privacy, and the handling of employee endpoint data, and its value collapses if the deployment is partial, the exclusions list is unmanaged, or nobody owns tuning. Effective programmes pair EDR with strong identity telemetry, network metadata and a documented triage workflow rather than treating the console as a self-contained security solution.
objectives: Explain what an EDR sensor collects at kernel and user level, and how that differs from classic antivirus file scanning.

topics.title: Eradication
topics.summary: Eradication is the incident response phase in which the team removes the adversary's ability to continue operating in the environment: malware, tooling, persistence mechanisms, created or compromised accounts, malicious configuration, and the initial access vector that let them in. It is the phase most often declared too early. Deleting a dropped binary or rebuilding a single workstation addresses a symptom rather than the foothold; if the adversary planted a scheduled task, a rogue service, a federated identity token, a malicious OAuth application, an additional SSH key or a shadow administrator account, that access survives the cleanup and the incident simply restarts. Sound eradication begins with scoping evidence: which accounts authenticated where, which persistence locations exist across the estate, which systems share the compromised credential or the vulnerable component. Root cause then has to be closed rather than merely observed - patching the exploited service, rotating every credential the adversary could have touched, removing malicious identity objects, and confirming that the initial access path no longer works. Eradication actions are destructive to evidence by nature, so forensic collection precedes them, and each action is recorded with a timestamp, an operator and a verification result. Verification is the crux: after cleanup the team must re-hunt using the adversary's known tactics, techniques and procedures to demonstrate absence rather than assume it. Only when eradication is verified does recovery begin, and even then detection coverage and monitoring are raised rather than relaxed.
objectives: Describe what eradication must remove beyond malware, including persistence, identity objects and the initial access vector.

topics.title: Evasion
topics.summary: Evasion is the set of techniques used to avoid, delay or defeat detection and analysis rather than to achieve an objective directly, and it is best understood as a tax on defenders' visibility rather than a single action. Practitioners group it by what is being evaded: signature matching, behavioural analytics, logging, and human investigation. Common patterns include altering the on-disk representation of code so known signatures no longer match, obfuscating scripts and command lines, abusing signed system utilities so actions appear under a trusted name, masquerading files and services as legitimate software, tampering with or blinding telemetry so evidence never reaches a central store, and encrypting or tunnelling command-and-control traffic so content inspection becomes useless. Because evasion targets the collection layer, the most effective counters are architectural. Centralised, append-only logging with strict access control removes the advantage of tampering on a single host. Tamper protection and health monitoring on endpoint agents expose attempts to disable them. Application control and script block logging shrink the space in which obfuscated code can run at all. Behavioural detections that correlate across hosts and identities survive cosmetic changes better than any signature. Finally, analysts should treat absence of evidence as a signal in itself: a host that stops reporting, a log source that goes quiet, or a gap in a timeline is a detection opportunity, and treating those gaps as alerts is one of the highest-value habits a security operations team can build.
objectives: You will be able to classify evasion techniques by whether they target signatures, behaviour, logging or investigation.

topics.title: Exfiltration
topics.summary: Exfiltration is the unauthorised transfer of data from an environment the organisation controls to a destination it does not, and it is usually the point at which an intrusion becomes a reportable breach. The activity normally follows a recognisable sequence: locating and collecting data of value, staging it on an intermediate system, reducing its size or obscuring its content through compression and encryption, splitting it into transferable chunks, and moving it over a channel that is likely to be permitted. Channel choice is a trade-off between volume and stealth. Large transfers over ordinary web or file-sharing protocols are fast but visible; low-and-slow transfers over DNS, commodity cloud storage or a long-lived command-and-control channel are quieter but take longer and depend on the destination remaining available. Defences fail most often at the egress boundary, where broad allow-lists for web traffic, personal cloud storage and remote access tools make almost any destination reachable. Detection combines data-side and network-side evidence: unusually large or oddly timed transfers, access to repositories the account does not normally touch, new external destinations, protocol use that does not match the port, and anomalous DNS query volumes or label lengths. Mitigations that work are egress filtering with explicit allow-lists, data classification with controls that follow the data, scoped credentials that limit what a single identity can read, and monitoring of cloud storage and collaboration platforms rather than only the corporate perimeter.

topics.title: Fileless Malware
topics.summary: Fileless malware is malicious logic that executes without a conventional malicious file ever being written to disk in a form that a scanner can inspect, instead living in memory, in registry values, in system configuration stores, or in the command lines and scripts passed to legitimate interpreters already present on the host. The category is best understood as a spectrum rather than a binary property. A purely memory-resident payload injected into another process leaves no artefact for a file-based scan, while a script launched from a registry key or a scheduled task leaves configuration artefacts that are fileless only in the narrow sense that no executable was dropped. The common thread is abuse of trusted, signed, ubiquitous components: the operating system shell, PowerShell or another scripting interpreter, Windows Management Instrumentation, the .NET runtime, and increasingly cloud-hosted script sources fetched at run time. Detection therefore shifts from content matching to behaviour and lineage. Analysts look at which parent process spawned which interpreter, whether the command line contains encoded or obfuscated content, whether a process downloaded and immediately invoked remote content, whether script block logging or module logging is even enabled, and whether memory contains executable regions that are not backed by a file on disk. Prevention leans on application control, constrained language modes, signed script enforcement and the removal of unnecessary interpreters from servers and user workstations. Memory acquisition capability and a solid understanding of logging gaps matter, because once the process exits the evidence often exits with it.

topics.title: Firewall
topics.summary: A firewall is a network security control that enforces an explicit policy over which traffic may pass between two zones by inspecting packet headers and, in modern products, application-layer content. Classic packet filters evaluated a five-tuple of source address, destination address, source port, destination port and protocol against an ordered rule list, stopping at the first match and falling through to an implicit deny. Stateful inspection added a connection table so that return traffic belonging to an established session is permitted without a matching inbound rule, which removed many of the permissive workarounds that plagued early deployments. Next-generation firewalls identify applications rather than ports alone, attach user and group identity to flows, decrypt selected TLS sessions, and integrate intrusion prevention and threat intelligence, so the operational boundary between firewall, proxy and IPS has largely dissolved. Defensive value depends almost entirely on policy quality. A rule base that ends in any-any, that carries shadowed rules which can never match, or that accumulates temporary exceptions long after a project closes provides little assurance regardless of the hardware. Effective programmes enforce default deny between zones, document the business owner and expiry of every permit, review the rule base on a schedule, and forward accept and deny logs to a central platform where volume and destination changes are correlated. Firewalls remain necessary but are not sufficient: they cannot see inside encrypted traffic they do not decrypt, they cannot reliably distinguish a trusted internal host that has been compromised, and they are bypassed entirely when users and workloads leave the perimeter.
objectives: You will be able to explain how stateful inspection differs from stateless packet filtering and why rule order determines the effective policy.

topics.title: Flash Report
topics.summary: A flash report is a short, time-sensitive threat intelligence product published quickly to warn recipients about an urgent development and prompt a defensive decision. It is deliberately narrow: one topic, minimal background, and heavy emphasis on what changed, why it matters now, what recipients should do, and when the next update is expected. Flash traffic typically covers newly exploited vulnerabilities, active campaigns against a sector, credible reports of imminent activity, or a significant change in an adversary's tooling. Because speed is the point, a flash report is usually built from incomplete information, so it must state its confidence and its sourcing plainly, and it must be updated or formally superseded rather than silently edited after release. A workable structure includes a headline that states the change, a one-paragraph bottom line up front, key judgements with confidence, the technical detail analysts need in order to hunt, recommended actions ranked by effort and impact, indicators with a clear validity window, handling and distribution markings, and points of contact. Distribution is governed by handling caveats so recipients know whether they may forward the material, and by a defined list of who must be reachable outside business hours. The most common failure is noise: publishing everything urgently destroys the value of urgency, so teams set explicit triggers for what qualifies as flash and keep routine developments in a daily summary. The second failure is actionability, where a flash tells recipients that an actor exists without giving them a detection, a mitigation or a question to answer. Well-run teams keep a standing template, pre-agree who may approve release, and rehearse the workflow so a flash can be written, reviewed and distributed within an hour during an incident.
objectives: You will be able to identify the situations that genuinely meet a flash reporting trigger and those that belong in routine reporting.
You will be able to draft a flash report with a bottom line up front, stated confidence and ranked recommended actions.
You will be able to apply handling and distribution markings and explain what recipients may do with the product.
You will be able to convert technical findings into detection and hunting guidance a recipient can act on immediately.

topics.title: Foothold
topics.summary: A foothold is the first durable, repeatable point of access an intruder establishes inside a target environment, giving command execution and a base from which further objectives are pursued. It is deliberately distinguished from full compromise: a foothold may be a single low-privileged shell on an internet-facing host, a valid credential pair, a session on a remote access appliance, or code running inside a user's active browser session, and its value lies in reliability rather than breadth. The paths that produce footholds are well documented and defensive teams should treat them as a checklist for exposure: phishing with an attachment or link, exploitation of public-facing services, abuse of stolen or guessed credentials against remote access services, trusted relationships with suppliers, and misconfigured cloud or container endpoints. Immediately after access is obtained, the intruder's priorities usually shift to understanding the local context, confirming that the access survives normal session end, and hiding the channel that will carry later stages. Detection therefore rarely depends on a single alert. It comes from correlating identity telemetry with endpoint and network evidence: authentications from unexpected geographies or protocols, new remote access sessions on appliances that normally see none, unusual parent and child process relationships, and outbound connections to infrastructure the organisation has never used before. Because a foothold is small by design, containment decisions hinge on whether the access is a one-off session or something that will re-establish itself, which is why rapid scoping and credential rotation accompany every confirmed incident.
objectives: You will be able to define a foothold and distinguish it from persistence, privilege escalation and full compromise.
You will be able to map common foothold vectors to the telemetry that each one generates.
You will be able to correlate identity, endpoint and network evidence to confirm whether an intrusion has established stable access.
You will be able to choose proportionate containment actions for a suspected foothold without destroying evidence.
You will be able to explain why remote access appliances and valid accounts dominate real-world initial access.

topics.title: GDPR
topics.summary: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union legal framework governing the processing of personal data, and it applies to organisations established in the EU as well as organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. Its obligations are built on principles rather than prescriptive controls: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality; and accountability, where the organisation must be able to demonstrate compliance rather than merely assert it. For security practitioners the regulation matters in four operational areas. Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures proportionate to risk, which is where encryption, pseudonymisation, access control, resilience and testing of those measures land. Articles 33 and 34 set breach notification duties, with a seventy-two hour window to the supervisory authority once the controller becomes aware, so incident response runbooks must be able to answer what data, how many people, what categories and what residual risk within hours. Chapter IV introduces the data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing and the records of processing activities that underpin it. Chapter V governs transfers outside the EU and drives data residency, standard contractual clauses and transfer impact assessments. The security team's artefact trail, including detection records, containment timelines and post-incident reviews, is frequently the evidence that a supervisory authority examines.
objectives: You will be able to map the data protection principles onto concrete engineering and operational controls.
You will be able to determine what Article 32 appropriate measures mean for a given processing activity and risk level.

You will be able to support a data protection impact assessment with accurate data flow and risk evidence.

topics.title: Hardware Security Module
topics.summary: A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside a boundary the host operating system cannot read across. Keys are created on the module, never leave it in plaintext, and are used through a constrained API that performs signing, decryption, key wrapping or random generation on behalf of an authorised caller. Because the key material exists only inside protected hardware, stealing the key requires physical or logical access to the module rather than a copy of a configuration file, and many modules zeroise their key store in response to detected tampering. HSMs underpin certificate authority private keys, payment key management, code signing, database transparent encryption, disk encryption key hierarchies and cloud KMS backends that offer dedicated or single-tenant hardware. The operational model introduces its own failure modes: poorly controlled administrator roles and quorum settings, weak or shared operator credentials that permit key export, misconfigured network exposure of the module's management interface, backup and restore procedures that either lose the key forever or replicate it into weaker storage, weak entropy on the first initialisation, and audit logging that is disabled or never reviewed. Availability also matters, since an HSM cluster that cannot fail over can take critical signing or payment flows offline, so redundancy and documented recovery are part of the security design rather than an afterthought.
objectives: Describe how an HSM protects key material through tamper resistance, restricted APIs and controlled key export.

topics.title: HIPAA
topics.summary: HIPAA is the United States federal law that governs the privacy and security of protected health information, and its security obligations are expressed through the Security Rule together with the Privacy Rule, the Breach Notification Rule and the Transactions and Code Sets Rule. The Security Rule is deliberately flexible and technology-neutral: it requires covered entities and their business associates to implement administrative, physical and technical safeguards that are reasonable and appropriate for their size, complexity and risk, and it sorts implementation specifications into required and addressable categories, where addressable means the organisation must either implement the specification or document why an equivalent alternative is reasonable and appropriate. The technical safeguards include access control, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication and transmission security, which in practice means unique user identification, role-based authorisation, emergency access procedures, automatic logoff, encryption in transit and at rest, and immutable audit logging of systems that touch electronic protected health information. Risk analysis is not optional and is the foundation of every other decision; a documented, current risk analysis tied to a remediation plan is the single artefact most often probed in an investigation. Business associate agreements extend obligations down the supply chain, and breach notification has a four-part risk assessment with defined timelines. Practitioners should treat ePHI data flow mapping as the prerequisite for meaningful segmentation and monitoring.

topics.title: HMAC
topics.summary: HMAC is a keyed message authentication construction defined in FIPS 198-1 and RFC 2104 that wraps an unkeyed hash function in a specific two-pass structure using inner and outer padding constants. It produces a message authentication code that proves both integrity and authenticity when the verifier holds the same secret key, and its security proof holds under weaker assumptions about the underlying hash than a naive secret-prefix construction, which is why it resists length extension attacks. HMAC-SHA-256 is the workhorse for API request signing, webhook verification, session token integrity, network protocol message authentication and key derivation through HKDF. Correct use depends on details that are easy to get wrong. The key must be generated randomly at an adequate length and stored as securely as any other credential, because possession of the key is possession of the ability to forge. Verification must be constant-time, since an early-exit byte comparison leaks how many leading bytes matched and enables forgery byte by byte. Truncated MACs reduce work for the attacker, and comparing a MAC that arrives in a client-controlled field without binding it to the request body, timestamp or nonce invites replay. Key rotation for HMAC secrets is operationally awkward when both sides must change simultaneously, so overlap windows and dual-key acceptance are standard practice, and log pipelines should alert on signature verification failures as a signal of tampering or credential misuse.
objectives: Explain the HMAC inner and outer padding structure and why it resists length extension attacks.
Implement secure MAC verification using constant-time comparison and explain the consequence of early-exit equality checks.

Choose appropriate MAC lengths and justify truncation only against a documented risk decision.
Plan an HMAC key rotation with overlapping key validity and no downtime for dependent services.
Analyse authentication failure telemetry to distinguish misconfiguration from active forgery attempts.

topics.title: IAM Policy
topics.summary: An IAM policy is a structured document that grants or denies permissions to a principal in a cloud platform, evaluated by the provider's authorisation engine on every API call. Policies typically bind a principal, an action or set of actions on a resource, and optional conditions such as source address, time, tags or whether multi-factor authentication was used, with an explicit effect of allow or deny. Cloud authorisation is generally default-deny, so access exists only where a policy grants it, and an explicit deny usually overrides any allow. Policies attach at several levels, including identity-based policies on users, groups and roles, resource-based policies on the target itself such as a bucket or key, permission boundaries, session policies and service control policies in an organisation hierarchy, which means the effective permission set is the intersection and union of several documents rather than any single one. Security professionals care because over-permissive policies are a leading cause of cloud compromise and because policy errors are invisible until an attacker or an auditor exercises them. Practical work includes least-privilege scoping, wildcard elimination, analysing cross-account trust relationships, reviewing role assumption chains, and detecting privilege escalation paths where one grant lets a principal modify a policy that grants more. Reviewing the effective permission of a principal, not the intent of a single document, is the discipline the topic teaches.

topics.title: IDS and IPS
topics.summary: An intrusion detection system monitors network or host activity and raises alerts on behaviour that matches known attack signatures, deviates from a statistical baseline, or violates an explicit policy, while an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can drop the offending traffic in real time. Network sensors are usually deployed at chokepoints such as the internet edge, the data-centre core and the links between trust zones, fed by spans, taps or packet brokers, while host agents inspect system calls, file writes and process lineage that never appears on the wire. Detection logic spans signature matching, protocol anomaly checks, reputation feeds and behavioural models, and each family carries distinct failure modes: signatures miss novel variants and encoded payloads, while anomaly engines generate volume that overwhelms analysts. The dominant operational problem is rarely sensor coverage but triage capacity. A poorly tuned signature set produces thousands of low-value alerts every day, so genuine events are buried and mean time to detect degrades rather than improves. Mature teams suppress noisy signatures, tune thresholds against real baselines, enrich alerts with asset criticality and identity, and validate detection content with controlled tests before enabling prevention. Prevention deserves particular caution, because an inline device with a false positive becomes an availability incident, and an inline device with a decryption or evasion blind spot provides false assurance. Fragmentation, TCP evasion, protocol tunnelling, encrypted channels and high-throughput asymmetric paths all degrade inspection quality, so effective programmes treat detection and prevention as one detection-engineering discipline, keep content updates under change control, measure precision as well as coverage, and document the blind spots that remain.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish signature, anomaly and reputation-based detection and describe the failure modes of each.
You will be able to triage a sensor alert set by asset criticality, direction and expected business traffic.
You will be able to tune or suppress noisy signatures without creating an evasion gap.
You will be able to explain the operational risk of inline prevention and the conditions under which fail-open is acceptable.
You will be able to describe how fragmentation, encoding and encryption reduce inspection fidelity.
You will be able to evaluate detection coverage against a technique matrix and document the remaining blind spots.

topics.title: Incident Response Playbook
topics.summary: A playbook in security operations is a documented, versioned procedure that specifies how a defined class of alert or incident is handled, from the first acknowledgement through to closure and follow-up. It exists so that response quality does not depend on which analyst is on shift. A usable playbook is more specific than a policy and more procedural than a runbook index. It states the trigger conditions that invoke it, the roles and who has authority to act, the required inputs such as the alert payload and enrichment sources, the ordered steps with the exact queries and commands to run, the decision points with explicit criteria for each branch, the containment options available and their blast radius, the evidence to preserve and where, the escalation path with contact conditions and timeframes, and the closure criteria including what must be recorded. Two design principles separate playbooks that survive contact with reality from those that do not. First, enrichment precedes action: gather asset ownership, identity privilege, business function and recent related activity before disabling an account or isolating a host, because the outage can be worse than the incident. Second, every irreversible step has a named approver and a documented reversal path. Playbooks also decay. Infrastructure changes, log sources move, contact lists age and query syntax drifts, so each playbook needs an owner, a review date, and validation through tabletop exercise or live-fire test. Response metrics such as time to detect and time to contain are only meaningful when the underlying procedure is consistent and actually followed, which is the operational argument for maintaining them.
objectives: You will be able to define the required sections of an incident response playbook, from trigger conditions through closure criteria.
You will be able to write ordered response steps with explicit decision points and branch criteria instead of vague instructions.
You will be able to place enrichment before containment and justify the ordering in terms of outage risk.

topics.title: Infostealer
topics.summary: An infostealer is malware whose primary purpose is to harvest and exfiltrate credentials and other valuable data from an endpoint quickly and with minimal footprint. Unlike ransomware, which seeks to disrupt, an infostealer is designed to be quiet: it typically runs for seconds or minutes, collects what it can, sends it out, and often removes itself. The target set is broad and highly specific at the same time. Browser stores are the richest source, including saved passwords, session cookies and authentication tokens, and the theft of live session cookies is particularly damaging because it lets an intruder reuse an already authenticated session and sidestep multi-factor authentication entirely. Beyond browsers, stealers target cryptocurrency wallet files, messaging and file-transfer application sessions, saved credentials in mail and remote-access clients, keylogging of anything typed, and bulk collection of documents and configuration files from user profiles. Distribution is usually opportunistic and consumer-oriented: cracked software, fake installers, malicious advertising, game cheat utilities and community-shared files, which is why an infostealer detections often first appear on a personal or unmanaged device before the stolen credentials are used against a corporate service. For defenders the implications are architectural rather than purely endpoint-focused. Stolen session cookies and tokens invalidate the comfortable assumption that multi-factor authentication makes credential theft survivable, so detection must include impossible-travel style session anomalies, first-time device and user-agent combinations, and token reuse from unexpected network locations. Response to a confirmed infostealer infection requires mass credential rotation, revocation of active sessions and refresh tokens, not just removal of the file.
objectives: Explain why infostealers prioritise browser credential and session-cookie theft over persistence or disruption.
Describe how stolen cookies and tokens let an attacker bypass multi-factor authentication at the session layer.

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code Scanning
topics.summary: Infrastructure as code scanning is the automated static analysis of declarative infrastructure and configuration definitions, such as cloud resource templates, Kubernetes manifests, container build files, serverless definitions and policy bundles, looking for misconfigurations that would create security exposure when the code is applied. Because infrastructure definitions are machine-readable and describe the intended end state, scanners can reason about them far more reliably than they can reason about application logic, checking properties such as publicly reachable storage, permissive identity policies, unencrypted data stores, containers running as privileged or as root, absent network policies, disabled audit logging and hard-coded registry credentials. The category is closely related to cloud security posture management, with the key distinction that posture management assesses what is deployed while IaC scanning assesses what is about to be deployed, which is why it belongs in the pull request and in the pipeline before apply or sync. For a practising engineer the practical difficulty is drift and context. A scanner cannot see values injected at deploy time from a variable file, cannot know that a resource is internet-facing by design in a specific environment, and cannot tell whether an exception was granted deliberately. Effective programmes express policy as code with the same review process as application code, use environment-aware rule sets, classify findings by whether they affect a trust boundary, and detect drift between the repository and what the provider actually reports. Common failure modes are scanning only a subset of repositories, ignoring modules and nested templates, allowing unbounded inline suppressions, and treating a clean scan as evidence that the deployed environment is compliant.
objectives: You will be able to explain how static analysis of infrastructure definitions differs from cloud posture assessment of deployed resources.

topics.title: Instance Metadata Service Version 2
topics.summary: Instance metadata service version 2 is the session-oriented revision of the link-local endpoint that cloud instances query to obtain information about themselves, most importantly the temporary credentials associated with their attached role. The original interface answered any request arriving from the instance, which meant that a server-side request forgery flaw in an application running on that instance was sufficient to read the instance role credentials and use them from anywhere on the internet. Version two changes the exchange in two ways: the client must first issue a PUT request to obtain a limited-lifetime token that is unique to that session, and every subsequent metadata request must present that token in a header, with a configurable hop limit that additionally restricts whether requests can traverse a proxy or container network layer. Because a naive request-forgery payload cannot set custom headers or perform the required PUT, the token requirement breaks the common exploit chain, while the hop limit constrains forwarding through intermediate proxies and container namespaces. Security teams track adoption by measuring how many instances still permit the older interface, since the setting is enforced per instance and inherited at launch, and they apply it to container platforms through the node launch configuration. The topic also covers the practical migration problems: software that read metadata directly, custom agents that proxy metadata to pods, and the need to monitor metadata requests as a detection signal.
objectives: You will be able to explain how the token and hop limit requirements break credential theft through a server-side request forgery flaw.

topics.title: IOC
topics.summary: An Indicator of Compromise (IOC) is a forensic or telemetry artefact that provides evidence a system, account or network has been compromised, ranging from a file hash or hostile domain name to an anomalous authentication pattern or a registry key created by a loader. IOCs are the most shareable and the most perishable product of threat intelligence. They are trivially expressible in structured patterning, easy to push into a SIEM or EDR, and quick to automate, which is why they dominate machine-to-machine sharing; they are also the easiest thing for an adversary to change. A domain can be rotated in minutes, a payload recompiled to a new hash in seconds, and infrastructure can be rented and discarded. Treating an indicator list as a permanent blocklist therefore produces both alert fatigue and a false sense of coverage. Mature programmes classify indicators as atomic, computed or behavioural. Atomic values such as an IP address, domain name or file hash are volatile and should carry a short validity window and a confidence rating. Computed indicators, such as a hash of a decoded malware configuration or a distinctive transport fingerprint derived from a family, survive longer and support hunting. Behavioural indicators describe sequences of action and overlap heavily with adversary techniques. Operationally, an indicator is only useful when it is enriched with context: which actor family used it, which campaign, when it was first and last observed, and whether it is a genuinely exclusive artefact or a shared hosting address. Low-specificity indicators, especially IP addresses from commercial hosting or content delivery ranges, should drive hunts and correlation rather than blocklists, because blocking them breaks legitimate traffic. Indicators also age, so a feed that has not been reviewed recently should be filtered by first-seen date before it is trusted. Finally, defenders should be able to state which detection each indicator feeds and how it will be retired, because an indicator whose only consumer is a dashboard produces no security value.
objectives: You will be able to classify indicators as atomic, computed or behavioural and explain the operational lifetime and confidence each class deserves.
You will be able to build an indicator lifecycle covering enrichment, validation, deployment, review and retirement instead of permanent blocking.

topics.title: ISO 27001
topics.summary: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard that specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an information security management system. It is a management-system standard rather than a control catalogue: it tells an organisation how to govern security through leadership commitment, documented scope, risk assessment, risk treatment, internal audit, management review and corrective action, while the accompanying guidance in ISO/IEC 27002 describes control objectives an organisation may select from. Certification is granted to the management system by an accredited certification body, not to a product, a data centre or a specific application, and it is issued against a declared scope and Statement of Applicability. For the security practitioner the practical consequences are concrete. Risk assessment must be repeatable and produce traceable treatment decisions; controls must be documented with owners, evidence and review cycles; Annex A control themes now cover organisational, people, physical and technological domains, and each selected or excluded control needs a justification. Auditors sample evidence rather than trust assertions, so operational artefacts such as access reviews, change tickets, incident records and supplier assessments become the real currency of the audit. Surveillance audits occur at least annually and a recertification audit happens on a three-year cycle, which means compliance is a continuous programme rather than a project with an end date. The standard pairs well with ISO/IEC 27017 and 27018 for cloud services and with ISO 27005 for risk methodology.
objectives: You will be able to explain how a risk assessment and risk treatment plan feed the Statement of Applicability and the audit programme.
You will be able to define an ISMS scope that matches the organisation's real legal, contractual and technical boundaries.
You will be able to map Annex A control themes onto existing operational controls and produce clause-level evidence.
You will be able to prepare for a stage 1 documentation review and a stage 2 evidence-based certification audit.
You will be able to run an internal audit and management review cycle that generates genuine corrective actions.
You will be able to identify the common failure modes where certification is achieved but security practice does not improve.

topics.title: Just-in-Time Access
topics.summary: Just-in-time (JIT) access is an access management pattern in which elevation to a privileged role or entitlement is granted only for a bounded period, on request, and only after the requester has satisfied whatever approval, justification and authentication conditions the organisation defines. It replaces standing privilege, where an administrator holds powerful entitlements permanently and therefore holds them equally at three in the morning during a phishing campaign and during a planned maintenance window. A JIT workflow typically has four phases: request, where the user states the scope and reason and often a ticket reference; approval, which may be automatic when the request matches a pre-approved template or manual when it does not; activation, where the entitlement is attached for a fixed duration and is frequently accompanied by step-up authentication and a session recording; and expiry, where the grant is removed automatically by the platform rather than by human discipline. The security gain is measurable, because the window during which a stolen credential is useful narrows from indefinite to hours, and the population of accounts holding privileged rights at any instant becomes small enough to enumerate and monitor. The pattern also produces high-quality telemetry that rarely exists elsewhere: every request, justification, approval decision, activation and expiry is logged, so defenders can alert on activations outside change windows, on self-approvals where separation of duties is required, on repeated activations that suggest a workflow is being used as permanent access, and on direct use of the underlying privileged account that bypasses the broker entirely.
objectives: You will be able to describe the request, approval, activation and expiry phases of a just-in-time access workflow.
You will be able to design approval policies that keep routine work fast while reserving manual review for high-risk elevation.

You will be able to identify bypass paths where a privileged credential is used directly instead of through the broker.
You will be able to measure the reduction in standing privilege achieved after a JIT rollout.

topics.title: Kerberos
topics.summary: Kerberos is a network authentication protocol built on symmetric cryptography and a trusted third party, in which a client proves its identity to a service without sending a password across the network. The key distribution centre, composed of the authentication service and the ticket granting service, issues a ticket granting ticket after the client authenticates, and the client then presents that ticket to obtain service tickets for individual resources. Tickets carry a validity window and are encrypted with keys derived from account passwords or machine secrets, which is why Kerberos security is inseparable from the hygiene of those secrets. In Active Directory the protocol underpins almost all domain authentication, and its abuse paths dominate enterprise intrusions: requesting service tickets and cracking them offline because a service account password is weak, forging tickets when a service account key is stolen, relaying authentication to a service that does not enforce mutual verification, and taking advantage of delegation configured too broadly. Defensive practice centres on detecting anomalous ticket requests, especially bursts of service ticket requests with unusual encryption types or for services that a principal never normally contacts, and on eliminating the conditions that make those requests valuable. That means long random passwords for service accounts managed automatically where possible, removal of unnecessary privileged service principals, restriction of delegation, and monitoring of the domain controller security log for the ticket and credential events that indicate a principal is attempting to obtain material it should not need.
objectives: You will be able to describe the role of the authentication service, ticket granting service and service tickets in a Kerberos exchange.

You will be able to explain relay and coercion risks against services that do not verify authentication properly.
You will be able to prioritise remediation for Kerberos-related findings by blast radius rather than by count.

topics.title: Key Management Service
topics.summary: A cloud key management service is a managed, hardware-backed system for creating, storing, rotating and auditing cryptographic keys, and for performing encryption and decryption without ever exposing the key material to the caller. Applications and services call an API to encrypt or decrypt, and the service enforces authorisation through the same identity and policy machinery as the rest of the platform, so control of a key is a control of the data it protects. Two design patterns dominate practice. Envelope encryption wraps data with a data key, then wraps that data key with a long-lived key that never leaves the service, which allows large objects to be encrypted efficiently while keeping the root secret in hardware. Customer-managed keys add an explicit policy and lifecycle that the customer controls, enabling rotation schedules, automatic rotation, grants, cross-account access and the ability to disable a key and render data unreadable. Security professionals focus on several recurring problems: keys with policies that allow broad principal access, keys shared across environments, disabled or scheduled-for-deletion keys that break services, missing audit trails on decrypt operations, and key material that is replicated into a region an organisation did not intend to use. Because destruction is irreversible, key lifecycle decisions are treated as high-risk change, and separation of duties between those who can use a key and those who can delete it is a standard control.
objectives: You will be able to explain envelope encryption and why data keys are wrapped rather than used directly on large objects.
You will be able to read a key policy and determine which principals can encrypt, decrypt, manage or delete a key.

topics.title: Key Rotation
topics.summary: Key rotation is the scheduled or event-driven replacement of cryptographic keys, secrets and certificates so that the exposure window of any single key is bounded. Rotation limits the blast radius of an undetected compromise, satisfies compliance requirements that demand defined cryptoperiods, and reduces the value of a stolen key to an attacker who may already have exfiltrated it. A workable rotation process has four parts: generating new key material in an approved location, distributing it to every consumer without downtime, accepting both old and new material during an overlap window, and retiring the old material with proof that nothing still depends on it. The hard part is almost never the cryptography; it is discovery of every place a key is used, including configuration files, environment variables, CI pipeline secrets, cached tokens, backups, third-party integrations and human-held copies. Rotation that breaks production is the reason teams avoid it, so mature organisations automate issuance, treat keys as short-lived credentials, prefer key derivation per message or per tenant over one long-lived shared key, and monitor decryption or authentication failures that would reveal a consumer missed a rotation. Emergency rotation after a suspected compromise is a different exercise from scheduled rotation, since it must assume the attacker holds the old material and can observe the overlap window.
objectives: Design a key rotation policy covering generation, distribution, overlap acceptance and retirement with evidence.

Detect incomplete rotation through authentication, decryption and signature verification failures in telemetry.

topics.title: KQL and SPL
topics.summary: KQL, the Kusto Query Language, and SPL, the Splunk Search Processing Language, are the two query languages most commonly used by detection engineers and SOC analysts to interrogate security telemetry. Both are pipeline languages: a search begins with a source of events and a filter, then passes a tabular result through a chain of operators that project, extend, summarise, join, order and visualise. Their shared idioms matter more than their syntax. Progressive filtering keeps queries fast because the earliest stage should eliminate the most data. Time bounding is mandatory rather than optional, both for performance and because an unbounded query over a long retention window will time out or return misleading aggregates. Summarisation collapses many raw events into per-entity counts, which is how thresholds, rarity analysis and first-seen or last-seen logic are expressed. Joins between datasets such as endpoint process events and identity sign-in logs are what turn a weak single-source signal into a defensible detection. The differences are practical. KQL uses a pipe-forward style with tabular operators, has strong support for dynamic and JSON-typed columns, and is used across Microsoft security products and Azure services. SPL uses a search-command model with a large command library, is central to Splunk, and offers macros and lookups that many teams use to build reusable detection content. Fluency in either language is really fluency in a set of habits: knowing which fields carry trustworthy values, understanding how each platform handles timestamps and nulls, and testing query logic against deliberately constructed sample data before trusting it to raise alerts.
objectives: You will be able to read and construct pipeline-style queries that filter, project, extend, summarise and join security telemetry.

topics.title: Kubernetes RBAC
topics.summary: Kubernetes role-based access control is the authorisation system that decides whether an authenticated request against the API server is permitted, by matching the requester's identity and group memberships against rules that name API groups, resources and verbs. Permissions are granted through Role objects scoped to a namespace or ClusterRole objects that apply cluster-wide, and they take effect only when bound to a subject by a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding. Because the API server is the control plane's single entry point, RBAC governs far more than reading object lists: a subject that can create pods can often arrange for a pod that mounts a service account token or a host path, a subject that can read secrets can obtain credentials for other workloads, a subject that can create role bindings can grant itself anything, and permission to exec into pods or read pod logs provides a direct path to application secrets and internal services. These compound paths mean that reviewing individual rules in isolation is misleading and effective privilege must be computed across the graph of bindings, service accounts and default roles. Security teams inventory cluster-admin bindings and wildcard rules, examine default service account usage, restrict who may create workloads and bindings, and monitor the audit log for privilege-sensitive verbs. Good practice pairs authorisation tightening with authentication controls, since RBAC decisions are only as trustworthy as the identity source feeding them.

topics.title: Lateral Movement
topics.summary: Lateral movement is the progression from one compromised system or identity to others inside the same environment, performed to reach valuable data, higher authority, or a position from which the final objective can be achieved without returning to the internet. It rarely relies on a novel exploit; most real intrusions reuse credentials, sessions and administrative tooling that already exist. Typical mechanisms include interactive remote access over desktop, terminal or remote management protocols, authenticated file sharing and remote service creation, execution frameworks that push jobs to many machines at once, and control-plane operations in cloud or virtualisation platforms that reach many workloads through a single API. Credential reuse drives much of it, whether the material is a plaintext password, a password hash, a cached ticket or a long-lived API key, and it is frequently shared service accounts and duplicated local administrator passwords that make the movement cheap. Detection depends on joining authentication events to host and network context: a workstation authenticating to another workstation, an account logging in from a system it never normally touches, remote service or scheduled task creation, and east-west traffic that crosses a segmentation boundary. Mitigations reduce the number of usable hops rather than the number of alerts: segmented networks with default-deny rules between tiers, unique local administrator credentials, dedicated privileged access workstations, just-in-time administration, and removal of legacy authentication protocols. In cloud estates the same logic applies to role assumption paths and to network reachability between workloads.

You will be able to identify the authentication and host telemetry that reveals movement between systems.

topics.title: LDAP
topics.summary: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services, and it remains the directory backbone behind Active Directory, OpenLDAP and most enterprise identity stores. Data is organised as a hierarchical tree of entries, each identified by a distinguished name and described by attributes constrained by a schema, with object classes determining which attributes are permitted. Clients bind to the directory to establish an identity and a level of access, then search with a base, a scope and a filter to retrieve or modify entries. Authentication outcomes depend on the bind and on transport: simple binds send credentials that are only protected by the transport, so LDAP over TLS or a SASL mechanism such as GSSAPI is required for any operation crossing an untrusted segment, and referrals and anonymous binds must be deliberately disabled unless a specific integration demands them. The dominant application-layer weakness in directory-connected software is filter injection, where unescaped user input is concatenated into a search filter so that an attacker can alter the logic of the query and, in badly written authentication code, bind as another user or enumerate the directory. Directory design carries its own risk: overly broad read permissions on the user object class enable reconnaissance of accounts, groups, service principals and delegation settings, and stale accounts or nested groups accumulate effective privilege that nobody intended to grant. Defenders monitor for anomalous bind failures, unusual search filters, high-volume enumeration and changes to privileged groups or directory-integrated objects.
objectives: You will be able to describe the directory information tree, distinguished names, schema and object classes well enough to read an LDIF entry.
You will be able to choose an appropriate bind mechanism and explain why simple binds require transport encryption.
You will be able to identify LDAP filter injection in application code and describe how input escaping prevents it.
You will be able to reduce directory exposure by restricting anonymous binds, referrals and overly broad read permissions.
You will be able to detect directory enumeration and privileged group modification from directory server logs.

topics.title: Living Off the Land Binary
topics.summary: A living-off-the-land binary, commonly shortened to lolbin, is a legitimate, usually signed and pre-installed executable that an intruder abuses to perform an action such as downloading content, executing a payload, compressing data, or establishing persistence, without introducing a file that a signature-based control would flag. The same idea applies to scripts and libraries, which is why the broader terms living-off-the-land techniques and abuse of built-in tooling are often preferred. The defensive problem is structural: an allow-list that permits the operating system's own utilities implicitly permits every capability those utilities possess, and many of them are considerably more capable than administrators expect. Common abuse patterns include signed binaries that fetch remote content, utilities that proxy execution of another program, management and scripting interfaces that run arbitrary code, archiving tools used to stage collected data, and troubleshooting or installer executables that were designed to raise their own privilege. Detection cannot rely on the tool being present or on its signature. It relies on context: the parent process, the user account, the working directory, the full command line, the network destination contacted, and whether the invocation matches the organisation's baseline of how that tool is normally used. Practical controls include application control policies scoped to specific binaries and argument patterns, blocking specific utilities on server roles that never need them, script block logging, and prompt patching to remove known privilege-escalation paths in installer and troubleshooting components. Analysts should also expect deliberate argument obfuscation and path trickery, since adversaries know these names are watched.
objectives: Define living-off-the-land techniques and explain why signed, pre-installed binaries defeat content-based detection.
Recognise the capability categories adversaries seek in built-in tooling: download, execute, archive, persist and elevate.

topics.title: Macro Malware
topics.summary: Macro malware is malicious logic delivered inside a document or spreadsheet that uses the host application's built-in scripting facility to execute when the file is opened or when the user enables content. The classic form targets office productivity suites, where a document containing an embedded macro reaches a user as an email attachment, a link to a shared file, or a file hosted on a legitimate service, and relies on social engineering to persuade the recipient to click through the security warning. The technique persists because it sits inside a trusted, signed, universally deployed application and because a document is a natural thing for a user to open. Modern variants have widened well beyond the original form: some rely on external content relationships that pull a remote template or resource on open without any macro at all, some abuse document features to launch a companion file, and some target spreadsheet or presentation formats that fewer organisations remember to restrict. Defensive control has three layers. First, reduce the capability itself by disabling macros in documents originating from the internet, using mark-of-the-web and policy-based blocking rather than relying on user judgement. Second, restrict what the host process may do through attack surface reduction rules, application control, and blocking of child process creation from productivity applications. Third, detect the residue: document processes spawning shells or scripting engines, unusual outbound connections from a workstation's office application, external template retrieval, and files written to startup or temporary locations immediately after a document is opened. Email and web filtering help, but user reporting and rapid containment matter because macro campaigns are frequently the initial access step of something larger.

topics.title: Memory Dump
topics.summary: A memory dump is a capture of the contents of a system's physical or virtual memory, preserved as an image file for later analysis. It is the primary source for evidence that never touches disk: running and recently terminated processes, injected code regions, loaded drivers, kernel structures, network connections, command histories, encryption keys and, in many intrusions, the only surviving copy of fileless malware and its configuration. Dumps are taken either from a live host with a trusted acquisition tool, from a virtual machine through the hypervisor, from a cloud instance through provider snapshot or capture mechanisms, or from a crashed system via a configured crash dump or hibernation file. Fidelity depends on the method: hardware-assisted or hypervisor-level capture generally produces the most complete image, while software tools running inside a potentially compromised operating system may themselves be tampered with by a kernel-mode rootkit, so the trustworthiness of the tool and the order of acquisition both matter enormously. A defensible acquisition records the tool and version, the exact command, the memory range captured, a cryptographic hash of the image, the time of capture and the identity of the collector, because the image becomes evidence the moment it is written. Analysis then reconstructs process trees, extracts strings and configuration, looks for injected or unbacked executable regions, recovers credential material, and correlates findings with disk, identity and network evidence. Memory images are large and sensitive, so handling, retention and access controls are part of the process rather than an afterthought.
objectives: Explain what evidence a memory dump can recover that disk and log sources cannot.
Compare live, hypervisor, cloud-provider and crash-dump acquisition methods and their fidelity tradeoffs.
Perform a documented memory acquisition that records tooling, scope, capture time and cryptographic hash.

Analyse a memory image to reconstruct processes, network connections and injected code regions.

topics.title: MFA
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is an authentication control that requires a principal to present evidence from two or more distinct factor categories before a session is granted. The categories are knowledge (something you know, such as a password or PIN), possession (something you have, such as a hardware token, smart card or registered phone), and inherence (something you are, such as a fingerprint or face geometry), with location and behavioural signals sometimes treated as additional context rather than true factors. Because a stolen password alone satisfies only one category, MFA directly disrupts credential replay, password spraying and credential stuffing against externally exposed services, and it is one of the few controls that measurably changes the economics of initial access for ransomware operators. The strength of an implementation depends far less on the label than on the binding between factors: push notification approval, SMS one-time codes and email codes are all phishable or relayable, and adversary-in-the-middle toolkits that proxy the legitimate login page can capture a session token after the user completes a genuine prompt. Practitioners therefore evaluate MFA by the assurance properties it actually delivers: phishing resistance, number matching, origin binding, device-bound keys, and the telemetry the identity provider emits so that anomalous enrolment, factor reset and impossible-travel events can be alerted on. Deployment also has to survive operational reality, including service accounts, legacy protocols that cannot present a second factor, break-glass accounts, and help-desk enrolment fraud, which is why conditional access policy, number matching and FIDO2 security keys are typically combined rather than deployed in isolation.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish authentication factor categories and explain why two prompts of the same category do not constitute MFA.
You will be able to evaluate push, SMS, TOTP and FIDO2 authenticators by their resistance to phishing and adversary-in-the-middle relay.

topics.title: MISP
topics.summary: MISP is an open-source threat intelligence platform designed for storing, correlating, sharing and consuming structured indicators together with the context that makes them usable. Its central data structure is the event, a container that groups attributes describing an incident, campaign or sighting. Attributes are typed key-value pairs covering network indicators, file hashes and names, email artefacts, registry keys, financial data and free text, and they carry a category, a distribution setting and optional identifiers used for correlation. Objects extend attributes into structured bundles, so a file object can carry hashes, size and filename together instead of as loose rows. Taxonomies provide controlled vocabularies for classifying events, while galaxies attach knowledge such as ATT&CK techniques and threat actor clusters, which is what lets an organisation pivot from raw indicators to behavioural intelligence. Correlation is a core feature: when a newly ingested attribute matches an existing one, MISP links the events, surfacing relationships that a flat feed would hide. Sharing is governed by distribution levels, sharing groups and synchronisation with partner servers, and feeds can be pulled from external sources at configurable intervals. Warning lists are the practical counterweight to that automation, flagging values such as common public resolvers, popular domains and shared hosting ranges that are almost always benign. Effective MISP use depends on hygiene rather than features: consistent tagging, honest confidence and distribution choices, curated feeds, and periodic review of stale events. Because instances frequently exchange data with partners and public feeds, every ingested attribute should be treated as untrusted input, and correlation output should never drive automatic blocking without a validation step.

topics.title: MTTD and MTTR
topics.summary: Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond are the two headline measures of security operations performance. Mean Time to Detect measures the elapsed interval between when malicious activity actually began and when it was first identified, while Mean Time to Respond measures the interval from identification to containment or resolution, depending on how the organisation defines the endpoint. Both are averages and both are therefore easily misread. A mean computed over a handful of incidents is dominated by outliers, so distributions, medians and percentiles communicate far more than a single number. The definitions themselves are the hardest part. Detection time cannot be measured from the alert timestamp unless you also determine when the activity started, which usually requires retrospective log analysis and often moves the start earlier once the incident is understood. Response end is equally ambiguous: is it containment of the immediate threat, eradication, restoration of service, or case closure. Without a written definition agreed with the business, teams optimise a metric they cannot compare over time. The measures are also gameable. Suppressing noisy detections lowers alert volume and can appear to improve response time while degrading detection. Closing cases quickly without corroboration improves the average and hides unresolved risk. The genuinely useful approach is to pair times with quality measures: the proportion of incidents found by internal detection rather than external notification, the fraction detected at each ATT&CK stage, dwell time distributions, and containment precision. Tracking MTTD and MTTR by incident class and detection source, and reviewing the specific incidents that set the extremes, converts an executive number into an engineering feedback loop.
objectives: You will be able to define detection start, detection point, containment and closure precisely enough that the metric is comparable over time.
