topics.title: Netflow and IPFIX
topics.summary: NetFlow and its open equivalent IPFIX are flow-export technologies that summarise network conversations rather than capturing every packet. A router or switch observes packets, groups them into flows keyed by source and destination address, ports, protocol and other fields, and periodically exports records that describe each flow with counters, timestamps and interface information. Because exports are aggregated, the storage and bandwidth cost is a small fraction of full packet capture, which makes it practical to retain flow data for weeks or months across an entire estate. That retention is the core defensive value. Flow records answer who talked to whom, when, how much and over which port, and they stay useful for retrospective investigation long after the packets are gone. Common analytical uses include detecting exfiltration by volume and direction, identifying beaconing through regular inter-arrival patterns, mapping external exposure during incident scoping, and proving that a segmentation policy is genuinely enforced. Flow data is deliberately lossy: it carries no payload, so it cannot confirm what was transferred or match content signatures, and sampling, aggregation timeouts and top-talker reporting on the exporting device all reduce fidelity. Adversaries and ordinary applications can tunnel over permitted protocols, so flow analysis often produces the hypothesis that packet capture or endpoint telemetry must confirm. Practical deployments must handle clock synchronisation, because flow timestamps are useless for correlation when devices disagree, asymmetric routing so both directions are collected, collector capacity and duplicate exports, and consistent interface naming so that a flow can be tied to a physical or logical path. Enrichment with asset inventory, geolocation and threat intelligence turns raw records into something an analyst can prioritise, and keeping flow data beside DNS, proxy and authentication logs resolves most incidents that no single source could explain.
objectives: You will be able to describe how flows are defined, aggregated and exported and what fidelity that costs.
You will be able to triage flow records for beaconing, exfiltration volume and unexpected lateral movement.

topics.title: Network Access Control
topics.summary: Network access control is the set of technologies that decides whether a device may join a network and what it may reach once connected. A typical deployment authenticates the device or its user before granting access, commonly through 802.1X with a RADIUS server, MAC authentication bypass for devices that cannot run a supplicant, or a captive portal for guests and unmanaged endpoints. After authentication the platform evaluates posture, covering operating system version, patch level, endpoint protection state, disk encryption and configuration compliance, and then places the device into a role-based segment or access control list. Devices that fail posture checks are quarantined to a remediation network where they can update but cannot reach production systems, and devices that cannot authenticate at all are denied or routed into a registration workflow. The result is that network admission becomes a policy decision with an audit trail rather than a physical fact. Projects fail more often for organisational than technical reasons. Discovery is the first hurdle, because most estates contain printers, cameras, badge readers, medical devices and building systems that predate any authentication requirement and may not support 802.1X, and each needs a documented exception with a compensating control. Rollout must be staged in monitor mode first, where the platform classifies devices and reports what would have happened, before enforcement is enabled, otherwise a misconfiguration locks out staff or takes critical systems offline. Link design also matters, because authentication on switch-to-switch and switch-to-controller uplinks requires careful configuration to avoid authenticating infrastructure. Once operating, network access control supplies valuable telemetry: it knows which device is on which port at which time, which helps incident response locate and isolate a compromised host quickly. Its limitation is that it secures the moment of connection, not the behaviour afterwards, so it complements segmentation and monitoring rather than replacing them.

topics.title: Network Segmentation
topics.summary: A network segment is a bounded group of systems that share a communication policy, and segmentation is the practice of inserting enforced boundaries between those groups so that a single compromised host cannot reach every other asset. Boundaries may be physical, built from separate switches and cabling, logical, built from VLANs with router or firewall access control lists, or identity-based, built from microsegmentation agents and policy engines that decide per workload rather than per subnet. The design goal is to limit blast radius and to create chokepoints where traffic can be inspected and logged. Flat networks fail catastrophically because one phished workstation inherits reachability to file shares, management interfaces, backup infrastructure and directory services. Good segmentation starts from data and service flows rather than from the organisational chart: classify assets by sensitivity, map which systems must talk to which on which ports, then enforce default deny and log the denials until the policy is proven. Segmentation is a programme rather than a purchase. Legacy applications with hard-coded addresses, unmanaged devices, and operational technology that cannot tolerate added latency all generate exceptions that erode the model over time, so each exception needs an owner and an expiry date. Attackers respond by tunnelling permitted protocols, chaining through dual-homed hosts and abusing management planes, which is why monitoring must exist on the boundaries themselves. Administrative tiering, jump hosts and dedicated management networks address the management-plane risk, while cloud security groups, network policies and service meshes reproduce the same ideas with their own drift problems. The practical test of any segmentation scheme is adversarial: assume a host inside a segment is already compromised and ask what it can still reach.

topics.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
topics.summary: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based framework that organises cybersecurity activity into a common vocabulary so that technical teams, executives, auditors and regulators can discuss risk using the same terms. Its core is a set of Functions, historically Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, each broken into Categories and Subcategories that describe desired outcomes rather than prescribing specific products. Around that core sits the Framework Implementation Tiers, which characterise how rigorous and repeatable an organisation's risk management practice is, and the Framework Profiles, which express current and target states so a gap analysis produces a funded roadmap instead of a vague maturity claim. Practitioners use the framework in three concrete ways. First, as a mapping hub: an organisation maps its existing controls from ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls and regulatory obligations onto Subcategories once, then reuses that mapping for every new questionnaire. Second, as a reporting device: Function-level scores give executives a defensible view of capability without exposing implementation detail. Third, as a design input for metrics, where each Subcategory outcome gets an operational measurement such as mean time to detect or percentage of assets with current agent coverage. The framework is deliberately technology-neutral and does not itself create legal obligations, which is why it is frequently used as the connective tissue between mandatory regimes rather than as a replacement for them.

topics.title: NIST SP 800-53
topics.summary: NIST Special Publication 800-53 is the United States federal control catalogue for information systems and organisations, and it has become the de facto reference control set for regulated industries well beyond government. Its structure is what makes it useful to engineers: controls are grouped into families such as Access Control, Audit and Accountability, Configuration Management, Incident Response, Risk Assessment and Supply Chain Risk Management, and each control carries a statement, supplemental guidance, assessment procedures drawn from SP 800-53A, and optional control enhancements that allow an organisation to dial specificity up or down. Controls are selected and tailored through the SP 800-37 risk management framework process, where a system is categorised for confidentiality, integrity and availability impact, a control baseline is chosen, and the resulting set is documented in a system security plan with a plan of action and milestones for anything not yet satisfied. The critical practitioner insight is that 800-53 is a catalogue, not a compliance regime by itself: it becomes mandatory through law, contract or agency policy, and the burden of evidence sits with the organisation. Control identifiers are stable and widely reused, which is why so many commercial and cloud compliance mappings, including the FedRAMP baselines, are expressed as 800-53 selections. Teams that implement it well automate evidence collection against assessment procedures rather than treating the catalogue as a documentation exercise.

topics.title: Nonce Reuse
topics.summary: Nonce reuse is the failure to supply a unique per-operation value to a cryptographic algorithm that requires one, and it quietly converts otherwise sound constructions into broken ones. The consequences depend on the mode. In counter-mode authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM, reusing a nonce with the same key leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and exposes the authentication subkey, which allows an attacker to forge messages and, in many deployment patterns, to recover plaintext outright. In stream ciphers, the same keystream is produced twice, so ciphertext XOR reveals plaintext XOR. In signature schemes that take a per-signature secret, reusing it across two different messages lets anyone recover the private key with straightforward algebra, which has caused real-world key compromises in wallets and embedded devices. Nonces are not required to be secret, only unique within the scope of a key, but they must be unpredictable wherever an attacker can influence or predict them. Production failures usually come from weak randomness on constrained hardware, virtual machine clones that resume with identical state, counters that reset after a restart or a snapshot rollback, or application code that derives a nonce from a field like a user identifier, timestamp with poor resolution, or an incrementing database value that resets. Defensive practice means deterministic nonce derivation where the standard permits it, per-message key derivation, hardware random sources, monotonic counters persisted with the key, and monitoring for the duplicate-value signatures of these faults in protocol logs and telemetry.

topics.title: OAuth 2.0
topics.summary: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework that lets a client application obtain limited access to a resource on behalf of a user or another service without handling that user's credentials. It defines roles (resource owner, client, authorisation server, resource server), grant types (authorisation code, client credentials, device code, and the deprecated implicit and resource owner password grants), and token types, most importantly the access token and the optional refresh token. The framework deliberately separates authorisation from authentication, which is why building a login flow on OAuth alone produces the confused-deputy problems that OpenID Connect was created to solve. Security depends heavily on implementation choices rather than on the framework's defaults: public clients must use proof key for code exchange to bind the authorisation request to the token request, redirect URIs must be matched exactly, state parameters must be unpredictable and verified, and bearer tokens must be protected in transit and at rest because anyone holding the token can use it. Common real-world failures include open redirectors leaking authorisation codes, permissive redirect URI matching with wildcards or path traversal, tokens stored in browser local storage where cross-site scripting can reach them, excessive scope grants that let a low-privilege client call high-value APIs, and consent phishing in which a user grants a malicious application durable access. Defenders focus on token lifetime, scope minimisation, sender constraint, and the authorisation server's audit log of grants, consents and token issuance.

topics.title: OpenID Connect
topics.summary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that gives clients a standardised way to verify a user's identity and obtain basic profile information. It adds an identity token, a JSON Web Token whose claims describe the authentication event and the subject, and it standardises discovery through a well-known configuration document, key distribution through a JSON Web Key Set, and user information retrieval through a dedicated endpoint. Because the identity token is signed and carries claims such as issuer, audience, subject, issue time and expiry, a relying party can validate it locally without a per-request round trip to the provider, provided it verifies the signature against the published keys, checks that the issuer and audience match its own registration, enforces nonce and expiry, and refuses to accept a token signed with an algorithm it did not expect. Failures cluster in exactly those checks: accepting a token with an unexpected signing algorithm, skipping audience validation so a token minted for a different application is accepted, trusting unverified claims taken from an access token rather than the identity token, and mixing up access tokens and identity tokens in ways that lead to privilege confusion. Hybrid flows, front-channel logout, and the handling of long-lived refresh tokens each introduce their own edge cases. Operational attention belongs on key rollover in the JSON Web Key Set, because a relying party that caches keys indefinitely will fail closed or, worse, fail open depending on its error handling.

topics.title: Operational Security (OpSec)
topics.summary: Operational security, usually shortened to OpSec, is the practice of controlling the observable traces an activity produces so that they do not reveal capability, intent, identity or infrastructure to an observer. The classic process has five steps: identify the information that must not be disclosed, analyse who is collecting against it, analyse the weaknesses in how the activity is conducted, assess the risk each weakness creates, and apply countermeasures in proportion. In security work the concept applies in two directions. On the adversarial side it explains why intrusions are often quiet, consistent and patient: infrastructure is separated by purpose, personas are maintained consistently across channels, timing follows the target's working rhythm, and released artefacts are sanitised of metadata before use. Understanding that discipline is directly useful to defenders, because every trace an intruder must suppress is a trace worth monitoring, and every inconsistency in a persona or infrastructure set becomes a pivot for attribution at a stated confidence level. On the defensive side, OpSec governs incident response itself: communications move off potentially compromised channels, actions that would alert an intruder are delayed until containment is ready, and information about the investigation is shared strictly on a need-to-know basis. Poor OpSec in either direction produces preventable loss, whether that is a burned capability or an intruder who destroys evidence after noticing that they have been detected.
objectives: You will be able to apply the five-step OpSec process to a security activity and its observable traces.
You will be able to identify which traces an intruder must suppress and convert them into monitoring requirements.
You will be able to explain how inconsistencies in infrastructure and persona support attribution at a stated confidence level.
You will be able to plan incident response communications that do not alert an active intruder.

topics.title: Passwordless Authentication
topics.summary: Passwordless authentication is a set of authentication methods in which the user proves possession of a registered authenticator bound to their identity and never supplies a shared secret that can be phished, reused or cracked offline. The two dominant families are asymmetric key credentials based on the Web Authentication standard, where the private key stays in a hardware security key or platform authenticator and the public key is registered with the relying party, and certificate-based authentication, where a device or smart card certificate issued by enterprise certificate authority replaces the password. Both defeat password-centric attacks structurally rather than by policy: there is no secret to spray, no hash to crack, no code to relay to a waitress-style adversary-in-the-middle proxy, and the signature is bound to the origin so that a lookalike domain cannot harvest a usable response. Passkeys extend the same primitive to consumer use by synchronising or device-linking credentials, which improves usability and recovery but changes the threat model, since the credential now follows the user's platform account rather than a single physical token. Deployment work is mostly in the unglamorous details: recovery and enrolment, because account recovery becomes the weakest authentication path once passwords are gone; attestation and device inventory, to decide which authenticators are acceptable; account identifier design, to avoid silently re-enrolling a credential to the wrong person; and legacy systems that cannot speak the protocol and therefore need a brokered or certificate-based compromise. Hybrid environments usually run passwordless for interactive users and retain vaulted secrets for machine identities, where the equivalent control is short-lived certificates and automatic rotation.

You will be able to compare hardware security keys, platform authenticators and synchronised passkeys by assurance and usability.

You will be able to detect suspicious authenticator registration, deletion and re-registration events in identity provider logs.

topics.title: Payload Staging
topics.summary: Payload staging is the practice of splitting the code or configuration that achieves an objective into a small delivery component and one or more larger components retrieved after execution begins. It exists because delivery channels impose constraints: an email attachment has a size ceiling, a landing page should look unremarkable, and a single large transfer to an unusual destination is easier to detect than several small ones that blend with normal traffic. A typical staged operation therefore uses a lightweight first stage, often a script or a signed system utility, to establish execution and then pull the remainder from a location the operator controls, frequently over ordinary web or cloud storage protocols. Staging also supports flexibility, because capabilities can be swapped or updated during an engagement without re-delivering the initial component. From a defensive standpoint, staging is a gift as much as a problem: it produces a distinctive chain of events that begins with a user action or an exploited service, continues through an interpreter or signed binary starting unexpectedly, and ends with an outbound fetch from an endpoint that has no business reason to contact that destination. High-value detections combine process ancestry with network context, especially where a document reader, archive tool or script host initiates an outbound connection, and where the destination is new to the estate. Mitigations limit both halves of the chain: blocking macros and script execution from user-writable locations, restricting which binaries may make outbound connections, tightening egress, and maintaining a software inventory so unexpected fetches stand out.
objectives: You will be able to explain why operators split delivery into stages and what each stage reveals to a defender.
You will be able to trace a staged delivery chain through process, file and network telemetry.
You will be able to write detections that pair suspicious parent processes with unexpected outbound connections.
You will be able to list the application control and egress controls that break staged delivery.
You will be able to distinguish in-memory execution from on-disk staging in endpoint evidence.

topics.title: PCI DSS
topics.summary: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is a contractual requirement imposed by the card brands and administered by the PCI Security Standards Council on any entity that stores, processes or transmits account data, or that can impact the security of the cardholder data environment. Unlike principle-based regimes, PCI DSS is prescriptive: it defines requirements for network security controls, secure configuration, protection of stored account data, encryption of transmission over open networks, malware protection, secure development, access restriction by business need to know, identification and authentication, physical security, logging and monitoring, security testing and an information security policy supported by risk assessment. Scope is the central engineering problem, and the standard explicitly encourages segmentation and other scope-reduction techniques so that systems neither connected to nor able to impact the cardholder data environment drop out of assessment. Practitioners should expect annual assessment by a Qualified Security Assessor or completion of a self-assessment questionnaire depending on transaction volume, plus quarterly network scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor and continuous evidence of logging, file integrity monitoring, change control and access review. Version 4.x introduced a customised approach allowing an entity to meet a requirement's intent using a documented compensating control methodology, and shifted many controls into a continually operating model rather than an annual evidence scramble.
objectives: You will be able to define the cardholder data environment and reduce scope through segmentation and data flow analysis.

topics.title: Persistence
topics.summary: Persistence is the collection of mechanisms an intruder uses to retain access across reboots, password changes, session expiry and partial remediation, so that initial access does not have to be won again. Host-based persistence attaches to legitimate startup behaviour: autostart entries, scheduled tasks, system services, logon scripts, shell profiles, and browser or office extensions. Identity-based persistence is often more valuable and harder to see, because it lives in the directory or cloud tenant rather than on an endpoint; examples include newly created accounts, added credentials or keys, modified federation settings, and application registrations with delegated permissions that outlive any single session. Network-based persistence covers configurations that survive host rebuilds, such as remote access profiles, tunnels and backup channels. Every mechanism trades stealth against resilience, and defenders can exploit that trade-off: the more durable the mechanism, the more likely it is to touch a monitored location, generate an audit record, or require a privileged change. Practical detection therefore starts from an accurate baseline of what is allowed to autostart, which scheduled tasks and services normally exist, and which principals hold privileged roles. Deviations from that baseline, combined with audit events for account creation, permission grants and application registration, give far better coverage than hunting for specific tools. Mitigation combines application control, privileged access management with approval workflows, credential hygiene, and centralised logging that an intruder cannot quietly edit.
objectives: You will be able to categorise persistence mechanisms as host-based, identity-based or network-based.
You will be able to explain the trade-off between resilience and stealth for common autostart mechanisms.
You will be able to build a baseline of legitimate autostart locations, services and scheduled tasks.
You will be able to spot tenant-level persistence through account creation, credential addition and application registration.

topics.title: PICERL
topics.summary: PICERL is a six-phase incident response lifecycle - Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery and Lessons Learned - that gives a security team a shared vocabulary and a gated decision path from the moment an alert fires to the moment an incident is formally closed. Preparation covers work done before anything happens: asset inventories, logging coverage, jump bags, out-of-band communication, standing authority to isolate systems, and rehearsed escalation paths. Identification is the analysis phase, where telemetry from endpoints, identity providers, network sensors and SaaS audit logs is correlated into a defensible statement of what is actually happening, which hosts and accounts are involved, and how confident the team is in that conclusion. Containment splits into short-term measures that stop immediate spread, such as network isolation or credential revocation, and longer-term measures that keep the business running while the adversary is still presumed present. Eradication removes the adversary's foothold - malware, persistence, created accounts, modified configuration - and is where teams most often declare victory too early. Recovery restores service under heightened monitoring, validates that the root cause is genuinely closed, and defines what normal looks like again. Lessons Learned converts the incident into durable change: detection gaps closed, playbooks updated, owners named, and remediation tracked to completion. The phases are not strictly linear. A persistence mechanism discovered during Recovery sends the team back to Containment, and that iteration is expected rather than a sign of failure. What matters is that each transition is justified by evidence, documented with timestamps, and communicated to the people who own the resulting risk decisions.
objectives: Explain each PICERL phase and the evidence-based entry and exit criteria that justify moving to the next one.
Build a Preparation checklist covering logging coverage, standing authority to isolate, out-of-band communications and evidence handling.
Write an Identification statement that separates confirmed fact from inference and states an explicit confidence level.
Choose between short-term and long-term containment actions and defend the tradeoff between spread reduction and business impact.
Distinguish eradication from recovery and explain why restored service is not proof that the adversary is gone.
Design a Lessons Learned process that converts findings into owned, dated remediation items.
Reconstruct a PICERL timeline from multi-source logs and identify the points where the team iterated backwards between phases.

topics.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
topics.summary: Post-quantum cryptography is the family of public-key algorithms designed to remain secure against an adversary equipped with a large-scale quantum computer, alongside the migration work required to deploy them. The threat is asymmetric in time: Shor's algorithm would break RSA and elliptic curve cryptography outright, while Grover's algorithm only modestly reduces the effective strength of symmetric primitives, so AES-256 and SHA-384 remain comfortable. The most urgent operational risk is harvest-now-decrypt-later, where traffic captured today is stored for decryption once the capability arrives, which makes long-lived confidentiality requirements the first migration priority. NIST standardised a set of algorithms for key encapsulation and digital signatures built on lattice, hash-based and code-based mathematics, with a hybrid deployment pattern that combines a classical and a post-quantum exchange so that security holds unless both are broken. Migration is harder than swapping a library. Organisations must inventory where public-key cryptography is used, including embedded devices that will never receive an update, hardware modules with fixed algorithm support, certificate and protocol size assumptions that break under larger keys and signatures, performance budgets on constrained links, and the certificate authority and code signing infrastructure that has to issue and validate new algorithm types. Governance questions follow, such as which algorithms are approved, how hybrids are represented in policy, and how long a cryptoperiod must be before quantum resistance becomes mandatory.
objectives: Explain how Shor's and Grover's algorithms affect public-key and symmetric cryptography differently.
Describe harvest-now-decrypt-later and identify which data classes justify early migration.

Perform a cryptographic inventory that finds public-key usage in code, devices, protocols and third-party services.
Plan a hybrid classical-plus-post-quantum deployment and explain what property the hybrid preserves.
Assess protocol and infrastructure changes needed for larger keys, including certificate handling and constrained links.
Build a migration roadmap with cryptoperiods, priorities and a defensible policy position on algorithm approval.

topics.title: Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Privilege escalation is the set of actions that convert ordinary user or service access into authority the account was never intended to hold, whether that means higher rights on the same host or rights that reach across a domain or cloud tenant. Vertical escalation raises the level of permission an identity holds, while horizontal escalation moves to a different identity with comparable rights and is often a stepping stone rather than an end in itself. The underlying causes are consistent across platforms: excessive standing privilege, misconfigured permissions on files, services or container runtimes, unpatched local software, credential material left in memory, configuration files or environment variables, and trust relationships that let a low-trust principal assume a high-trust role. Cloud and container estates add their own variants, including over-broad role assumption policies, instance metadata reachable from a workload, and container configurations that expose the host. Because escalation usually abuses legitimate functionality, signature-based detection alone is inadequate. Useful signals include process trees in which a user-facing application spawns a shell or administrative utility, changes to local or directory group membership, newly granted roles or permissions, and access to privileged interfaces outside a change window. Effective mitigation is architectural rather than detective: least privilege, removal of standing administrative rights in favour of just-in-time elevation, unique local administrator credentials, timely patching, and application control that limits what an unprivileged user can execute. Detection then concentrates on the residual cases where those controls fail or are bypassed.

topics.title: Privileged Access Management
topics.summary: Privileged access management (PAM) is the discipline and tooling set that controls, brokers, records and audits the use of accounts with elevated rights, including domain administrators, root, database superusers, cloud root and organisation owner roles, and the service accounts that hold equivalent power. The core problem PAM addresses is that privileged credentials are shared, rarely rotated, widely copied into scripts and configuration files, and almost never attributable to an individual, so a single disclosure can be replayed indefinitely with the full authority of the account. A mature programme removes standing privilege wherever possible by vaulting credentials and checking them out for a bounded window, injecting them into sessions so the human never sees the secret, brokering interactive sessions through a jump host that records keystrokes and commands, and replacing human-held credentials with short-lived certificates or tokens. Just-in-time elevation, approval workflows and break-glass procedures with mandatory post-use review are the mechanisms that make this workable when a human genuinely needs emergency access. Beyond vaulting, PAM covers the secrets that machines use: application credentials, API keys and certificates stored in a managed vault with automatic rotation rather than committed to repositories or baked into images. The detection value is substantial, because privileged session recordings, checkout logs and vault audit trails give defenders a well-defined baseline against which unusual hours, unusual source hosts, direct use of an unvaulted credential, or elevation outside the approved workflow stand out sharply.

topics.title: Process Injection
topics.summary: Process injection is a family of techniques in which code is placed into the address space of another running process so that it executes under that process's identity, privileges and trust context. Attackers use it for three overlapping reasons: to hide malicious execution inside a legitimate process that security tooling already trusts, to inherit access tokens and privileges the injected process already holds, and to survive elementary cleanup because the host process is not the malicious file. The general mechanism is consistent across implementations even when the specific interfaces differ: obtain a handle to a target process, allocate or repurpose memory inside it, write the payload, change that memory to an executable state, and redirect execution there. Variants differ in how visible each of those steps is — remote thread creation requires cross-process handles and leaves distinct artefacts, while approaches that use shared sections, asynchronous procedure calls, or the process's own already-loaded libraries produce different telemetry. Detection depends heavily on visibility into memory and into cross-process operations, so defenders combine endpoint sensor callbacks, memory scanning for executable regions that are not backed by a file on disk, thread creation anomalies, and behavioural signals such as an unexpected process making network connections or reading credential material. Injection alone is not an objective; it is an enabler that usually appears adjacent to credential access, defence evasion and command-and-control. Understanding the mechanism precisely is what allows an analyst to decide whether a flagged event reflects a genuine intrusion or one of the many legitimate products that also inject code.

topics.title: Proxy
topics.summary: A proxy is an intermediary that receives a client request, applies policy, and forwards that request to the destination on the client's behalf, so the client never communicates directly with the remote server. Forward proxies serve outbound traffic and are the classic control point for URL filtering, malware blocking, authentication, logging and caching, while reverse proxies sit in front of servers to terminate TLS, balance load and shield applications from direct exposure. Because a forward proxy sees the full request, including hostname, path, headers and, where transport encryption is terminated, the body, it can enforce category and content rules that a packet filter cannot express. Proxies are also a natural place for authentication, so access decisions can be tied to a user identity rather than an address, and for inspecting protocols that negotiate their own transfers, such as web traffic carrying file downloads or application programming interface calls. The operational challenges are bypass and scale. Applications that ignore system proxy settings, mobile devices that roam off the corporate network, and encrypted protocols on non-standard ports can all sidestep a proxy unless it is combined with egress control that blocks direct outbound connections, so enforcement of proxy use matters more than the feature list. Explicit proxies require client configuration, while transparent interception redirects traffic without client knowledge, which simplifies rollout but breaks certificate-pinned applications and creates privacy obligations. High availability is essential because an inline proxy failure becomes an outage, and capacity must account for decryption overhead. Logging is where the proxy earns its keep: full URLs, identities, response codes, byte counts and file metadata are among the richest sources for detecting beaconing, staged downloads and exfiltration over web services, though the volume makes retention and indexing a real design constraint.

topics.title: Public Key Infrastructure
topics.summary: Public key infrastructure is the combination of certificate authorities, registration authorities, certificate repositories, revocation services and the policies that bind public keys to identities so that parties who have never met can authenticate each other. A certificate is a signed data structure containing a subject public key, an issuer, a validity period, extensions that constrain usage, and the issuer's signature over all of it; a relying party validates that structure by building a chain to a trusted root, checking signatures, validity times, key usage and extended key usage, name constraints, and revocation status through CRL or OCSP. In practice most PKI incidents are not cryptanalytic. They are trust-store problems: an over-broad enterprise root installed on endpoints, a subordinate CA with no name constraints, an internal CA whose private key sits on a network-reachable server, a certificate issued to an unverified requester, a revocation path that clients never actually check, or a machine identity that outlives the employee who owned it. Lifecycle management is equally important, because expiring certificates cause outages while forgotten long-lived ones become stable footholds. Modern practice pushes towards short-lived certificates, automated issuance through ACME-style protocols, hardware-backed CA keys, certificate transparency monitoring for rogue issuance, and continuous inventory of everything presenting a certificate on the network.

topics.title: Ransomware
topics.summary: Ransomware is malicious software or an intrusion campaign whose objective is to deny an organisation access to its own data or systems and then sell that access back, typically by encrypting files, locking virtualisation or backup infrastructure, or threatening to publish stolen data. Modern incidents are rarely a single executable. They are operations that begin with access brokering, phishing, exposed remote services or valid credentials, proceed through discovery, privilege escalation and lateral movement, often harvest data for double extortion before encryption starts, and only then deploy the payload across many hosts at once. The encryption phase is quick and loud, but the preceding dwell time is where defenders have the best chance to intervene, which is why detection strategy emphasises the precursors: mass file rename behaviour, deletion or disabling of shadow copies and recovery catalogs, unexpected use of backup administration interfaces, credential dumping, and the disabling of endpoint protection. Recovery depends far more on preparation than on any live response. Organisations need offline or immutable backups whose restore path has genuinely been rehearsed, a documented decision process for isolation versus shutdown, and pre-negotiated legal, regulatory and communications roles. Paying a demand is discouraged because it funds further crime, does not guarantee restoration, and in some jurisdictions carries sanctions or reporting implications. Because exfiltration frequently precedes encryption, incident scoping must assume data theft even when no leak site is mentioned, and breach notification timelines should be assessed from the moment of first unauthorised access rather than the moment files were encrypted.
objectives: Describe the typical ransomware intrusion lifecycle from initial access and discovery through exfiltration and encryption.
Detect pre-encryption precursors such as recovery-inhibition behaviour, credential access and mass file modification.

topics.title: Reconnaissance
topics.summary: Reconnaissance is the disciplined collection and organisation of information about a target before and during an engagement, producing the map of systems, identities and technologies that every later phase depends on. Practitioners divide it into passive work, which draws on third-party and public sources and leaves no trace on the target, and active work, which sends traffic to target-owned infrastructure and is therefore visible to defenders. Passive sources include domain registration records, certificate transparency logs, DNS history, public code repositories, cloud storage naming conventions, marketing material, job advertisements that name internal platforms, and breach corpora that reveal credential exposure. Active work includes port and service enumeration, protocol fingerprinting, virtual host and content discovery, and banner or TLS inspection; each of these produces network, firewall and web server evidence that a mature security operations centre can alert on. The output is normally a structured inventory annotated with ownership, exposure and business value rather than a raw list of addresses. For defenders, reconnaissance matters because it is the phase with the longest lead time before exploitation: high volumes of denied flows, sequential destination sweeps, unusual user agents, and monitoring of certificate transparency entries for the organisation's own domains all provide early warning. Reconnaissance quality also determines engagement safety, because scope, rate limits and prohibited techniques are agreed before any packet is sent. Understanding what an adversary can learn from open sources is the most honest route to reducing an attack surface rather than cosmetically hiding it.
objectives: You will be able to separate passive from active reconnaissance and state what evidence each leaves in network and application logs.
You will be able to inventory the open sources that reveal an organisation's naming conventions, technology stack and staff identities.
You will be able to describe how enumeration traffic appears in firewall, netflow, DNS and web server telemetry.
You will be able to rank attack surface findings by business impact rather than by count.
You will be able to explain how certificate transparency and historical DNS monitoring feed an early warning capability.
You will be able to draft reconnaissance limits for a rules-of-engagement document, including rate limits and excluded assets.

topics.title: Risk Register
topics.summary: A risk register is the controlled record of identified risks that an organisation has decided to track, each entry capturing the risk statement, the affected assets and business processes, the threat and vulnerability that make it credible, the existing controls, the assessed likelihood and impact, the resulting inherent and residual rating, the risk owner, the treatment decision and the target date. It is the operational heart of a risk management programme because it converts assessment into accountable action: an entry without a named owner and a due date is an observation, not a managed risk. Practitioners should treat the register as a living engineering artefact rather than an annual spreadsheet. Good registers express risk in a consistent grammar such as cause, event and consequence, so that two analysts score similar situations similarly; they attach evidence such as detection coverage gaps, vulnerability findings, control test results and near-miss incident data; and they record risk acceptance explicitly, with the accepting authority, the rationale and the expiry. Risk scoring should be calibrated against real incident and loss data where it exists, because uncalibrated five-by-five matrices drift toward subjective optimism. Registers also need lifecycle discipline: risks are reviewed on a defined cadence, escalated when treatment slips, closed with evidence, and linked to the frameworks in use, whether ISO 27001 clause six, NIST SP 800-30 or a sector regulator's expectations. Effective registers are visible to engineering, not locked in a GRC tool only compliance staff can open.
objectives: You will be able to write risk statements in a consistent cause, event and consequence structure that different analysts score the same way.
You will be able to attach control evidence, detection coverage and vulnerability data to support likelihood and impact ratings.
You will be able to assign risk owners with authority to accept or treat, and set meaningful target dates.

You will be able to run a review cycle that escalates overdue treatment and closes risks only with evidence.
You will be able to calibrate a risk matrix against incident and loss data rather than unfounded opinion.

topics.title: Role-Based Access Control
topics.summary: Role-based access control (RBAC) is an access control model in which permissions are assigned to roles rather than directly to users, and users receive permissions only through the roles granted to them. The model is usually decomposed into users, roles, permissions, operations and objects, with role hierarchies allowing a senior role to inherit the permissions of a junior one and constraints preventing conflicting combinations from being held simultaneously. In practice RBAC is the default model for Active Directory groups, Linux groups, Kubernetes role bindings, cloud IAM policies and nearly every commercial application, and it succeeds or fails on the quality of role design rather than on the model itself. Roles that accumulate permissions over years, roles that are granted for convenience rather than function, and role explosion where hundreds of near-duplicate roles exist because exceptions were encoded as new roles rather than handled as exceptions, all produce effective privilege that far exceeds intent. Role mining and periodic recertification are the corrective processes: derive candidate roles from observed entitlement usage, consolidate what overlaps, and require an accountable owner to affirm every assignment on a schedule. The persistent gap is that RBAC answers whether a subject holds a permission but not whether the request is appropriate for the moment, which is why organisations layer attribute-based or context-based conditions over role assignment for sensitive operations. Segregation of duties and least privilege are both expressed through RBAC, so careful attention to role-to-permission mapping and to the aggregation of inherited roles is where real assurance comes from.
objectives: You will be able to model users, roles, permissions and role hierarchies for a representative application.
You will be able to explain how role inheritance and the aggregation of multiple roles produce unintended effective privilege.
You will be able to run role mining and recertification to consolidate role explosion and remove unused entitlements.
You will be able to design segregation-of-duties constraints that keep conflicting duties out of one identity.
You will be able to review cloud IAM policies and Kubernetes role bindings for overly permissive or wildcard grants.

topics.title: Rootkit
topics.summary: A rootkit is a set of techniques and components designed to keep malicious presence on a system hidden while retaining privileged control, typically by subverting the very mechanisms an administrator would use to observe the machine. That subversion takes several forms. User-mode rootkits hook or patch library functions so that directory listings, process enumerations and registry queries omit the intruder's artefacts. Kernel-mode rootkits load a driver that filters system calls, hides handles, or unlinks entries from kernel data structures, which can make the compromise invisible to ordinary tooling running above them. Bootkits extend persistence into the boot chain, surviving reinstallation of the operating system on the same disk, and firmware implants sit below that in platform code. Virtualisation-based rootkits move the operating system into a guest and let a thin hypervisor mediate what the guest can observe, which is powerful but fragile in practice. The defensive consequence is that on a suspected rootkit host, a negative result from host-resident tooling proves very little. Trustworthy examination requires either an out-of-band method such as booting the system from known-good external media, offline disk analysis, or cross-referencing independent telemetry: network flow records, remote authentication logs, hypervisor-level events and endpoint agent data that does not rely on the compromised operating system's own APIs. Removal is generally a rebuild decision rather than a cleaning exercise, because a partially removed kernel implant leaves an unverifiable system. Prevention focuses on driver signing enforcement, secure boot, measured boot attestation, and blocking the privileged access that rootkit installation requires in the first place.
objectives: Differentiate user-mode, kernel-mode, bootkit, firmware and virtualisation-based rootkit approaches by their position in the stack.

Assess driver signing, secure boot and measured boot controls as barriers to kernel and boot-level persistence.

topics.title: RSA
topics.summary: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem whose security rests on the presumed hardness of factoring the product of two large primes, combined with modular exponentiation over that product. A key pair consists of a modulus derived from two secret primes, a public exponent usually 65537, and a private exponent derived through the extended Euclidean algorithm. RSA supports both encryption and digital signatures, and it is normally used inside a padding or encoding scheme rather than on raw data, because textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable. Encryption uses OAEP padding; signatures use PSS or the older PKCS#1 v1.5 scheme, and the padding choice is where most real-world breaks have occurred. Practical risks include small key sizes that are within reach of well-resourced factoring efforts, shared or non-random primes generated by faulty entropy sources, Bleichenbacher-style padding oracle attacks against v1.5 encryption, and signature verification code that ignores algorithm identifiers or accepts the wrong hash. Signing is also much slower than verifying, which shapes how RSA is deployed in certificate chains and protocol handshakes. Throughout their lifecycle, RSA keys must be protected against exfiltration, rotated before weakness accumulates, and retired with their certificates, which is why hardware modules and inventory of key material are operational controls rather than cryptographic footnotes.
objectives: Explain the mathematical structure of an RSA key pair and why factoring the modulus compromises both confidentiality and authenticity.
Distinguish OAEP encryption padding from PSS and PKCS#1 v1.5 signature schemes, and state when each is acceptable.
Describe how a padding oracle attack against RSA encryption is exploited and how constant-time error handling mitigates it.

Interpret certificate chain and signature algorithm fields during a review of TLS or code-signing infrastructure.

topics.title: RTO and RPO
topics.summary: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective are the two commitments that translate continuity intent into engineering requirements. The recovery time objective is the targeted duration of time within which a business process, system or service must be restored after a disruption; it is a deadline, not a duration target, and it must sit inside the maximum tolerable period of disruption derived from the business impact analysis. The recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, expressed as how far back the last usable copy may be; it constrains backup frequency, replication mode and journaling design. The relationship between them is where most programmes break down. An aggressive recovery point objective of minutes implies continuous or near-continuous replication and therefore a second site, transactional log shipping or storage-level mirroring, all of which carry cost, operational complexity and their own failure modes. An aggressive recovery time objective implies pre-provisioned capacity, automated failover, tested runbooks, current infrastructure as code and staff who have actually executed the procedure. Practitioners should treat both figures as properties of a service tier, published with the dependent services and any exclusions, and validate them with regular restoration and failover tests, because an untested objective is a claim rather than a capability. Finally, recovery objectives must account for integrity as well as availability: restoring clean data after destructive or ransomware activity requires immutable or offline copies whose own recovery point is understood.
objectives: You will be able to explain the difference between a recovery time objective and a recovery point objective using concrete service examples.

topics.title: S3 Bucket Policy
topics.summary: An S3 bucket policy is a JSON resource-based policy attached directly to an object storage bucket that controls which principals may perform which actions against that bucket and the objects inside it, optionally under conditions. Because it is resource-based it can grant access to principals outside the owning account, which is what makes it the standard mechanism for cross-account sharing, public content delivery, and service integrations such as logging or content delivery networks. The policy is evaluated together with identity-based policies, access control lists, block-public-access settings, and any service control policies, and an explicit deny in any of those layers prevents the action. The most consequential failure modes are well known: a wildcard principal combined with a wildcard action, a listing permission that reveals object names, a condition intended to restrict access that does not actually match the request shape, and an object that was public before public access blocks were enabled. Security teams monitor bucket policy changes as high severity events because a single edit can expose an entire dataset, and they combine policy review with classification of what the bucket holds, encryption requirements, versioning, logging and lifecycle rules. Effective practice is to prefer identity-based access and role assumption over cross-account wildcards, to enforce encryption and TLS in the policy itself, and to keep public access blocks on unless a documented exception exists.

topics.title: Salt
topics.summary: A salt is a unique, non-secret random value that is combined with an input before hashing so that identical inputs produce different digests, and it is a mandatory component of any password storage scheme. Salting defeats precomputed lookup structures such as rainbow tables and prevents an attacker who obtains a password database from learning which accounts share a password, because the same password hashed under different salts yields unrelated digests. Salts must be generated with a cryptographically secure random source, must be long enough to make collisions across a large user base statistically irrelevant, and must be stored alongside the resulting hash so verification remains possible. Salting does not slow down guessing, so it must be paired with an adaptive, memory-hard password hashing function; a salted fast hash is still a fast hash. Other contexts use the term differently. In key derivation a salt binds derived material to a context or generation, and in signature schemes a random per-signature value is sometimes loosely called a salt even though its uniqueness requirements are far stricter and its exposure is catastrophic rather than merely weakening. Common implementation defects include a single global salt shared by every account, salts derived from the username or a timestamp with insufficient entropy, truncated salts, salts generated with a non-cryptographic random function, and migration routines that re-hash existing passwords with a fixed salt during a framework upgrade.

topics.title: SAML
topics.summary: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service provider, and it remains the dominant federation protocol in enterprise and government environments. In the common web browser profile, an unauthenticated user is redirected to the identity provider, authenticates there, and is returned to the service provider carrying a signed assertion posted to an assertion consumer service endpoint. The service provider must validate the XML signature over the assertion, confirm the audience restriction matches its own entity identifier, verify the NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter conditions and the subject confirmation method, and reject any assertion that is replayed. Those checks are exactly where real breaches have occurred: libraries that parse untrusted XML without disabling external entity resolution, service providers that trust an unsigned assertion because it arrived over TLS, and implementations that accept a signature covering only part of the document while the attacker modifies another part. Signature wrapping, XML external entity injection, comment-field confusion and assertion replay are the recurring failure modes, and they are implementation defects rather than flaws in the protocol. Metadata, certificate rotation and clock skew are the operational problems that cause outages, while attribute mapping and name identifier format issues cause the subtle authorisation errors that let a user reach an application they should not. For defenders, SAML troubleshooting means reading identity provider sign-in logs alongside the service provider's own assertion handling, and treating any change in signing certificate or assertion consumer endpoint as a change worth alerting on.

topics.title: Scope and Rules of Engagement
topics.summary: Scope and rules of engagement are the written boundary that defines what may be tested, when, how, by whom, and what happens when something goes wrong; without documented authorisation from someone entitled to give it, the same activity is simply unauthorised access. A workable document names in-scope assets precisely enough to be unambiguous, lists excluded systems and data categories, and states testing windows with time zones. It defines permitted and prohibited techniques, for example whether denial-of-service testing, social engineering, physical entry or third-party hosted services are allowed, and it records the source addresses that defenders may allow-list. It sets escalation rules: emergency contacts on both sides, stop conditions such as discovery of an unrelated active intrusion or unexpected service degradation, and the obligation to report critical findings immediately rather than at the final readout. It also covers handling of sensitive data encountered during testing, evidence retention and destruction, deconfliction with the security operations centre, and the treatment of cloud or outsourced services where the provider may require separate notification under a shared responsibility model. Practically, the document protects the tester, the client and the defenders: it reduces false positives because the security operations centre knows when legitimate testing is scheduled, gives a tested route for stopping work, and provides the audit trail that regulators and insurers request. Scope should be reviewed whenever the environment changes materially.

topics.title: Secret Scanning
topics.summary: Secret scanning is the practice of detecting credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys and other sensitive material that has been committed to source control, embedded in build artifacts, written into logs, or left in configuration files and container layers. It operates in three places: pre-commit or pre-receive hooks that block a secret before it enters history, continuous scanning of repositories and pipelines that catches what got through, and artifact and runtime scanning that finds secrets baked into images or exposed through debug endpoints. Detection usually combines high-confidence provider-specific patterns with entropy heuristics and verification calls that confirm whether a discovered credential is still live. For a practising engineer the critical insight is that a secret written to version control should be treated as disclosed, because rewriting history does not undo the copies already fetched by every clone, fork and CI cache. The response is therefore rotation first, cleanup second, and only then rewriting history if it is worth the disruption. Effective programmes pair scanning with a secrets manager, short-lived credentials issued by workload identity, and pre-commit enforcement so the cheap prevention happens before the leak. The usual failure modes are scanning only the default branch, ignoring pipeline logs and issue attachments, alerting into a channel nobody owns, and treating the problem as solved once a scanner is installed while long-lived static keys remain the primary authentication method.
objectives: You will be able to explain why a credential committed to version control must be treated as disclosed and rotated rather than merely deleted.

topics.title: Secrets Manager
topics.summary: A secrets manager is a managed service for storing, controlling access to, and automatically rotating credentials such as database passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates and private keys, so that applications retrieve them at runtime instead of embedding them in code, images or configuration files. The service encrypts stored values with a key management service key, authorises retrieval with the platform identity system, versions every change, and can run scheduled rotation by invoking a function that creates a new credential and updates both the secret store and the target system. The security value comes from removing long-lived static secrets from build artefacts and repositories, from giving each workload a distinct credential that can be revoked individually, and from producing an audit trail of which identity read which secret and when. Practitioners must still address several hard problems. Workloads need a trustworthy identity to authenticate to the store, which in cloud environments usually means instance or workload identity rather than a bootstrap credential, otherwise the initial secret simply moves rather than disappearing. Caching matters because a rotated credential must not break running services, and rotation must be atomic enough that the old value stops working only after the new one is distributed. Also important are scoping read access so that one compromised workload cannot read every secret, detecting secrets that leak into repositories and images, and monitoring for unusual retrieval patterns.
objectives: You will be able to explain how runtime retrieval, versioning and automatic rotation remove static credentials from build artefacts.

topics.title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
topics.summary: The Secure Software Development Lifecycle is a structured way of weaving security activities into every phase of how software is planned, built, tested, released and maintained, rather than bolting security on at the end. In a mature SSDLC, requirements work establishes abuse cases and security acceptance criteria alongside functional ones, design work produces threat models and data-flow diagrams, implementation follows approved patterns and hardened libraries, verification combines static analysis, dependency review and dynamic testing, and release gates confirm that findings are triaged and that artifacts are signed. Operations closes the loop through monitoring, vulnerability intake and a defined patch cadence. For a practising security engineer the importance of the SSDLC is organisational rather than technical: it converts a series of ad hoc code reviews into a repeatable set of gates with named owners, entry and exit criteria, and evidence. That evidence is what makes the process auditable and what lets a security team argue for design-time intervention instead of endless reactive reviews. Typical failure modes are well known. Security work is defined as a gate rather than a service, so developers route around it. Threat models are produced once and never revisited when architecture changes. Tooling generates thousands of findings with no triage SLA, producing alert fatigue and eventual ignoring of the whole pipeline. Exceptions are granted verbally and never expire. The strongest programmes measure how early defects are caught and how quickly accepted risks are revisited, and they treat a blocked release as a process defect to be fixed, not a hero moment.

topics.title: SHA-256
topics.summary: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family that maps an arbitrary-length input to a fixed 256-bit digest, and it is specified in FIPS 180-4. It belongs to the Merkle-Damgard construction with a Davies-Meyer compression function, processing 512-bit message blocks through 64 rounds over eight 32-bit state words. The function is designed to be preimage resistant, second-preimage resistant and collision resistant, so it is suitable for integrity verification, digital signature pre-hashing, message authentication when combined with a key, and content addressing. It is not a password storage function: its speed makes offline guessing cheap, and password hashing should use a memory-hard, salted construction instead. Integrity use cases bring their own failures, because comparing digests with a non-constant-time equality check leaks information and because hashing a downloaded artifact without binding it to a trusted signature only proves the artifact matches whatever digest was served alongside it. File integrity monitoring, software supply chain attestation, SBOM identification and forensic evidence records all rely on SHA-256 as a common language, so defenders need to know when a digest comparison is meaningful and when it is merely decorative. Extension-attack resistance is also relevant: because plain SHA-256 is a Merkle-Damgard construction, naive secret-prefix MACs built from it are forgeable, which is precisely why HMAC exists.
objectives: Explain the Merkle-Damgard structure of SHA-256 and what preimage, second-preimage and collision resistance each protect.
Distinguish integrity verification from authenticity and state what additional control is required for a trustworthy digest comparison.
Identify why SHA-256 must not be used directly for password storage and which construction to use instead.
Explain how length extension defeats secret-prefix construction and why HMAC is the correct keyed alternative.
Apply SHA-256 correctly in forensic evidence handling, file integrity monitoring and software supply chain records.
Assess the risk from deprecated hash functions still present in a certificate or signature policy.

topics.title: Shared Responsibility Model
topics.summary: The shared responsibility model is the contractual and architectural division of security duties between a cloud service provider and its customer, in which the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in the cloud. The split is not uniform: for infrastructure as a service the provider owns the physical facilities, hosts, hypervisor and network fabric, while the customer owns the guest operating system, patching, identity, data and application; for platform as a service the provider absorbs the runtime and middleware, leaving the customer identity, configuration and data; for software as a service the provider operates nearly the whole stack and the customer retains responsibility for accounts, access grants, data classification and how the service is used. Security professionals rely on the model because most cloud incidents occur in the customer's portion of the stack, particularly identity misconfiguration, overly permissive policies, exposed storage and unpatched workloads. Applying it demands more than reading a marketing diagram: teams must map each control in their own framework to a named owner, record the evidence source, and confirm the split for every managed service they adopt, since the boundary shifts service by service and even feature by feature. Auditors expect this mapping to be documented and traceable, and incident responders need it to know who to contact and what telemetry the provider will and will not expose.

topics.title: SIEM
topics.summary: A Security Information and Event Management platform is a centralised system that ingests logs and telemetry from across an estate, normalises them into a common schema, correlates events over time, and evaluates detection rules to raise alerts that a security operations centre can triage. In practice a SIEM is three coupled capabilities: collection and parsing, a searchable hot and warm store with a query language, and a rules and correlation engine with alerting, case management and reporting on top. Its value depends far less on the vendor than on data quality and coverage. A rule is only as good as the fields it can rely on, so normalisation decisions, timestamp handling, and reliable identity resolution across endpoints, identity providers, cloud control planes and network sensors determine whether detections are precise or noisy. Detection engineers therefore treat the SIEM as a product with a content pipeline: they map log sources to what MITRE ATT&CK techniques they can observe, write and version rules, measure precision and recall against known-good and known-bad telemetry, and retire content that only produces fatigue. Common failure modes are predictable. Ingesting everything without enrichment produces volume without context; ignoring time zone and clock skew breaks correlation windows; broad rules with single-event triggers flood analysts; and quiet log sources create blind spots that adversaries exploit precisely because nobody alerted. Effective operators tune the platform deliberately, using allow-lists with expiry dates, entity risk scoring rather than raw severity, and periodic purple-team validation to prove that a technique which should be detected actually is.

topics.title: Sigma Rules
topics.summary: Sigma is a vendor-neutral, YAML-based signature format for describing log-based detections, intended to be written once and translated into the query language of whichever SIEM or log platform an organisation runs. A rule separates two concerns that many native rule formats entangle: the detection logic, expressed as named search identifiers with field modifiers such as contains, startswith, endswith, base64offset, re and cidr, and a condition that combines those identifiers with boolean and aggregation operators. Around the logic sits metadata that makes the rule maintainable and machine-readable: a title and description, a stable id, a status, a logsource block naming the product, service or category the rule requires, references, an author, a date, a level and tags that commonly include ATT&CK technique identifiers. The logsource abstraction is what enables portability, because the translator maps product and category onto concrete field names for the target platform, for example expanding a Windows process creation rule into the vendor's specific process, command-line and parent-process fields. The pipelining feature turns Sigma into a small language for composed detections: a base rule can be chained with filters that add exclusions, or several rules combined to require correlated events. Practical advantages are reviewable diffs, reuse of a rule estate across multiple platforms, and coverage tracking. Practical limitations deserve equal weight: translation quality varies, so a converted rule must be validated on real telemetry before it is trusted; generic field mappings can lose fidelity for platforms whose schema differs substantially; and Sigma describes log detections only, so it says nothing about network, memory or endpoint-behaviour detection that never reaches a log pipeline. Treat Sigma as a shared, reviewable source of truth rather than as a guarantee of deployable accuracy.

topics.title: SOAR
topics.summary: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response is the discipline and tooling category concerned with turning detection output into repeatable action. Where a SIEM answers what happened, a SOAR platform asks what should happen next and then does as much of it as is safe without a human. Three capabilities are usually bundled: orchestration, meaning integration with other systems through APIs and playbooks; automation, meaning execution of those playbooks with minimal analyst input; and response, meaning the enrichment, containment and case-management actions that result. Typical first automations are unglamorous and high value: enriching an alert with asset ownership, user directory data, threat-intelligence reputation and recent sign-in history; de-duplicating and grouping related alerts into one case; notifying the right on-call queue with a consistent summary; and posting a structured timeline into the ticketing system. The hard part is not the integration, it is the decision boundary. Automations that take destructive action such as disabling an account, isolating a host or blocking an indicator can cause outages and can be abused by an adversary who learns what triggers them, so mature teams stage actions by confidence and reversibility, require approval for anything irreversible, and log every automated decision with its inputs for later review. SOAR also institutionalises response quality: a playbook is a documented, versioned procedure, so junior analysts execute the same steps as seniors, and post-incident review can show exactly which step failed. Common pitfalls include automating a process nobody had defined, brittle integrations with no error handling, and relying on threat-intelligence indicators that expire before the playbook runs.
objectives: You will be able to distinguish orchestration, automation and response capabilities and map each to concrete SOC workflows.

topics.title: SOC 2
topics.summary: SOC 2 is an attestation report issued under the AICPA Trust Services Criteria that describes how a service organisation designs and, in a Type 2 report, operates controls relevant to the security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy of customer data. It is not a certification and there is no pass or fail: an independent CPA firm expresses an opinion on whether management's description of its system is accurate and whether the selected controls operated effectively over a defined review period. Two report types exist. A Type 1 report speaks to control design at a single point in time and is frequently used to unblock early enterprise deals; a Type 2 report covers design and operating effectiveness across a window, commonly three to twelve months, and is what mature buyers demand. The Common Criteria, organised around control environment, communication and information, risk assessment, monitoring activities and control activities, map closely to how engineering teams already work, which is why SOC 2 readiness often reduces to formalising change management, access review, vulnerability management, incident response and vendor risk processes that already exist informally. For practitioners the practical work is defining the system boundary, producing a control matrix with named owners, gathering evidence on a schedule rather than in a panic, and being precise in the description of the system. Bridge letters and complementary user entity controls matter because responsibilities split between the provider and the customer.

topics.title: Software Bill of Materials
topics.summary: A software bill of materials is a machine-readable inventory of the components that make up a piece of software, typically listing each package with its name, version, supplier, unique identifier and the relationships that describe how components nest. The two dominant interchange formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, both of which support integrity hashes and licence metadata, and both of which can be produced per build or per released artifact. The operational purpose is rapid answerability: when a critical vulnerability or a compromised package is disclosed, an organisation that holds accurate SBOMs can determine exposure in minutes by querying inventories rather than by rebuilding and reviewing manifests by hand. That is also why SBOM accuracy, completeness and freshness matter far more than format choice. An SBOM generated once at a release and never regenerated drifts from reality as soon as a hotfix rebuilds a base image. For a practising engineer the practical problems are transitive completeness, identifier normalisation across ecosystems, correlating components to vulnerability data with trustworthy package identifiers, and handling the volume of inventory data without turning it into an unreadable dump. Useful programmes generate SBOMs automatically in the build pipeline, store them alongside the artifact they describe, sign them so their provenance can be checked, and test the whole path with a tabletop exercise that asks how fast the organisation could answer a specific exposure question. Formats without ingestion tooling or a query surface produce compliance artefacts that nobody can use during an incident.
