topics.title: Software Composition Analysis
topics.summary: Software composition analysis is the automated identification of third-party and open-source components in a codebase or built artifact, together with an assessment of the known vulnerabilities, licence obligations and maintenance risks attached to those components. A typical SCA engine resolves the dependency graph from manifests and lock files, matches resolved versions against vulnerability advisories, and reports the direct and transitive path that introduces each affected package, which matters because most findings arrive through dependencies the team never chose explicitly. Modern supply-chain expectations extend SCA to artifact-level analysis of containers and binaries, where the tool inspects package databases inside an image rather than trusting the build manifest alone. For a practising engineer the hard parts are reachability, version-range ambiguity and remediation logistics. A flagged transitive dependency may never be loaded at runtime, an advisory may apply only to a configuration the project does not use, and the fixed version may be blocked by an incompatible major upgrade somewhere else in the graph. A workable programme therefore gates on new critical findings with an available fix, tracks unfixable findings as accepted risk with an expiry, and uses override or exclusion mechanisms deliberately rather than pinning stale versions forever. The recurring failure modes are reporting the same vulnerable library dozens of times because it appears in several images, ignoring transitive dependencies entirely, and treating an empty scan result on a project that vendors its dependencies as evidence of safety.

topics.title: SSO
topics.summary: Single sign-on (SSO) is an authentication architecture in which one identity provider authenticates a principal once and then issues assertions or tokens that multiple relying-party applications accept in place of their own credential stores. Instead of every application holding a password database, each application trusts a federated identity provider such as Entra ID, Okta, Ping or a Keycloak deployment, and receives a signed statement about who the user is and, increasingly, what context the authentication occurred in. The security benefit is concentrated and easy to understate: credentials live in one hardened location with one MFA policy, one lockout policy, one session lifetime and one revocation path, so deprovisioning a leaver becomes a single disable action rather than a hunt through dozens of local account stores. The corresponding risk is that the identity provider becomes a tier-zero system whose compromise grants access to every federated application, and that the session cookie or refresh token becomes the real credential that adversaries pursue. Most real-world SSO incidents therefore involve token theft, consent phishing against the authorisation endpoint, misconfigured assertion validation on the relying-party side, or stale accounts that survive offboarding because a shadow application was never federated. Practitioners must be able to reason about session lifetime, token binding, sign-out propagation, identifier normalisation and the difference between an application that validates a signature correctly and one that merely decodes it. Logging quality matters here: the identity provider's sign-in and audit logs, not the application logs, are usually the authoritative record of who authenticated and from where.

topics.title: Statement of Applicability
topics.summary: A Statement of Applicability is the document that records, for every control in the applicable catalogue, whether the organisation includes it, why that decision was made, and where the implementation lives. In an ISO/IEC 27001 management system it is a mandatory artefact that ties the risk assessment and risk treatment process to the controls actually operated, and it acts as the table of contents an auditor follows through the rest of the evidence. A defensible entry contains the control reference and title, an inclusion or exclusion decision, the justification for that decision, the implementation status, a reference to the specific implementation such as a policy section, system configuration or process document, and the control owner. Exclusions are where most documents fail. An organisation cannot legitimately exclude a control simply because it is inconvenient; the justification must show that the control is not applicable to the scope, that the risk it addresses does not exist in the scope, or that an alternative treatment reduces the risk to an acceptable level. Practitioners should keep the statement traceable in both directions: every selected control should map back to at least one assessed risk, and every treated risk should map forward to at least one control or a documented acceptance. Version control matters because the document is audited against a period, and reviewers should be able to reconstruct what the statement said when a given audit took place. It is also useful beyond certification as a concise inventory of the control estate.

topics.title: Static Application Security Testing
topics.summary: Static application security testing is the automated analysis of source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program, looking for patterns that indicate a security defect such as injection sinks reached by untrusted input, unsafe deserialisation, hard-coded cryptographic material or broken access control. Modern SAST engines combine pattern matching with dataflow and taint tracking, so a rule can follow a value from a source such as an HTTP parameter through assignments and function calls to a sink such as a database query. Because it works on the code itself, SAST can find defects on code paths that no test exercises, and it can be run on every commit, which makes it attractive as a pull-request gate. Its central limitation is the false positive rate: without whole-program context and runtime configuration, the engine cannot know whether a path is reachable or whether a sanitiser it cannot model already applies. For a practising engineer the discipline is therefore triage, not detection. A workable programme baselines existing findings, gates only on new high-confidence rules, tunes rules per repository, suppresses with expiring annotations, and assigns rule ownership so that noisy rules are fixed rather than ignored. The common failure modes are treating the raw finding count as a metric, enabling every rule at once and drowning the team, running SAST only on a nightly build so feedback arrives too late to change the design, and allowing unbounded suppressions that silently disable entire rule classes. Pairing SAST with dependency analysis, dynamic testing and code review covers the gaps each tool leaves.
objectives: You will be able to explain how taint tracking differs from pattern matching and what each approach can and cannot detect.
You will be able to configure a SAST scan as a pull-request gate that blocks on new high-confidence findings without failing on legacy debt.

topics.title: STIX and TAXII
topics.summary: STIX is a structured language for expressing cyber threat intelligence and TAXII is the transport protocol that moves it between organisations, and together they are the standards that make machine-to-machine sharing practical. STIX is a graph-based data model, serialised as JSON, whose objects fall into domain objects, cyber observable objects and relationship objects. Domain objects describe high-level intelligence such as threat actors, campaigns, intrusion sets, malware, attack patterns, indicators, reports, courses of action and identities. Cyber observable objects describe the technical artefacts an analyst records, including files, processes, network traffic, domain names and registry keys. Relationship objects connect them, so an indicator can reference an attack pattern and a report can bundle the whole product. Patterning gives indicators a precise, testable expression language, which is what allows a detection platform to consume them without hand translation. TAXII is the transport layer: a client polls or subscribes to a server, and the server exposes API roots containing collections of STIX objects. TAXII collections are browsable sets of objects, while channels support publish and subscribe exchange. Versioning and identifier discipline matter operationally. Every object carries a stable identifier and a modified timestamp, and consumers deduplicate and resolve updates on that basis, so sloppy identifier generation causes silent divergence between sharing partners. Real deployments also need trust decisions, because receiving a bundle is receiving attacker-influenced content. Analysts must honour handling markings that express sharing caveats, and they must decide what tooling does when an object is malformed or uses extensions the consumer does not implement. A working pipeline therefore combines schema validation, deduplication, enrichment, confidence handling and a documented policy for what is automatically blocked, what is only hunted, and what is discarded.

topics.title: STRIDE
topics.summary: STRIDE is a threat enumeration mnemonic that groups threats into six categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. It was developed so that designers without a deep attack background could still systematically ask the right questions about each element of a data-flow diagram. The categories map neatly onto security properties, which is what makes the framework teachable: spoofing attacks authenticity, tampering attacks integrity, repudiation attacks non-repudiation of actions, information disclosure attacks confidentiality, denial of service attacks availability and elevation of privilege attacks authorisation. In practice the mnemonic is applied per element and per flow, with a common convention that processes, data stores, data flows, external entities and trust boundaries each attract a characteristic subset of the six. For a practising engineer STRIDE is most useful as a completeness check rather than a rating scheme, because it deliberately says nothing about likelihood or impact and produces no prioritisation on its own. Teams normally pair it with a scoring method and with attack-library mapping to connect abstract categories to observed adversary behaviour. The known weaknesses are worth stating plainly. STRIDE was framed for classical component-and-network designs and fits cloud identity, serverless and machine-learning pipelines awkwardly. It has no privacy or supply-chain category. Its output is highly dependent on the facilitator's skill, and groups tend to over-report the categories they understand and under-report repudiation and availability. Reviewing a STRIDE session for concrete preconditions and observable failure modes is the cheapest way to raise its quality.
objectives: You will be able to name the six STRIDE categories and state which security property each one attacks.
You will be able to apply the mnemonic element by element to a data-flow diagram without missing entire categories.
You will be able to explain the conventional mapping between diagram element types and the STRIDE categories most likely to apply.
You will be able to convert a bare STRIDE label into a concrete threat statement with preconditions and impact.
You will be able to identify design situations where STRIDE fits poorly, such as cloud identity graphs and machine-learning pipelines.
You will be able to critique a completed STRIDE worksheet for over-reporting and under-reporting bias.

topics.title: Supply Chain Attack
topics.summary: A supply chain attack is an intrusion that reaches a target indirectly by compromising something the target trusts: a software dependency, a build system, a package registry, an update mechanism, a managed service provider, or a hardware or firmware supplier. The attraction for an adversary is leverage. One compromised package or build job can yield access to thousands of downstream organisations, and the resulting code or update often arrives already signed, already approved and already allow-listed. Documented patterns include malicious package versions published to public registries, typosquatted and dependency-confusion package names that resolve to attacker-controlled artifacts, compromised maintainer accounts, injected code in build pipelines that never touches the repository, and tampered vendor updates delivered through legitimate channels. For a practising engineer the defences are layered and mostly about provenance rather than detection: pin and verify dependencies with lock files and integrity hashes, generate and review build provenance, require signed artifacts with verification at install and deploy time, restrict who can publish and with what credentials, and monitor registries and build systems as production infrastructure. Attribution is genuinely hard because the activity happens inside trusted workflows; logs from build systems, registry publish events and artifact signing services often provide the only visibility. The most common organisational failure is assuming that internal dependence on well-known vendors removes the risk, when in practice the exposure is determined by how much unverified code and configuration is consumed, and how quickly a compromised component could be identified and removed from production.
objectives: You will be able to describe the main supply chain attack patterns, including malicious packages, dependency confusion, compromised maintainers and build pipeline injection.
You will be able to explain why signed and approved artifacts still require verification and provenance checks rather than blind trust.

You will be able to assess an organisation's time to identify and remove a compromised dependency from production.
You will be able to distinguish third-party and vendor risk that is genuinely mitigated from assurance that rests on reputation alone.

topics.title: Tabletop Exercise
topics.summary: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based rehearsal in which a team walks through a realistic scenario and makes the decisions it would face during a real incident, without touching production systems. Participants are given an inject, such as a triggering event involving a suspicious file server notification, an unexpected identity consent grant, or a reported business email compromise, and the facilitator advances the scenario in stages while asking who would be notified, what evidence would be collected, who has authority to isolate a system, how customers or regulators would be informed, and where the organisation's own procedures break down. Its value lies less in testing tooling than in exposing the seams between teams: security operations, IT operations, legal, communications, HR, executive leadership and third-party providers all have to agree on roles before a real crisis forces the question. Well-run tabletops are grounded in a written scenario and explicit objectives, use a documented playbook as the reference standard, and produce findings with named owners and dates. They differ from functional and simulation exercises, which do exercise live systems and response tooling, and most mature programmes alternate between the two. Frequency and scope should follow risk profile and regulatory expectation, and results feed back into the incident response plan. Because these exercises surface uncomfortable truths, including unclear decision rights, untested contact trees and unowned log sources, their findings are only valuable if remediation is tracked like any other risk treatment.
objectives: Define the purpose of a tabletop exercise and distinguish it from functional, simulation and full-scale testing.
Design a scenario, objective set and inject sequence grounded in risks the organisation actually faces.
Facilitate an exercise that surfaces unclear decision rights, communication gaps and untested assumptions.
Use the incident response playbook as the reference standard and capture where practice diverges from it.

Convert observations into findings with named owners, due dates and a tracked remediation path.

topics.title: Terraform Drift
topics.summary: Terraform drift is the divergence between the infrastructure state recorded in a Terraform state file and the actual configuration of the resources deployed in a cloud account, arising when something changes a resource outside the pipeline that created it. The change might be a console fix during an incident, a script in a legacy automation path, a provider-side default that shifted, an imported resource never brought under management, or an attacker deliberately relaxing a control such as a firewall rule or bucket policy. Drift matters because the infrastructure-as-code repository stops being a trustworthy description of reality: a plan run after drift will silently revert the out-of-band change, reviews of pull requests no longer describe the live environment, and a security control that appears present in code may have been removed in production. Detection normally relies on scheduled plans or a refresh-only plan that reports differences without applying them, remote state with locking to prevent concurrent writes, and consistent provider versions so that cosmetic differences do not obscure real ones. Handling drift requires judgement rather than blind application, because some drift is legitimate emergency remediation that should be codified back into the repository, while unreviewed drift in security-relevant attributes is an incident indicator. Mature teams track drift as a metric, alert on changes to sensitive attributes, and reconcile by importing or amending code rather than by overwriting production.

topics.title: Threat Hunting Hypothesis
topics.summary: A threat hunting hypothesis is a falsifiable statement about adversary behaviour that is expected to be present in an environment if a specific technique is being used, written so that telemetry can confirm or refute it. It is the element that separates hunting from browsing dashboards. A usable hypothesis names the behaviour rather than a tool, states the observable artifacts that behaviour would create, identifies the data sources required to see those artifacts, and defines in advance what evidence would count as a hit and what would count as absence. A well-formed example is that an adversary using valid accounts for lateral movement will produce authentication events from atypical source hosts or at atypical times for that identity, which can be tested against identity logs joined to asset inventory. The discipline around the hypothesis is as important as its content. Before hunting, the analyst verifies the required log source is actually collected, parsed and retained for the period of interest, because a great many hunts end with the discovery that the question cannot be answered with current telemetry. During the hunt, findings are documented as they are made, including negative results, since knowing that a technique was sought and not found is itself informative for coverage decisions. After the hunt, hits are converted into durable value: a new or tuned detection rule, a logged coverage gap with an owner, or a data source onboarding request. Hunting without that loop produces interesting sessions and no lasting improvement, which is why mature programmes track hunts by hypothesis, data source, technique coverage and number of detections produced rather than by hours spent.
objectives: You will be able to write a falsifiable hunting hypothesis that names behaviour, observable artifacts, required data sources and refutation criteria.
You will be able to derive hypotheses from ATT&CK techniques, threat intelligence reporting and known gaps in existing detection coverage.

topics.title: Threat Modelling
topics.summary: Threat modelling is a structured design-time technique for reasoning about what can go wrong in a system, who would want to make it go wrong, and which controls would reduce that risk, producing a documented set of threats that engineering teams can act on. The usual workflow has four parts: scope the system and draw its data flows across trust boundaries, enumerate plausible threats against each element and flow, rate them by likelihood and impact, and record a decision for each one as mitigate, transfer, accept or eliminate. Frameworks such as STRIDE help teams avoid blind spots by prompting per category, while attack-library mapping grounds the exercise in techniques that real adversaries use. For a practising engineer the value is not the diagram but the argument it forces: where does authentication actually terminate, which component can impersonate another, what happens when a message is replayed, who can read this store, and what does the audit trail miss. Good threat models are living artifacts tied to architecture decisions, reviewed when data flows or trust boundaries change, and written in language the delivery team already uses. Failures are predictable. The exercise becomes a compliance ritual with no owner and no follow-through. Models are built by a single architect and never validated against the running system. Threats are described abstractly, with no asset, actor or preconditions, so no control follows. Ratings are inflated until everything is critical and prioritisation collapses. Structured abuse-case derivation, adversarial review by a second team, and tracking threat entries to backlog items with acceptance criteria are what separate a useful model from a wall diagram.
objectives: You will be able to scope a system into components, data stores, flows and trust boundaries before enumerating any threat.

topics.title: Timeline Analysis
topics.summary: Timeline analysis is the forensic practice of ordering events drawn from multiple evidence sources onto a single, comparable chronological axis so that an investigator can establish sequence, duration, causality and gaps in an intrusion. It is the discipline that turns a pile of artefacts into a story: which account logged in first, when the payload was written, what process created it, whether an outbound connection preceded or followed credential theft, and how long the adversary held access before anyone noticed. Source material includes file system metadata such as creation, modification and access times, file system journals and change records, registry hives and their key last-write values, operating system event and process telemetry, authentication logs from identity providers, browser and application histories, shell histories, container and cloud control-plane audit logs, and network flow or proxy records. The hard parts are rarely tooling and usually interpretation: clocks drift, time zones differ, some sources record local time while others use UTC, several timestamps are updated by ordinary activity, and artefacts can be deliberately manipulated by an adversary who understands the same metadata. A sound timeline states its normalisation decisions, records uncertainty rather than smoothing it away, and distinguishes corroborated events from single-source ones. Analysts typically build a full super-timeline for scoping and a filtered, focused timeline to answer one specific question such as dwell time, lateral movement path or data access. The output feeds incident scoping, legal and regulatory reporting, and detection engineering.

topics.title: TLS Inspection
topics.summary: TLS inspection is the practice of terminating or intercepting encrypted sessions inside a controlled boundary so that security controls can examine the plaintext that would otherwise be opaque. Because most malicious traffic now uses the same transport encryption as legitimate traffic, signature-based network detection, data loss prevention and URL filtering are blind without decryption. Two broad techniques exist. An active proxy terminates the client connection, presents a certificate the client must trust, and opens a separate connection to the server, while passive decryption uses key material or session keys supplied out of band to decrypt copies of traffic without altering the flow. Both depend on trust: active interception requires a private certificate authority whose root is installed on every endpoint, which makes that authority a high-value target and a frequent source of operational breakage when applications use certificate pinning, mutual TLS or embedded trust stores. Inspection is not free. Decryption consumes substantial processor and memory capacity, so throughput, latency and sizing change materially, and uninspected encrypted traffic becomes a growing blind spot as the inspection ratio falls. Privacy and legal constraints are equally important, because intercepting employee banking, health or personal traffic carries regulatory exposure in many jurisdictions, and an internal certificate authority must be protected, logged and audited like any other signing authority. Bypass categories are necessary for pinned applications, software update channels and regulated third parties, and each bypass should have a documented owner. Monitoring must cover the inspection platform itself, since an expired root certificate, a failed cipher negotiation or a silent fail-open policy can disable decryption without anyone noticing.
objectives: You will be able to compare active interception with passive decryption and state the trust requirements of each.

topics.title: True and False Positives
topics.summary: A true positive is an alert that correctly identifies the behaviour the detection was written to find; a false positive is an alert raised on activity that does not match that behaviour. The pairs that matter operationally are richer than that binary. A true positive may still be benign in context, which is why analysts distinguish a detection that fired correctly on authorised administrative work from one that fired on genuine adversary activity. A false negative is the more dangerous case: malicious behaviour occurred and nothing alerted, either because the log source was absent, the rule logic did not cover the variant, or the telemetry was normalised into a shape the rule never matched. Detection engineers therefore evaluate content on two axes, precision, meaning what fraction of alerts are genuine, and recall, meaning what fraction of real occurrences are caught. Improving one usually costs the other, which is why tuning is an explicit trade-off documented with its rationale rather than an accumulating set of exclusions. Practical classification requires ground truth, and ground truth requires work: confirming with asset owners whether a process is sanctioned, checking change records for scheduled jobs, validating whether an account was legitimately used, or replaying controlled test activity to prove a rule fires. The vocabulary also covers near misses and true negatives, and it is worth stating plainly that a closed alert labelled false positive is a claim of fact, not a dismissal. Teams that keep a labelled corpus of past alerts, including the reasoning, build the empirical basis for tuning, for measuring detection coverage, and for demonstrating improvement over time.
objectives: You will be able to classify alerts into true positive, false positive and false negative with an evidence-based rationale rather than intuition.

topics.title: TTP
topics.summary: A TTP is the behavioural layer of threat intelligence: the tactics, techniques and procedures an adversary uses to achieve an objective, expressed independently of the specific tools, hashes or domains observed in any single intrusion. Tactics describe the goal, such as gaining initial access or exfiltrating data. Techniques describe how the goal is achieved, such as abusing a valid account, injecting into a trusted process, or tunnelling command and control inside a protocol the network already permits. Procedures describe the specific implementation an actor prefers, including the exact command line shape, the order of operations and the operational security habits around them. Because TTPs are constrained by how software and operating systems actually work, they change far more slowly than infrastructure. An actor can re-register a domain overnight but cannot easily abandon the need to persist after reboot or to move laterally with stolen credentials. That asymmetry is why behavioural intelligence retains value for months or years while atomic indicators decay in hours, and why the widely used pyramid of pain ranks TTPs near the top for the difficulty they cause an adversary when defenders detect them. In practice, TTP intelligence is codified as technique mappings, detection-as-code rules, hunting hypotheses and control requirements rather than as blocklists. The defensive translation step matters: a report stating that an actor abuses signed system binaries is not actionable until an engineer identifies which telemetry would capture it, which legitimate activity resembles it, and what the detection will cost in analyst time. TTP-driven detection also supports coverage reasoning, because defenders can measure which techniques are instrumented and which are blind spots. The main risks are over-generalisation, where a technique is treated as unique to one group, and abstraction drift, where a mapping is recorded without the procedure detail that would make it detectable.
objectives: You will be able to separate tactics, techniques and procedures and explain why each layer has a different detection lifetime.

topics.title: Volatile Data
topics.summary: Volatile data is state that exists only while a system is powered, running or connected: processor registers and cache contents, random access memory, running processes and their loaded modules, open network sockets and routing tables, logged-on sessions, mounted encrypted volumes, clipboard contents, and in-memory credentials or keys. Because it disappears on shutdown, reboot, logoff, container termination or network disconnection, it is both the most perishable and often the most probative evidence in an investigation. Memory is where fileless malware, injected code, decryption keys, command-and-control configuration and unencrypted artefacts frequently live, and where a rootkit's tampering may be visible even when the file system looks clean. Established practice follows an order of volatility, collecting the fastest-decaying sources first: processor and memory state, then network and process state, then temporary file systems, then disk, then archival media. Acquisition must be planned before the responder types a single command, because ordinary administrative actions such as listing directories, opening a file or running a built-in utility overwrite memory and alter timestamps. Captured data is hashed, documented and stored under chain of custody, and analysis must account for the fact that memory contents are a snapshot of a live and constantly changing system. In virtualised and cloud environments the practical techniques differ, relying on hypervisor snapshots, managed capture APIs and provider tooling, but the ordering logic and the documentation obligations do not change.
objectives: Classify data sources by volatility and apply the correct collection order at an incident scene.
Explain why memory, session and network state often carry evidence that the file system does not.

topics.title: VPN
topics.summary: A virtual private network establishes an encrypted tunnel between endpoints or gateways so that traffic crossing an untrusted network cannot be read or modified in transit, and so that the endpoints can be treated as members of a logical private network. Site-to-site tunnels join branch offices or cloud networks using IPsec or comparable protocols, while remote-access VPNs connect individual users through a concentrator that authenticates them and places them on an internal subnet. The security properties come from the cryptographic handshake, mutual authentication of peers, and integrity protection of each packet, but the trust model is the weak point. A remote-access VPN that grants full internal reachability reproduces the flat network for every connected device, so a compromised laptop inherits the same access as a workstation on site. Split tunnelling compounds the problem by allowing the endpoint to talk directly to the internet while holding an internal tunnel, which turns the endpoint into a bridge between the two. Operationally, VPN concentrators concentrate risk. They are internet-facing, they authenticate users, and they are frequently targeted by credential stuffing, password spraying and exploitation of unpatched appliances, so they must be patched aggressively, protected with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, and monitored for unusual session behaviour such as logins from unexpected geographies or impossible travel. Capacity planning matters because a saturated concentrator becomes an availability incident. Many organisations are reducing reliance on broad network-level access in favour of application-level access brokers that authorise a specific service rather than placing a device on the internal network. Where VPNs remain, good practice includes per-user authorisation profiles, session timeouts, device posture checks before access is granted, and complete logging of tunnel establishment and termination.
objectives: You will be able to explain what a VPN does and does not protect once a device is connected.
You will be able to compare site-to-site and remote-access designs and their trust assumptions.
You will be able to assess split tunnelling and full tunnelling against endpoint risk.
You will be able to triage VPN authentication logs for spraying, stuffing and anomalous session behaviour.
You will be able to harden a concentrator with multi-factor authentication, patching discipline and per-user profiles.
You will be able to justify moving sensitive access from network-level tunnels to application-level brokers.

topics.title: WDAC and AppLocker
topics.summary: Windows Defender Application Control and AppLocker are the two application control mechanisms Microsoft provides for Windows, and understanding their difference matters more than knowing either in isolation. AppLocker is policy-based, configured through Group Policy or a similar management channel, and enforces rules that permit or deny executables, installers, scripts, packaged applications and dynamically loaded libraries on the basis of publisher signature, file path or file hash. It is straightforward to operate, easy to audit in a reporting-only mode before enforcement, and widely used because it can be piloted on a subset of users without touching the underlying platform configuration. WDAC operates at a lower level and expresses policy as a signed binary policy that the kernel enforces, which makes it substantially harder for a local administrator or a malicious process with administrative rights to disable, and it can be used to protect the integrity of the code that is allowed to run at boot and in the kernel. In practice the two are complementary and both are frequently deployed together, because WDAC's strength is its resistance to tampering while AppLocker's strength is granular, easily reasoned-about rules for user-facing applications. The hardest part of either deployment is not the technology but the operational discipline: maintaining accurate inventory of what legitimately runs, designing publisher-based rules rather than brittle path rules, adopting managed installer concepts so that approved deployment tooling can introduce new software without policy churn, running in audit mode long enough to catch the long tail, and planning a change process for the inevitable application that must be allowed next week. A policy that is too permissive provides no protection; one that is too brittle is bypassed by an exception list nobody reviews.
objectives: Compare WDAC and AppLocker across enforcement location, tamper resistance, rule granularity and management model.
Choose between publisher, path and hash rule types and explain the maintainability consequences of each.
Design an audit-then-enforce rollout that gathers the legitimate software inventory before blocking anything.
Explain how managed installer and signed policy concepts reduce operational churn after enforcement.
Detect attempted policy tampering or the abuse of allowed binaries to execute unapproved code.
Plan an exception and change process that keeps the policy tight without blocking business operations.

topics.title: XDR
topics.summary: Extended Detection and Response (XDR) is the practice of fusing telemetry from multiple security domains — endpoint, identity, email, cloud workload, network and SaaS audit logs — into a single detection and response platform so that correlated evidence from several sources produces higher-fidelity incidents than any one source could alone. Where EDR answers host-level questions, XDR is defined by the correlation itself: an email gateway recording a delivered message with an external link, an identity provider logging a successful sign-in from an unusual geography with a satisfied multi-factor challenge, and a cloud audit log showing a new OAuth grant to an unfamiliar application become one incident rather than three unrelated alerts. That consolidation is attractive because it directly attacks alert fatigue and the mean time to detect, but it also concentrates risk. A single platform that holds identity, email and endpoint data becomes a high-value target, its normalisation pipeline can silently drop fields that a responder later needs, and its correlation logic is often opaque enough that analysts cannot explain why two events were joined. Many vendors ship a native XDR that works best with their own sensors, and open or hybrid approaches exist that stitch together existing tools through a data lake and a detection-as-code layer. Practitioners should evaluate XDR on ingestion coverage and latency, schema fidelity, the ability to write and version custom detections, the depth of the response actions available per integration, and how gracefully the platform degrades when one source goes dark. XDR does not replace investigation discipline; it changes where the analyst starts.
objectives: Define XDR precisely and distinguish it from EDR, SIEM and SOAR by the correlation and response scope each provides.
Map the telemetry sources that must be onboarded before cross-domain correlation can produce actionable incidents.
Explain how identity, email and endpoint signals combine to raise confidence above that of any single-domain alert.
Assess schema normalisation risk, including field loss and timestamp skew that degrade correlated detections.
Write and version a custom cross-domain detection rule and describe how it should be tested before production rollout.
Evaluate a vendor XDR deployment against data concentration, response-action depth and graceful degradation requirements.

topics.title: YARA
topics.summary: YARA is a pattern-matching language and tool for identifying files and memory regions by their content, widely used by malware analysts, incident responders and detection engineers to classify samples by family, capability or campaign. A rule consists of a metadata block, a set of string definitions, and a boolean condition that decides whether the rule matches. Strings may be text, hexadecimal byte patterns with wildcards and jumps, or regular expressions, and each can carry modifiers that change matching semantics, such as nocase for case-insensitivity, wide for UTF-16 encodings, ascii, fullword to prevent substring hits, and xor to handle simple single-byte obfuscation. Conditions can reference string counts, offsets, file size, the values of the PE header, module imports, and matches from other rules through the of and for...of constructs, which allows composition from weak indicators into stronger composite logic. That compositional ability is the feature that separates useful rules from fragile ones: a single suspicious string is weak evidence, whereas a condition requiring several independent strings, a specific file size range and a particular section characteristic resists trivial modification. YARA is also a source of operational mistakes. Rules written against one sample overfit and miss variants; broad string sets produce false positives across legitimate software; large rule sets slow scanning to the point of being unusable and are often loaded with performance warnings that operators ignore; and short strings without fullword matching collide with unrelated binaries. Authoring quality therefore means testing rules against known-good corpora before deployment, documenting their provenance, retaining a rationale for each indicator, and treating a match as an investigative lead that must be corroborated rather than as automatic proof of malice.
objectives: You will be able to explain the structure of a YARA rule and the roles of the metadata, strings and condition blocks.
You will be able to select appropriate string modifiers and explain how each changes matching behaviour and false-positive risk.
You will be able to write compositional conditions that require independent evidence instead of relying on a single weak indicator.
You will be able to test a rule set against known-good files and quantify the false positives before deployment.
You will be able to identify overfitting to a single sample and rewrite the rule so that it generalises to likely variants.
You will be able to treat a YARA match as an investigative lead and state the corroboration needed before calling a file malicious.
You will be able to assess the performance cost of a rule set and reduce scanning overhead without losing meaningful coverage.

topics.title: Zero Trust
topics.summary: Zero trust is a security model that removes implicit trust from network location and instead evaluates every request against identity, device posture, context and policy before granting the least access needed. The traditional perimeter assumed that anything inside the corporate network was trustworthy and anything outside was not, and remote work, cloud services and mobile devices destroyed that assumption. Zero trust replaces it with explicit verification, so a request from a corporate subnet receives no more privilege than the same request from a home network. Core components include a strong identity provider with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, a policy decision point that consumes signals from device management and threat detection, segmentation that constrains lateral movement, and pervasive logging so that every decision can be audited after the fact. Reference architectures describe the model in terms of a policy engine, a policy administrator and policy enforcement points, which gives architects shared vocabulary when planning a migration. Migration is incremental, because few organisations can rebuild identity, endpoint management and network policy at the same time. A realistic sequence strengthens identity first, then device assurance, then application-level access brokers that replace broad network reachability, and finally workload-level policy for the highest-value systems. The hard parts are cultural and operational rather than technical: legacy applications that cannot express fine-grained authorisation, service accounts holding standing privilege, and business processes that depend on unrestricted file-share access. Zero trust also fails when telemetry is poor, because a policy engine fed stale or incomplete device data will either block legitimate work or wave through compromised endpoints. Mature implementations measure the share of access decisions made by policy, count standing privileged accounts, and test how quickly access can be revoked.
objectives: You will be able to explain why network location is not an authentication signal and what replaces it.
You will be able to describe the roles of the policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement point.
You will be able to identify standing privilege and implicit trust relationships in a real environment.
You will be able to design an incremental migration order across identity, device assurance and application access.
You will be able to evaluate whether telemetry quality is sufficient for policy decisions and where it misleads.
You will be able to measure zero trust progress with defensible metrics rather than vendor claims.

topics.title: Account Use Policies
topics.summary: Account use policies constrain how, when, from where, and through which session type an identity may authenticate, rather than what that identity is permitted to read or change. Typical controls include conditional access that demands a compliant device, a trusted network location, an acceptable risk score, or a phishing-resistant authenticator; logon-hour and source-address restrictions; session lifetime and idle timeouts; limits on concurrent sessions; denial of interactive logon for service and shared accounts; and automatic disconnection of dormant or orphaned identities. In practice the difficult part is not writing the rule but keeping it true. Hybrid estates evaluate policy in several places at once, so a rule that is strict in the cloud can be undermined by an on-premises path that still accepts the same credential, and legacy protocols plus emergency break-glass accounts routinely sit outside enforcement. Vendor and batch service accounts resist restriction because their scheduled work cannot satisfy interactive conditions, so teams either carve out permanent exceptions or move the workload onto a managed identity. Understanding what an account is actually used for normally has to precede meaningful restriction, which is why sign-in and privileged-role reporting carry so much weight. The control attacks the value of stolen credentials directly: a valid account is far less useful when the credential cannot be used from an unmanaged host, at an unusual hour, or into a remote desktop service from the internet. It reduces the yield of brute-force and spraying campaigns by removing the paths they target and it damages lateral movement by denying interactive logon where it is not required. Its failure modes are common and honest: exclusions that outlive their justification, session tokens stolen after a correct policy decision, legacy authentication paths, and misconfigured rules that either lock out operations or quietly apply to nobody.
objectives: Explain how account use policy differs from permission policy and why both are required for a defensible posture.

topics.title: Antivirus/Antimalware
topics.summary: Antivirus and antimalware controls are the endpoint and gateway technologies that identify, block, quarantine, and remediate malicious files, scripts, and behaviour before or during execution. A modern deployment is rarely signature-only: it combines static signatures and hashes, emulation and unpacking of obfuscated content, heuristic and machine-learning scoring, script-scanning interfaces that inspect interpreter content at runtime, behavioural monitoring of process trees and file operations, and cloud reputation lookups for samples the local engine has not seen. Protection is placed at several chokepoints, including the endpoint agent with on-access and on-write scanning, mail gateways that strip or detonate attachments, web proxies that block known-malicious downloads, and server or container layers where scanning is often omitted for performance reasons. Operationally the control is dominated by tuning and by exclusions. Build directories, database data paths, backup volumes, and vendor application folders produce constant false positives, and every documented exclusion becomes a place where an intruder can operate unobserved, which is why exclusion lists deserve the same review discipline as firewall rules. The control reliably defeats commodity and mass-market malware, script-based loaders, well-known ransomware families, and infostealers, and it frequently supplies the first detection signal for an intrusion that other controls missed. Its limitations are structural: novel or lightly modified samples evade signatures, living-off-the-land execution and in-memory payloads leave little on disk to scan, attackers target the agent itself for tampering, encrypted archives and some delivery paths escape inspection entirely, and agents left disabled or excluded on server tiers create large unprotected areas.
objectives: Explain how signature, heuristic, behavioural, and reputation layers complement each other and where each one fails.
Tune detection and exclusions for production workloads without creating blind spots an intruder can exploit.
Interpret malware alerts alongside process, script, and network telemetry during initial triage.

Assess why script-based, in-memory, and living-off-the-land execution evade file-based detection.

topics.title: Application Developer Guidance
topics.summary: Application developer guidance is the set of practices, standards, and tooling that cause security requirements to be expressed in code rather than bolted on after release. It begins with threat modelling during design, where the team enumerates trust boundaries, data flows, and the abuse cases a feature enables, and continues through secure coding standards that name the safe primitive for each risky operation: parameterised queries instead of string-built statements, contextual output encoding, framework-provided session and anti-forgery handling, safe deserialisation, and explicit allow-lists for file paths and redirects. In delivery pipelines the guidance is enforced by automated checks, including static analysis, dependency and container scanning, secret detection, composition analysis against a maintained inventory, and infrastructure-as-code policy evaluation, with a severity threshold that actually fails a build instead of producing a report nobody reads. Durable programmes also govern build artifacts, signing releases and verifying dependencies so the build path itself is not a supply-chain vector, and they invest in developer enablement through security champions and lightweight review rather than pure gatekeeping. The control removes whole classes of exploitable weakness from public-facing applications, shrinking the reachable initial-access surface and the injection, authorisation, and deserialisation flaws that follow. It also constrains privilege-abuse paths that depend on flawed authorisation logic and reduces the chance that a product ships insecure defaults. Its honest limits are that scanners miss logic and business-flow flaws, false positives breed desensitisation, transitive dependencies are difficult to govern, remediation debt accumulates faster than it is cleared, and guidance changes nothing unless it changes the code that ships.
objectives: Run a design-stage threat model that produces security requirements a team can implement and test.

topics.title: Audit
topics.summary: Audit is the control that makes an environment observable: the deliberate collection, retention, and review of security-relevant events so that unauthorised activity can be detected, reconstructed, and attributed. Implementation in a real estate spans several layers that must be joined together. Operating system audit policy is tuned to capture process creation with command-line arguments, authentication outcomes, account and group changes, service installation, scheduled task creation, and privilege use. Directory and identity services capture sign-in events, token issuance, and administrative role assignment. Network infrastructure contributes flow records, proxy and DNS logs, and firewall decisions. Cloud control planes contribute API activity trails for every subscription, account, and project. Endpoint agents contribute process lineage, driver and module loads, and file integrity information. All of it converges into centralised storage with normalised time, retained long enough to support an investigation that begins months after initial access, and protected from the very accounts it is meant to observe. Audit is the foundational control behind every other detection capability: without it, threat hunting, incident response, and forensics are guesswork. It directly supports detection of remote service use, account creation and discovery, autostart persistence, defence impairment, and data staging or exfiltration behaviour, because those actions leave configuration and authentication traces. The honest limitations are volume and quality. Default audit policy is either too sparse to be useful or so verbose that signal drowns in noise and licensing cost, and collecting events without a review process produces archives nobody reads. Failure modes include logging only on servers and not on workstations or build agents, leaving audit records in a writable location for any local administrator, failing to synchronise clocks so timelines cannot be correlated, expiring retention before an intrusion is discovered, and disabling a noisy audit subcategory after a false alarm instead of tuning the detection.

topics.title: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
topics.summary: Disable or remove feature or program is the reduction of attack surface by eliminating software, protocols, services, and interpreter features that the business does not need. It is the least glamorous control and consistently one of the most effective, because every removed component is a class of vulnerability, a persistence location, and an execution path the adversary can no longer use. In real environments it is implemented as a hardening baseline applied through configuration management: removing or blocking legacy scripting hosts and command-line download utilities where they are not required, disabling macro execution from internet-sourced documents, turning off deprecated authentication protocols and unauthenticated file sharing versions, uninstalling unused agents and management tools that carry their own privileged services, removing sample applications and default accounts from internet-facing systems, disabling unnecessary remote access features and file-transfer endpoints, and pruning optional operating system capabilities and kernel modules on servers. The control is powerful because it works before detection matters: the technique fails outright rather than generating an alert that someone must triage. It addresses user execution through document and script features, abuse of command and scripting interpreters, exploitation of public-facing applications that would not exist in a minimal build, and remote services that only function because an unnecessary protocol is enabled. It also removes the defence-impairment surface, since tooling that is not installed cannot be tampered with. The honest limitations are organisational. Nobody wants to be the team that broke a business process, so removal requests are contested, and the knowledge of who depends on a legacy component is usually incomplete. Applications are frequently reinstalled silently by a vendor update, a configuration baseline that is applied once drifts back within a quarter, and the hardened image is rarely the one used for the emergency build during an incident. Failure modes include disabling a feature only on workstations while servers keep it enabled, relying on a registry setting that a per-application local override can bypass, forgetting the disaster recovery and test environments, and removing a component with no inventory record so that no one can tell whether it came back.
objectives: Explain how to build a hardening baseline from an accurate software, protocol, and service inventory.
Identify the interpreter features, legacy protocols, and default components that most reliably reward removal.
Describe how configuration management and compliance scanning keep a hardened baseline from drifting back to default.
Explain how disabling an unnecessary feature changes detection requirements by removing an execution path entirely.
Describe how per-application overrides and vendor updates can silently re-enable a component that was disabled.
Explain why test, disaster recovery, and emergency build environments must receive the same baseline as production.

topics.title: Encrypt Sensitive Information
topics.summary: Encrypting sensitive information means ensuring that data is unreadable to anyone who does not hold the corresponding key, both while it is stored and while it travels between systems. In production the requirement resolves into a small set of concrete patterns: full-disk encryption bound to a hardware root of trust so a stolen laptop yields nothing without the platform, database and column-level encryption for regulated fields, object storage configured for server-side encryption under a customer-managed key, secret managers that remove plaintext credentials from configuration files and build pipelines, and modern TLS with validated certificates for every service-to-service and client connection. Key management is where such programmes succeed or fail. Envelope encryption through a key management service or hardware security module keeps data keys short-lived and auditable, rotation schedules and a cryptographic agility plan limit the blast radius of a compromised key, and separation of duties prevents the team that operates the data from also controlling the keys that protect it. The control blunts exfiltration over command-and-control channels and public web services by reducing what stolen bulk data is worth without its keys, protects credentials and tokens at rest so that an exposed file share or backup does not immediately become account takeover, and makes salted, deliberately slow storage of password material expensive to attack offline. Its limitations are real: data must be decrypted somewhere, and that endpoint, its memory, and its logs are the practical attack surface; keys stored beside the data reduce encryption to presentation; a legitimate session used by an intruder is unaffected; and aggressive inspection or key escrow can quietly undo the protection. Encryption changes the economics of a breach rather than preventing one.
objectives: Explain the difference between encryption at rest, in transit, and at the application layer, and where each genuinely helps.
Design an envelope-encryption scheme with a key management service or hardware security module that keeps data keys short-lived.

Assess certificate lifecycle and cipher configuration as continuing operational risks rather than one-time build tasks.
Evaluate how key custody, escrow, and separation of duties determine the real strength of an encryption deployment.

topics.title: Execution Prevention
topics.summary: Execution prevention is the set of endpoint and policy controls that stop unauthorised code from ever running, rather than detecting it after it starts. In practice it is implemented as a layered stack: application allow-listing through Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker, PowerShell constrained language mode and script block logging paired with a hardened execution policy, Microsoft Office macro restrictions enforced by group policy, and on Linux systems mount-level noexec flags plus integrity tooling. The control works because it denies the final common step of nearly every intrusion: the moment a payload is handed to a scripting host, a signed binary proxy, or an office application. It breaks behaviours such as user execution of a malicious attachment, abuse of command and scripting interpreters, and the broad family of living-off-the-land binary abuse where legitimate signed tools are repurposed to launch attacker code. Operational reality is unforgiving. Effective allow-listing requires months of audit-only telemetry, a disciplined change process for every legitimate software update, and a publisher-certificate strategy that survives vendor re-signing. Blocking PowerShell outright is rarely feasible; constrained language mode and AMSI integration are the practical compromise, and both are trivially weakened by an unmanaged host or an excluded directory. Common failure modes include allow-listing only the user-writable portions of the filesystem while leaving temporary and download directories executable, forgetting that signed interpreters such as mshta and rundll32 can load remote content, and deploying policy to workstations while leaving jump servers and build agents in audit mode indefinitely. Attackers adapt by moving to in-memory execution, signed binary proxy chains, and interpreter features that fall outside the constrained set, so execution prevention must be paired with memory-level detection and strict egress control to remain meaningful.
objectives: Explain how application allow-listing policies such as WDAC and AppLocker are designed, piloted in audit mode, and enforced without breaking business software.
Describe the practical difference between blocking a scripting interpreter outright and constraining its language mode, and when each is defensible.
Identify the signed binary proxy execution paths and interpreter features that most often bypass execution prevention controls.
Explain how Office macro, ActiveX, and add-in policy settings reduce user-execution risk and where they are commonly misconfigured.
Describe how noexec mounts, integrity verification, and package trust work on Linux and Unix endpoints as execution prevention.
Evaluate the operational cost of allow-listing in a changing environment and design a change-management path that keeps policy current.
Explain why execution prevention must be complemented by memory-level detection and egress control rather than treated as a complete control.

topics.title: Exploit Protection
topics.summary: Exploit protection is the family of host and process hardening features that make memory-corruption and similar software flaws harder to turn into reliable code execution. It is implemented through operating system mitigations that are compiled into binaries and enforced at load time, including address space layout randomisation, data execution prevention, control-flow integrity and control-flow guard, stack and heap integrity checks, structured exception handling overwrite protection, and arbitrary code guard, alongside runtime exploit protection settings that can be applied per process through platform tooling. In practice a security team defines a baseline of mitigations, audits which production binaries and third-party agents opt out, and remediates the opt-outs through vendor updates or configuration. The control raises the cost of vulnerability exploitation and, critically, causes attacks that depend on predictable memory layouts or writable executable regions to fail outright or to crash the target process, which generates high-value telemetry. It addresses exploitation of public-facing applications, client-side exploitation, and privilege escalation that relies on memory corruption in privileged services, and it complicates process injection techniques that require executable memory in a remote process. Honest limitations matter here. Mitigations are not a patch: a logic flaw, a design weakness, or a misuse of legitimate functionality is entirely unaffected. Whole classes of modern attacks, including those abusing legitimate scripting hosts and credential access through operating system interfaces, do not touch memory corruption at all. Mitigations are frequently disabled during troubleshooting and never re-enabled, and older in-house or line-of-business binaries often cannot be rebuilt with control-flow integrity. Failure modes include system-wide opt-outs applied to make a single legacy application run, per-process exclusions that quietly accumulate, and treating a mitigation audit as a one-time project rather than a continuous control that must be re-verified after every application update.
objectives: Explain each major exploit mitigation and the specific exploitation primitive it is designed to disrupt.
Describe how to audit per-process mitigation opt-outs across a production estate and prioritise remediation.

Explain how mitigation-related crashes appear in endpoint telemetry and how to triage them as potential exploitation attempts.
Evaluate the operational tradeoffs of enforcing strict mitigation policy against legacy line-of-business software.

topics.title: Filter Network Traffic
topics.summary: Filtering network traffic is the practice of permitting only the protocols, destinations, ports, and services an organisation has explicitly justified and denying everything else at control points the defender owns. In production it is never one device but a stack of them: perimeter and internal firewalls enforcing zone-to-zone policy, web proxies and secure web gateways applying category and reputation decisions, recursive resolvers with policy zones that block or sinkhole unwanted domains, cloud security groups and network ACLs, Kubernetes network policies and service mesh authorisation, and host firewalls that drop traffic before it reaches the wire. The engineering reality is that filtering is a change-management problem at least as much as a technical one. Rules accumulate, business owners resist removals, emergency openings become permanent, and a single any-any rule quietly rebuilds the flat network that segmentation was meant to replace. Mature teams therefore keep rule ownership metadata, review rulesets on a schedule, use hit counters to retire rules that never match, and ship denied traffic into detection pipelines instead of leaving it in a device buffer. The control interrupts command-and-control over common application-layer protocols by forcing beacons toward destinations the organisation does not permit, and it makes DNS-based tunnelling visible and blockable by channelling all resolution through controlled resolvers. It raises the cost of exfiltration over C2 channels and public web services, constrains remote service abuse such as unrestricted RDP or SMB across zones, and removes reachable services that opportunistic exploitation depends on. Its limitations are honest: inspection degrades against encrypted traffic, attackers ride allowed SaaS and cloud endpoints, domain fronting and fast-changing infrastructure defeat static allow-lists, and a filter that generates constant false positives will eventually be bypassed by the operators it inconveniences.
objectives: Explain how traffic filtering policy is enforced at perimeter, internal, cloud, cluster, and host layers, and where each layer's blind spots sit.
Design an egress allow-list that constrains command-and-control over web protocols and DNS without breaking legitimate business traffic.

topics.title: Multi-factor Authentication
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication is the requirement that a login present at least two independent evidence types, so that possession of a password alone is insufficient to establish a session. In real environments it appears in several forms with very different security properties: hardware-backed phishing-resistant factors using FIDO2 or platform credentials, push notifications through an authenticator application, time-based one-time codes, and legacy telephony methods such as SMS or voice callbacks. It is deployed for interactive user sign-in, for privileged and administrative access through a bastion or privileged access workstation, for remote access gateways including VPN and virtual desktop entry points, and increasingly for machine identities where certificate or workload identity stands in for a second factor. The control directly breaks password spraying, credential stuffing, and the reuse of harvested credentials, and it removes the immediate value of most credential phishing because the stolen password cannot complete a session. It also meaningfully constrains lateral movement that depends on reusing captured password hashes or plaintext credentials, since the second factor is not present in memory. The honest limitations are where most breaches still occur. Push-based and code-based factors are vulnerable to real-time relay, where an attacker proxies the authentication prompt to the victim and the victim approves it. Legacy protocols that cannot present a second factor become a bypass path unless they are disabled or brokered. Service accounts, scheduled tasks, and API clients typically cannot perform interactive multi-factor authentication and are excluded, creating a large credential-only attack surface. Failure modes include enrolling users but never enforcing, allowing remembered sessions for months, leaving a break-glass account with a static password, and treating the presence of any second factor as equivalent to a phishing-resistant one.
objectives: Explain the difference between phishing-resistant hardware-backed factors and relayable factors, and the risk each carries.
Describe how to roll out multi-factor authentication for interactive sign-in, remote access, and privileged administration in phases.
Identify the legacy authentication paths and non-interactive accounts that bypass multi-factor enforcement and describe how to close them.
Explain how real-time prompt relay and adversary-in-the-middle proxying defeat push and code factors in practice.
Describe how conditional access, device state, and session lifetime policy combine with multi-factor authentication.
Evaluate an authentication estate and rank the residual risks that multi-factor authentication does not remove.

topics.title: Network Intrusion Prevention
topics.summary: Network intrusion prevention is the inline inspection and blocking of traffic that matches known attack patterns, malicious infrastructure, or anomalous protocol behaviour, usually delivered through a next-generation firewall, a dedicated prevention appliance, or a cloud-native inspection service. Unlike intrusion detection, which only alerts on a copy of the traffic, prevention sits in the path and can drop a session, reset a connection, or quarantine a source, which raises both its value and its risk. Detection content combines signature and protocol-anomaly rules for exploitation attempts and malware callbacks, reputation and threat-intelligence feeds for addresses and domains, transport fingerprinting that can distinguish suspicious clients even inside encryption, and behavioural thresholds for scanning, brute force, and tunnelling. Teams enable signature sets selectively, tune and suppress noise until a blocking policy is trustworthy, and frequently run in detect-only mode first to measure what a block would have broken. The control provides virtual patching for vulnerable public-facing services that cannot be fixed immediately, interrupts command-and-control over web protocols and DNS, cuts off large-scale exfiltration toward known or suspicious external services, and contains fast-moving ransomware by dropping the file-sharing and remote-service traffic it uses to spread laterally. Its limitations are equally concrete: encryption and evasion techniques such as fragmentation, encoding, and polymorphic payloads reduce inspection fidelity, traffic that stays inside an allowed cloud service is hard to distinguish from legitimate use, east-west blind spots and sensor placement gaps leave internal movement uninspected, capacity limits force bypass under load, and every false positive is an outage that erodes the organisation's willingness to keep the control in blocking mode.
objectives: Explain the operational difference between detection-only and inline prevention and when each posture is appropriate.
Tune signatures, suppressions, and thresholds until a blocking policy is safe to enforce in production.
Triage prevention alerts for exploitation attempts, beaconing, and tunnelling rather than closing them as noise.
Apply virtual patching to an exposed service while the underlying vulnerability remains unremediated.
Assess the fidelity limits created by encrypted traffic, evasion techniques, and permitted cloud services.

topics.title: Network Segmentation
topics.summary: Network segmentation is the practice of dividing an enterprise network into zones with defined trust levels and restricting traffic between them to what each zone genuinely needs. In modern environments it is implemented less by firewall interfaces and more by a combination of internal micro-segmentation policy enforced on the host or in the virtual network fabric, virtual local area network and routing separation, private endpoints that remove public reachability from data services, and identity-aware proxies in front of administrative interfaces. The purpose is to convert a single compromised host from a launching point for the whole estate into a contained incident. Segmentation breaks the behaviours that carry most intrusions from foothold to impact: internal reconnaissance that depends on broad reachability, lateral movement over remote service protocols such as remote desktop, server message block, and secure shell, and command-and-control that relies on unrestricted outbound access from user subnets. It also constrains exfiltration, because staging servers must reach a route that policy permits rather than any internet destination. The operational reality is that segmentation is a data problem before it is a firewall problem. Nobody can write correct policy without an accurate, current map of which systems talk to which on which ports, and that map is almost never in the documentation. Failure modes are predictable: allow rules written once for a migration and never removed, a broad any-to-any rule between two production zones created during an incident and left in place, flat management networks where hypervisors, backup infrastructure, and jump hosts share a broadcast domain with user devices, and cloud security groups that permit the entire corporate range because enumerating real sources was inconvenient. Segmentation also creates a false sense of safety when the identity plane remains flat, since a single set of reusable administrative credentials can still cross every zone boundary. Segmentation must therefore be paired with privileged access management, multi-factor authentication, and outbound egress filtering rather than treated as a standalone control.

topics.title: Password Policies
topics.summary: Password policies are the enforced rules that govern how credentials are created, stored, transmitted, throttled, and retired across an identity estate. Current practice has moved away from mandatory rotation and character-mix requirements toward minimum length, screening against corpora of known-breached passwords, per-account throttling and lockout, and secure storage using salted, deliberately slow hashing. Forced periodic changes with symbol substitution reliably produce predictable mutations that add little entropy, while punishing users and generating helpdesk load. Implementation spans several planes that rarely share one policy: on-premises directory domains with both domain-wide and fine-grained settings, cloud identity providers with their own complexity, lockout, and banned-password controls, hybrid synchronisation that can silently preserve legacy behaviour, service and machine accounts that frequently sit under a separate or exempt policy, and application-local credential stores that no central policy reaches at all. Lockout thresholds deserve deliberate tuning because a low threshold hands an adversary a denial-of-service lever against any username they can guess, so risk-based throttling is usually the better trade than a hard lockout. The control raises the cost of online brute force and password spraying, and breached-password screening at set and change time makes credential stuffing materially less productive. It also reduces the chance that a weak or reused credential becomes the valid account an intruder needs. Its limits are decisive: once stored hashes leave the estate, policy protects nothing, spraying under the lockout threshold remains viable, legacy authentication protocols can bypass modern settings, helpdesk resets are a social-engineering target, and credential reuse on external sites is outside the organisation's control entirely.

topics.title: Privileged Account Management
topics.summary: Privileged account management is the discipline of limiting, controlling, and monitoring the accounts and roles that can change security-relevant configuration, access sensitive data, or administer other systems. Real implementations combine several mechanisms: a tiered administrative model that separates directory, server, and workstation administration so that no single credential can cross tiers, dedicated administrative accounts that are never used for mail or browsing, credential vaulting with automatic rotation for shared and service accounts, just-in-time elevation that grants a role for a bounded window with approval and full session recording, and the removal of standing local administrator rights from standard user workstations. The control removes the two conditions attackers rely on most: reusable credentials with broad reach, and quiet elevation paths that leave no approval trail. It breaks behaviours including account discovery and enumeration of privileged groups, credential access through cached secrets and process memory on administrative workstations, exploitation of elevation control mechanisms such as user account control misconfiguration and setuid binaries, and the use of remote services to move laterally with administrative shares. It also directly constrains impact, because destructive actions such as recovery inhibition and mass encryption require privileged reach that a tightly brokered model does not grant by default. Honest limitations are mostly organisational. Tiered models collapse when administrators reuse a single identity across tiers because it is convenient, and vaulting is defeated if the vault becomes a single unmonitored credential store reachable from the same flat network as everything else. Just-in-time access fails when approval becomes a rubber stamp or when emergency break-glass accounts retain permanent standing privilege. Service accounts remain the hardest case, because they cannot always be rotated without an outage and are frequently excluded from management scope. Failure modes include allowing interactive logon for service identities, leaving former administrators in privileged groups, permitting administrative sessions from ordinary workstations, and never reviewing who actually used the privilege that was granted.
