topics.title: Software Configuration
topics.summary: Software configuration as a mitigation is the deliberate hardening of applications, operating systems, and cloud services away from their permissive defaults, followed by the work of keeping that hardened state true over time. It covers disabling features that exist mainly as attack surface, such as legacy file-sharing dialects, name-resolution fallbacks that answer broadcast queries, obsolete scripting engines, and macro execution from internet-sourced documents; constraining command interpreters with logging and restricted language modes; requiring elevation through a separate administrative account for management tooling; and configuring services so that authentication, transport security, cipher suites, and audit settings match a defined baseline. In cloud estates the same idea appears as account-level and resource-level settings, public-access blocks, instance metadata hardening, and organisation policies that stop a workload owner from reverting a control by accident. The operational reality is drift. Baselines are applied at build time and then eroded by an application that needs an exception, an upgrade that resets a value, a container image that still ships the old configuration, or an operator under pressure who weakens a control to restore service. Teams that succeed treat baselines as code, scan continuously against them, alert on drift, and route exceptions through a named owner with an expiry date instead of leaving them undocumented. The control weakens defence-impairment attempts directly, because central logging configuration and tamper-protected agents remove the easiest routes to silencing telemetry, and it closes the autostart, macro execution, and script-interpreter behaviours that commodity intrusions depend on. Its limits are practical: an exception-heavy baseline is theatre, hardening that breaks operations gets rolled back, and no organisation controls the configuration of every third-party service it relies on.

topics.title: Update Software
topics.summary: Updating software is the systematic replacement of vulnerable code with vendor-fixed versions across every asset class an organisation operates, from operating systems and hypervisors through network appliances, container base images, firmware, and third-party libraries. The operational reality is dominated by inventory and scheduling rather than by the patch action itself, because you cannot update what you do not know exists. The control therefore rests on authoritative asset discovery, software composition analysis, a bill of materials for everything the organisation builds, and a change process capable of reaching production servers, field devices, remote laptops, and appliances that are only manageable through a vendor console. Effective programmes rank risk instead of chasing one score: vendor severity, evidence of exploitation in the wild, and whether the asset is internet-facing jointly decide what enters an emergency channel with a short deadline, while lower-risk internal findings wait for a scheduled ring. Where patching is genuinely impossible, teams apply compensating controls and record time-boxed risk acceptance with a named owner. The control breaks the most common initial-access path, exploitation of unpatched public-facing applications and remote-access gateways, and it removes the client-side and local privilege-escalation flaws that follow user execution. Its limitations are well understood: firmware and industrial systems rarely tolerate a reboot, shadow IT and embedded appliances escape inventory, vendors ship delayed or partial fixes, zero-days exist before patches do, and the update channel is itself a supply-chain target. Updating also fails quietly when installation reports success but the service is never restarted, or when an old container image is rescheduled from a registry that still holds it.

topics.title: User Account Management
topics.summary: User account management is the lifecycle control over identity: how accounts are requested, approved, provisioned, reviewed, and removed. In practice it means a governed joiners, movers, and leavers process tied to the authoritative human resources system, role-based entitlement templates that grant least privilege by default rather than cloning an existing colleague, periodic access recertification with real evidence of manager review, prompt and verifiable disabling of accounts on termination, and explicit handling of the accounts that have no human owner, including service, shared, vendor, and emergency identities. It also covers the hygiene properties of identity itself: unique named accounts rather than shared logins, strong password policy with breach-list checks and no forced rotation without cause, and detection of dormant or orphaned accounts that still hold access. The control matters because stale and excessive accounts are a durable attacker advantage. A valid account obtained from a data breach, a leftover contractor login, or a service identity with a static password provides legitimate-looking authentication that blends into normal activity, and it directly enables initial access through valid accounts. It also reduces the value of account discovery, makes the creation of an attacker-controlled account stand out against a clean baseline, and limits the reach of credential access because there are fewer credentials with access worth stealing. Its honest limitations are that identity governance is slow, political, and expensive: recertification campaigns generate rubber-stamped approvals, entitlement templates drift as people change roles, and exception processes quietly accumulate. Failure modes include leavers disabled but not deleted with their sessions and tokens still valid, vendor accounts shared among several engineers with no attribution, service accounts exempted from password rotation and monitoring, unreviewed privileged group membership, and no alerting at all on dormant account reactivation, which is often the first observable sign of an intrusion.
objectives: Explain how to build a governed joiner, mover, and leaver process anchored to an authoritative source of identity.
Describe how role-based entitlement templates and least-privilege defaults prevent access accumulation.
Explain how to run access recertification that produces real evidence rather than rubber-stamped approvals.
Identify the account categories that routinely escape lifecycle control and describe monitoring for each.
Describe how account discovery, creation, and dormant reactivation appear in identity telemetry.
Explain how account hygiene properties such as uniqueness and password policy reduce credential-based risk.

topics.title: User Training
topics.summary: User training is the deliberate programme of awareness, simulation, and reinforcement that changes how staff behave when they encounter social engineering, credential harvesting, or anomalous requests. It is implemented as more than an annual slide deck: mature organisations combine role-specific curricula, regular phishing simulations with per-department reporting metrics, a genuinely frictionless report-phishing button wired into the security operations queue, and targeted deep-dive sessions for high-risk populations such as finance, executives, help desk, and developers. The control matters because the overwhelming majority of intrusions still begin with a human decision, and because trained users become a detection source rather than only a victim population. Well-run programmes shorten the time between a lure landing and an analyst investigating, which directly reduces dwell time. It breaks spearphishing behaviours, including attachment and link variants, and it degrades follow-on actions such as user execution and credential submission to attacker infrastructure. The honest limitations are significant. Training decays quickly without reinforcement, simulation results are easily gamed by anxious staff who report everything or by teams that game click rates, and no amount of awareness defeats a well-crafted pretext aimed at a tired employee at the end of a quarter. Training also shifts blame toward users when the real failure is missing technical control: an organisation with no multi-factor authentication, no attachment sandboxing, and no egress filtering should not treat awareness as its primary defence. Failure modes include measuring completion rather than behaviour, running simulations that punish reporting, ignoring the report queue so that employees learn their reports go nowhere, and delivering generic content that never reflects the actual lures targeting the sector.
objectives: Explain how to design a role-specific security awareness curriculum and measure behavioural change rather than course completion.
Describe how to run phishing simulations ethically and use reporting rate and time-to-report as operational metrics.
Explain how a report-phishing workflow should connect end users to the security operations queue and what triage must look like.
Identify the high-risk populations that warrant targeted deep-dive training and the scenarios most relevant to each.
Describe how awareness failure modes such as blame culture and unreviewed reports undermine the control.
Explain why user training must be paired with technical controls such as multi-factor authentication and attachment handling to be credible.
Evaluate training programme results against phishing-resistant control gaps and recommend a sequenced remediation plan.

topics.title: Collection
topics.summary: Collection is the tactic covering the adversary's staging of information of interest before exfiltration, including locating, gathering, and organising data from endpoints, file shares, mail systems, databases, and cloud storage. Behaviours include searching volumes and shares for keywords and file extensions, archiving and compressing selected files into a single staging container, capturing screen or clipboard content, collecting email from mailboxes, dumping database contents, copying data from software-as-a-service platforms into personal locations, and using built-in utilities to enumerate and read files at scale. This tactic is where defenders still have a reasonable chance of catching an intrusion before data leaves, because collection is usually noisy relative to normal user behaviour. Useful telemetry includes file access and creation events with volume metrics, archive utility execution and the size of what it produced, bulk download and share actions in cloud audit logs, mailbox export and delegated access events, and abnormal read patterns on file servers or databases. Detection in isolation is difficult because archiving and bulk reads are ordinary business activities for backup software, developers, finance teams, and administrators. What distinguishes malicious collection is concentration and mismatch: a single workstation compressing hundreds of documents it has never touched before, a service account reading an entire database schema, or a user downloading their whole mail archive shortly before resigning. Judging those cases requires peer-group baselines and business context as much as technical rules.
objectives: Describe how adversaries locate and stage data across endpoints, file shares, mail systems, databases, and cloud services.
Identify the telemetry that reveals collection, including file access volume, archive creation, mailbox export, and bulk download events.

topics.title: Command and Control
topics.summary: Command and Control is the tactic that describes how an adversary maintains communication with compromised systems, tasking them and receiving results through channels that must remain usable while looking as ordinary as possible. Behaviours include beaconing over web protocols to attacker-controlled or compromised sites, tunnelling through DNS, using application layer protocols such as mail or messaging services, abusing legitimate remote monitoring and management tooling and cloud services as relays, and encrypting or encoding traffic to defeat content inspection. From a defender's perspective, this is one of the richest tactics for network and endpoint analytics because sustained communication has structural properties: regularity of timing, consistency of payload size, long-lived sessions to destinations that are new to the environment, and repeated resolution of domains that no user or service should need. Endpoint evidence complements it through process-to-network correlation, showing which binary opened the connection, and through anomalous child processes that inherit a network session. Detection is difficult in isolation because beaconing to a content delivery network resembles software updates, because DNS tunnelling looks like ordinary recursive queries until volume and entropy are considered, and because adversaries deliberately use the same services and protocols as the business. Practical detection combines flow analytics, DNS and proxy logs, TLS metadata such as certificate and JA3-style fingerprints, and endpoint context, plus the discipline to build a baseline of expected egress before hunting for what should not be there.
objectives: Describe the main command and control channels and how each appears in network, DNS, proxy, TLS, and endpoint telemetry.
Analyse beaconing behaviour using interval regularity, jitter, payload size consistency, and destination history rather than content inspection alone.
Detect DNS tunnelling and covert channels by examining query volume, subdomain entropy, and response characteristics.
Correlate endpoint process data with network sessions to attribute an outbound connection to the process that opened it.
Baseline expected egress so that new destinations, unusual protocols, and long-lived sessions stand out.
Explain how egress filtering, protocol allow-listing, and TLS inspection trade off against operational cost and privacy.

topics.title: Credential Access
topics.summary: Credential Access is the tactic covering the theft, guessing, or interception of account secrets, and it is frequently the single most valuable step in an intrusion because a valid credential can bypass controls that would stop everything else. Behaviours include brute force and password spraying against exposed authentication services, credential stuffing with data from unrelated breaches, dumping stored secrets from operating system memory or credential stores, reading browser and password manager databases, extracting keys and tokens from files, configuration stores, and container environments, intercepting authentication traffic, and abusing directory services to obtain or relay credentials. Defenders can see a great deal here if identity and endpoint telemetry is centralised. Repeated authentication failures followed by a success, logon attempts with unusual logon types, access to the memory of security-sensitive processes, bulk reads of credential files, suspicious use of directory replication or ticket-granting operations, and secrets exposed in code repositories all map to concrete events. The tactic remains hard to detect in isolation because spraying stays below account lockout thresholds by design, because legitimate administrators run the same tooling that attackers do, and because stolen credentials produce successful authentications that look healthy. Detection requires combining authentication analytics, endpoint behavioural monitoring, secret-scanning in source control, and monitoring of where secrets are stored, with priority given to protecting the highest-value credentials first.
objectives: Explain the main credential access paths, from spraying and stuffing to memory dumping and secret extraction, and how each generates evidence.
Analyse authentication telemetry to identify spraying and stuffing patterns that stay below lockout thresholds.
Identify endpoint behaviours that indicate credential dumping and explain what must be logged to see them.
Design secret-scanning and key-management controls that reduce the value of a stolen credential or key.
Prioritise protections for privileged, service, and machine identities rather than treating all accounts equally.
Build a triage path from a suspicious authentication to confirmation of credential theft and the actions taken with it.

topics.title: Defense Evasion
topics.summary: Defense Evasion is the tactic that groups everything an adversary does to avoid being seen, analysed, or stopped, and unlike most other tactics it is defined by intent rather than by a single technical primitive. Behaviours include disabling or tampering with security tools and logging, clearing or editing event records, obfuscating scripts and payloads, masquerading files by renaming or matching legitimate system paths, abusing signed binaries to proxy execution, uninstalling or suppressing agents, using alternate data streams, rootkits and bootkit techniques, and, increasingly, manipulating cloud audit settings or identity controls so that activity is never recorded. Defenders face a structural problem here: the telemetry that would prove evasion is often the telemetry the adversary is trying to remove. Detection therefore leans on independent evidence sources that are hard to reach, such as remote log shipping to a collector the endpoint cannot modify, EDR heartbeats and tamper protection events, agent health monitoring, service and driver load records, and configuration drift checks against a known baseline. Because much of this tactic consists of removing or weakening controls, absence of expected data is itself the signal: a host that stops reporting, a sensor whose configuration changed outside change control, or an audit policy quietly reverted. Analysts must treat these gaps as findings rather than as noise, and must be able to reconstruct what happened from the residual artifacts and the surrounding timeline.
objectives: Describe the main defense evasion behaviours and explain why the tactic is defined by intent rather than by a specific technique.
Design independent telemetry paths, such as remote log shipping and agent health monitoring, that survive local tampering.
Treat missing data, stopped agents, and reverted security configuration as high-priority detections rather than gaps to ignore.
Recognise obfuscation and masquerading patterns in process, file, and command line data without over-relying on signatures.
Investigate tampering with audit policy, log retention, or cloud control-plane logging and reconstruct the surrounding timeline.
Assess which evasion techniques would defeat the current tooling and propose concrete compensating controls.

topics.title: Discovery
topics.summary: Discovery is the tactic that covers the internal reconnaissance an adversary performs after gaining a foothold, mapping users, systems, shares, permissions, security controls, and network topology so that the next move is informed. Behaviours include enumerating local and domain accounts, querying directory services, listing remote systems and open shares, scanning internal address space for live hosts and services, reading configuration and cloud metadata, and checking for the presence of security tooling. The volume of telemetry is deceptive: almost all of this activity is native to the platform, produces normal-looking events, and is generated constantly by legitimate administration, inventory, monitoring, and software deployment. Command line and script block logging capture many of the queries, but only if enabled and centrally collected, since local logs are easily lost. Authentication records reveal lateral enumeration through logon types and target patterns, while cloud audit logs show unusual describe, list, or permission-enumeration calls from a principal that has never made them before. Detecting Discovery in isolation is close to impossible because the primitives are not malicious. Progress depends on baselining which hosts and accounts normally run which discovery commands, scoring breadth over any single action, and correlating a burst of enumeration from one identity with the privileged access or lateral movement that follows it. High-fidelity signals are rare, so prioritisation must be ruthless.
objectives: Enumerate the main discovery behaviours across endpoint, directory, network, and cloud environments and the evidence each produces.
Explain why native enumeration activity cannot be detected with signature-style rules and what baseline data is required instead.
Score discovery by breadth and rarity, for example a single host issuing many distinct enumeration commands in a short window.

topics.title: Execution
topics.summary: Execution is the tactic that covers adversary attempts to run their own code or abuse legitimate command interpreters on a victim system, and it is the bridge between having access and actually doing something with it. Concrete behaviours include launching PowerShell, cmd.exe, Windows Script Host, bash or other interpreters, using scheduled tasks and service creation to trigger payloads, exploiting client applications so that a document or archive executes code, and abusing built-in administration utilities that are already trusted and signed. Defenders see this tactic in process creation telemetry, command line logging, script block logging, module and image load events, application whitelisting or WDAC events, and, depending on maturity, EDR behavioural detections rather than simple indicator matches. The central problem is that execution telemetry is enormously high volume and heavily polluted by legitimate administrative activity. Management tooling, software deployment, monitoring agents, and helpdesk automation all spawn the same interpreters and utilities that attackers prefer, often with long encoded parameters. Detection in isolation therefore fails: a single encoded PowerShell command is weak evidence, whereas the same command spawning from an Office process, on a server that never runs interactive scripts, minutes after a new service was created, is a defensible finding. Effective work on this tactic means establishing a clean baseline of what runs where, enriching process events with parent-child lineage and signer information, and then hunting deviations from that baseline rather than chasing individual suspicious commands.
objectives: Describe the range of execution behaviours, from interpreter abuse and script hosts to scheduled task and service-based triggering.
Interpret process lineage and signer information to separate normal administrative execution from adversary execution.

topics.title: Exfiltration
topics.summary: Exfiltration is the tactic covering the removal of data from the victim environment after it has been collected and staged, and it is usually the last point at which defenders can still prevent business harm rather than only measure it. Behaviours include transferring files over the existing command and control channel, uploading data to legitimate cloud storage, file-sharing, code-hosting, or webmail services, sending it over alternative protocols such as file transfer or mail, using physical media on endpoints, and throttling transfers to stay under volumetric alerting thresholds. Telemetry is abundant but concentrated at the boundary: proxy and web gateway logs with upload volume and destination category, netflow records showing large asymmetric transfers, data loss prevention alerts on content or volume, cloud audit logs recording file uploads and sharing changes, mail gateway records of outbound attachments, and endpoint events for removable media and archive creation. Detection in isolation is hard because organisations legitimately move large amounts of data to those same services every day, and because the most damaging exfiltration is often small and targeted, such as a handful of documents leaving through an approved channel. Analysis therefore depends on joining collection and exfiltration evidence, comparing transfer volume against the account's own history and peer group, and knowing which destinations and volumes are normal for each business function before an incident begins.
objectives: Describe the main exfiltration channels and the specific telemetry each generates at the network, cloud, mail, and endpoint boundary.
Analyse transfer volume, direction, timing, and destination reputation against per-user and per-host baselines.

Explain how egress control, data loss prevention, and cloud sharing restrictions complement each other and where each fails.

topics.title: Impact
topics.summary: Impact is the tactic covering the actions an adversary takes to degrade, disrupt, destroy, or manipulate the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of systems and data, and it is where an intrusion becomes an operational and often physical business event. Behaviours include encrypting data for extortion, deleting or overwriting data and backups to prevent recovery, inhibiting system recovery features, defacing public sites, disrupting services through denial of service or resource exhaustion, manipulating or falsifying records to undermine trust, and using destructive wiper-like techniques. Defenders receive the clearest signal of any tactic here, but usually far too late: mass file modifications and rename storms, volume shadow copy deletion, backup catalogue changes, hypervisor or virtual machine snapshot removal, service stops across many hosts at once, account and permission destruction, and storage or compute consumption spikes. Endpoint and storage telemetry, backup system logs, hypervisor events, and cloud control-plane audit records all show these actions, and alerting on the earliest of them, especially anything touching backups or recovery capability, buys the only meaningful response time available. Detection in isolation is less of a problem than acting fast enough and having a tested recovery path; the practical challenges are distinguishing destructive intent from a failed deployment or a legitimate maintenance window, preserving evidence while containing, and knowing in advance the order in which to disconnect, isolate, and restore.
objectives: Describe the range of impact behaviours, from encryption and destruction to manipulation and service disruption.
Identify the earliest observable signals of destructive activity, especially those touching backups and recovery capability.
Explain how backup architecture, offline copies, and restore testing determine whether any response can succeed.
Design alerting that separates a genuine destructive campaign from failed deployments and maintenance activity.
Sequence containment correctly to stop propagation while preserving the evidence needed for recovery and investigation.

topics.title: Initial Access
topics.summary: Initial Access is the tactic that describes how an adversary first gains a foothold in a target network, and it is the point at which preparation on attacker-controlled infrastructure converts into presence on victim systems. The behaviours grouped here include sending phishing messages with malicious attachments or links, abusing valid accounts whose credentials were guessed, sprayed, stuffed, or purchased, exploiting public-facing applications such as web servers, VPN concentrators, and file transfer services, and using trusted external remote services with legitimate credentials. Telemetry defenders can rely on is unusually rich for this tactic because most of these paths touch perimeter and identity systems: web and reverse proxy logs, WAF alerts, VPN and remote access authentication records, mail gateway verdicts, endpoint process creation for parent processes that are email clients or browsers, and cloud identity sign-in logs showing impossible travel or unfamiliar user agents. The difficulty is not a shortage of data but a shortage of discrimination. Failed authentication attempts are constant, exploit probes against exposed services are relentless, and a successful credential-based intrusion can look exactly like an employee working from a new location. Detection therefore depends on correlation, baseline behaviour, and knowledge of which of the organisation's own assets are genuinely reachable from the internet, plus rapid triage of the small number of events that combine an unusual source, an unusual identity, and a subsequent post-access action.
objectives: Explain how Initial Access converts off-target preparation into on-target presence across phishing, valid accounts, exploitation, and external remote services.
Identify the highest-value telemetry sources for this tactic and the specific fields that make an event actionable.

topics.title: Lateral Movement
topics.summary: Lateral Movement is the tactic describing how an adversary moves between systems inside a network, using stolen credentials, remote management protocols, and trusted administrative channels to reach higher-value targets. Behaviours include remote desktop sessions, server message block and administrative share access, secure shell logins, remote service creation and scheduled task deployment, execution framework agents, and pivoting through compromised hosts to reach network segments that are not directly accessible. The telemetry picture is mixed. Authentication events across directory services and endpoints record the source, target, account, and logon type for most remote access, and service creation, remote process start, and file writes to administrative shares show what the adversary did on arrival. Network flow data identifies new host-to-host relationships and unusual internal fan-out. The core detection problem is that lateral movement is largely indistinguishable from normal administration by design: administrators use exactly these protocols and credentials. What separates them is context, such as an account authenticating from a workstation it never uses, administrative protocols appearing on endpoints where they were previously absent, or a single source touching many targets in sequence. Detection therefore relies on relationship baselines, careful use of honeypot or decoy credentials, segmentation that limits what is reachable, and rapid correlation of authentication, process, and flow evidence into a movement path rather than a list of isolated alerts.
objectives: Describe the remote access protocols and administrative mechanisms adversaries use to move between systems and what each leaves behind.
Correlate authentication, process creation, service installation, and network flow data into a coherent movement path.
Baseline legitimate host-to-host and account-to-host relationships so unexpected pairings become detectable.
Explain how network segmentation and just-in-time administrative access change what lateral movement is even possible.
Use decoy credentials and canary hosts to raise detection confidence without adding analyst load.

topics.title: Persistence
topics.summary: Persistence is the tactic that covers everything an adversary does to keep access across reboots, credential resets, and partial remediation, and it is the reason incidents that appear contained often resume weeks later. Behaviours in this tactic include modifying registry run keys and startup folders, installing services or daemons, creating scheduled tasks and cron entries, adding accounts or SSH authorised keys, abusing external remote services such as VPN or remote desktop gateways, planting web shells in application directories, and hijacking legitimate authentication pathways so that a token or certificate continues to work after the original password is changed. Defenders have good theoretical telemetry here because persistence usually requires a write to a durable location, and those writes are visible in registry auditing, file integrity monitoring, service and task creation events, directory service change logs, and cloud identity audit records. The practical difficulty is a very high legitimate baseline. Software deployment, agent updates, and administrators constantly create the same artifacts, so each event in isolation is weak. Compounding this, sophisticated adversaries prefer persistence that is indistinguishable from normal platform behaviour, such as a new OAuth application consent or a certificate added to an enterprise application, which may leave no endpoint trace at all. Detection therefore depends on inventories, change control correlation, and reviewing every new durable artifact against a known-good baseline, ideally with the identity and process that created it.
objectives: Enumerate the main persistence locations and mechanisms across endpoints, directories, cloud identities, and network services.
Explain which logging and auditing configurations are prerequisites for detecting persistence, and what gaps remain without them.
Correlate a newly created durable artifact with the identity and process responsible for creating it.
Use change management and asset inventory data to suppress expected persistence-like activity without losing genuine anomalies.
Recognise identity-layer persistence such as application consent, federated trust changes, and long-lived credentials.
Produce a remediation checklist that removes persistence rather than only the visible malware.

topics.title: Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Privilege Escalation is the tactic covering the steps an adversary takes to move from a foothold with ordinary user rights to something far more powerful, whether that means local administrator on one host, domain-wide control, or an equivalent role in a cloud tenant. Behaviours include exploiting misconfigured services and file permissions, abusing elevation control mechanisms such as user account control bypasses, injecting code into higher-privileged processes, stealing tokens, taking advantage of overly broad sudo or role assignments, and exploiting vulnerable kernel or driver components. The defender's view differs sharply by platform. On endpoints, escalation generates process access events, token manipulation, unusual child processes of privileged services, new service or driver installation, and integrity-level changes. In identity and cloud environments it appears as role assumption, policy attachment, group membership change, or a sudden expansion of what a principal can do. This is one of the hardest tactics to detect in isolation because legitimate administration produces the same primitives, and because many escalations are simply the use of permissions that were granted too generously rather than an obvious exploitation event. Meaningful detection requires modelling what each principal should be able to do, alerting on capability changes rather than individual actions, and correlating an escalation with whatever access it enabled next, such as credential dumping or lateral movement.
objectives: Map the privilege escalation paths that matter most on Windows, Linux, and major cloud platforms, and explain how each is normally abused.
Explain what process access, token, and integrity-level telemetry reveals about escalation attempts and where it is blind.
Model expected privileges per principal so that capability expansion is detectable without relying on signature-style rules.
Correlate an escalation event with the credential access or lateral movement that follows it to establish intent and impact.
Identify the configuration weaknesses, excessive permissions, and unpatched components that make escalation possible in the first place.
Prioritise hardening actions by realistic exploitability rather than by scanner severity alone.

topics.title: Reconnaissance
topics.summary: Reconnaissance is the set of adversary activities that gather information about a target before and alongside intrusion attempts, and it is the one tactic where most of the work can happen entirely outside the victim's visibility. Attackers enumerate publicly reachable services, harvest employee names and email addresses from social media and conference sites, fingerprint technology stacks from HTTP responses and TLS certificates, review job postings for named products, and search breach data and code repositories for credentials that were never meant to be public. Active variants cross into the target's own address space: port and service scanning, directory brute forcing, DNS zone transfer attempts, and probing of VPN or webmail portals that leave firewall, load balancer, and web server logs. Telemetry available to defenders is thin and noisy. Internet-facing sensors, honeypots, passive DNS, certificate transparency monitoring, and brand monitoring can reveal scanning or credential-harvesting infrastructure, while email security gateways may show early directory-harvest attempts or spoofed display names. Detection is difficult in isolation because scanning traffic is indistinguishable from vulnerability scanners, search engine crawlers, and researchers on most networks, and because the highest-value reconnaissance often produces no packets to the target at all. Effective defence is therefore mostly preparation: reducing the public attack surface, keeping an accurate external asset inventory, monitoring certificate and DNS changes, and correlating low-severity internet telemetry so the earliest stage of a campaign is not silently discarded.
objectives: Explain how the Reconnaissance tactic maps to adversary information gathering before initial access, and why most of it never touches victim-owned infrastructure.

Identify the telemetry that genuinely exists for this tactic: internet-facing scan logs, honeypot hits, passive DNS, certificate transparency records, email gateway anomalies, and brand monitoring feeds.
Distinguish opportunistic scanning noise from targeted enumeration using source reputation, timing, target selection, and request content.
Correlate several low-severity external observations, such as certificate issuance for a lookalike domain plus a login-attempt spike, into one campaign hypothesis.
Assess how much of an estate is discoverable from the public internet and prioritise attack-surface reduction accordingly.
Write and tune triage logic that suppresses crawler and vulnerability-scanner noise without discarding targeted probing.

topics.title: Resource Development
topics.summary: Resource Development is the tactic covering the infrastructure, identities, and tooling an adversary establishes or acquires before and during a campaign, almost all of which sits on systems the victim does not own and therefore cannot monitor directly. Typical behaviour includes registering lookalike or typosquatted domains, obtaining free or stolen cloud and virtual private server capacity, acquiring code-signing certificates through fraudulent registrations, staging payloads on legitimate file-sharing or code-hosting services, purchasing or renting access from initial-access brokers, and compiling or buying tooling that matches the target's defensive stack. From the defender's side the observable surface is indirect and mostly external: newly registered domains that resemble the brand, certificate transparency entries, DNS resolutions pointing at commodity hosting, mail authentication failures from previously unseen sending infrastructure, and abuse reports from third parties. Threat intelligence platforms, domain monitoring, and collaboration with registrars or hosting providers carry much of the detection weight, while internal telemetry usually only shows the consequences of this preparation, such as phishing sent from aged accounts or payloads downloaded from reputable content networks. The tactic is hard to detect in isolation because none of the preparatory actions are inherently malicious, because infrastructure is often recycled and shared between unrelated customers, and because attribution depends on correlating weak signals over time rather than on any single high-fidelity event.
objectives: Describe the adversary goal behind Resource Development and why most of its activity is invisible to internal monitoring.
Enumerate the observable external artifacts of campaign preparation: new domains, certificates, hosting changes, staged payloads, and broker activity.
Explain how domain and certificate monitoring can be tuned to a specific brand without generating unusable alert volume.
Correlate external infrastructure indicators with inbound email and authentication telemetry to identify a campaign before payload delivery.
Evaluate the limits of attribution when adversaries reuse commodity hosting, compromised legitimate sites, and shared tooling.
Draft an escalation path that turns an external infrastructure observation into a monitored defensive action.

topics.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
topics.summary: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism describes adversary actions that subvert the way an operating system gates privilege rather than exploiting a memory-safety flaw to obtain it. The parent technique covers bypassing or spoofing user consent prompts, abusing setuid and setgid binaries on Unix-like systems, manipulating sudo configuration and policy, and any other path where a legitimate elevation mechanism is misconfigured, induced to load attacker-controlled content, or simply presented to a user as routine. On Windows the central target is the consent and credential prompt that separates a standard user session from administrative rights; on Linux and macOS it is the set of binaries, capabilities and configuration files that grant controlled privilege transitions. The mechanism is usually one of three things: a component that elevates automatically without prompting, a signed or otherwise trusted process that can be induced to load content from a user-writable location, or a configuration entry that permits a low-privileged user to run a command as another account. The artefacts are configuration and process evidence rather than exploit signatures: process creation showing unusual parentage for privileged processes, command lines invoking elevation utilities with unexpected arguments, modifications to sudoers files, setuid bits or service definitions, audit records of consent prompt outcomes, and file integrity alerts on the binaries and configuration involved. Legitimate administration generates a large volume of genuine elevation, so triage should focus on who performed the elevation, from which session and host, whether the elevated process was expected there, and whether the same account also produced other post-exploitation behaviour such as credential access or defence impairment.
objectives: Explain how consent prompts, setuid binaries, capabilities and sudo configuration each mediate privilege and where each can fail.
Identify configuration drift such as unexpected setuid bits or sudoers entries as an elevation risk.
Read process lineage for privileged processes to spot unusual parents and argument patterns.
Distinguish routine administrative elevation from adversary abuse using session, host and timing context.
Prioritise hardening of auto-elevating components and elevation policy against observed gaps.
Correlate elevation events with credential access, persistence or defence impairment on the same host.

topics.title: Account Discovery
topics.summary: Account discovery is the enumeration of user, service and machine identities that exist in an environment, usually early in an intrusion, to identify accounts worth targeting for credential access or lateral movement. The mechanism is straightforward: the adversary queries whatever directory, database or operating system interface is reachable and returns identity information. On Windows systems this includes local account enumeration through command line utilities and remote procedure calls, domain enumeration through directory service queries and management cmdlets, and reading cached or configuration stored identity data. On Linux and Unix it includes reading local account and group files, querying directory services, and inspecting configuration management and orchestration data. In cloud environments the equivalent is calling identity provider interfaces to list users, groups, roles and service principals, and examining policy documents to learn who can assume what. Telemetry differs by platform but shares a shape. Endpoint logs capture the responsible process, its command line and parent, and whether the query tool ran from an unusual location such as a temporary directory. Directory services record the bind account and the volume of search operations, and large or unusually broad queries stand out against the routine lookups that applications and helpdesk tools perform. Cloud audit logs record the calling principal, the interface operation and its result, and the source address. Investigations rarely treat a single enumeration as conclusive. Asset inventory agents, identity governance tooling, backup software, monitoring systems and legitimate administration all enumerate accounts. Analysts look instead at breadth and intent: an account listing that covers the whole directory from a workstation that normally queries nothing, enumeration performed by a service account outside its application context, queries immediately following a new foothold, or results quickly followed by authentication attempts against the accounts that were discovered. Combining the identity of the caller, the scope of the query and the sequence of subsequent actions is what separates reconnaissance from routine housekeeping.
objectives: Explain how local, domain and cloud identity enumeration differ in mechanism and in the telemetry they generate.
Interpret directory service search volume and cloud identity interface calls to identify unusually broad enumeration.
Baseline which applications, agents and administrators legitimately enumerate accounts in your environment.
Correlate enumeration with subsequent authentication attempts against the accounts that were discovered.
Distinguish service account misuse from expected application behaviour using context and source host role.
Prioritise discovery alerts by caller privilege, query scope and position in the incident timeline.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol
topics.summary: Application layer protocol abuse is the embedding of command and control inside protocols that networks and users expect to see, so the traffic resembles ordinary application use. The mechanism is protocol mimicry. An implant formats its tasking and responses to fit a legitimate carrier such as a web request, a name resolution query, a mail protocol or a file transfer service, then follows that carrier's conventions closely enough to survive inspection: valid request structure, plausible headers, expected ports, and timing that resembles a human or an agent rather than a metronome. Encrypted carriers hide payload contents but not the metadata around them, so detection shifts to connection characteristics such as destination reputation and age, certificate properties, client fingerprints that disagree with the claimed application, user agent strings that never appear elsewhere in the estate, uniform request sizes, and beacon intervals with low jitter sustained over long periods. Unencrypted or partially visible carriers expose more. Name resolution tunnelling encodes data in query names, producing long high entropy labels, elevated query rates and concentration on a single authoritative server, while web based tasking often shows repeated URI patterns, unusual content types and cookie values that carry state. The technique appears on every platform, from Windows workstations and Linux servers to containers, network appliances and cloud workloads, and it is frequently paired with exfiltration over the same channel. The investigative difficulty is that the same protocols carry enormous legitimate traffic. Software updates, telemetry agents, cloud synchronisation, package repositories and partner integrations all generate steady outbound requests. Analysts distinguish malicious use by prevalence and ownership: whether the destination is seen anywhere else in the organisation, which process makes the connection, whether the domain was registered recently or resolves to hosting with no business relationship, and whether the beacon survives reboots or follows a specific user between systems. Enrichment and deviation from baseline, not the choice of protocol, drive the verdict.
objectives: Explain how implants shape command and control traffic to conform to web, name resolution and other application protocols.
Use connection metadata such as certificate properties, client fingerprints and destination age when payload contents are encrypted.
Detect name resolution carried tasking through label entropy, query rate and authoritative server concentration.
Establish prevalence baselines for destinations, user agents and client fingerprints across the estate.
Attribute outbound connections to the responsible process and separate implant traffic from update and telemetry agents.
Map command and control findings to exfiltration and follow-on activity within a single incident timeline.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
topics.summary:
DNS command and control describes adversary use of the Domain Name System to carry instructions and data between an implant and its controller, usually by encoding information into the queried name itself and receiving instructions in resource records returned by the authoritative server. The technique works because outbound name resolution is permitted almost everywhere, is rarely inspected beyond reputation filtering, and is often logged with more consistency than other egress protocols. Variants include high-volume subdomain encoding for data transfer, low-and-slow single-label lookups for tasking, and the use of DNS over HTTPS to hide the query content inside ordinary web traffic.

The strongest artefacts are in resolver and naming data. Atypical query characteristics include very long or high-entropy labels, unusually deep label hierarchies under a single parent domain, a very high count of unique subdomains for one registered domain from a small set of hosts, and query types that a normal client population never emits in volume, such as text or null record requests. Timing analysis is equally important: automatic retry behaviour in the client stack, which yields near-constant intervals across a few resolver replicas, is a recognisable pattern. Where responses can be observed, unusually large answer sections or records carrying encoded payload deviate from normal caching behaviour. Endpoint evidence is often the decisive layer, since the process making the queries can be identified and tied to a file origin and command line.

Legitimate high-volume DNS exists in the form of content delivery networks, security vendors performing lookups, and misconfigured applications that fail repeatedly against the same name. Investigations separate these by host population, domain registration age, absence of the domain from any approved service inventory, and whether the queried labels decode to structured data rather than readable service names.
objectives: Explain how encoded labels and resource record responses allow bidirectional communication over name resolution.
Identify query entropy, label length, unique subdomain counts, and record type anomalies as detection signals.
Interpret DNS retry timing patterns caused by client resolver behaviour and why they appear so regular in logs.
Correlate resolver telemetry with endpoint process data to attribute queries to a specific binary or script.
Evaluate the visibility loss introduced by encrypted DNS transports and describe compensating controls.
Map DNS command and control to ATT&CK and rank resolver policy, egress restriction, and host telemetry by effectiveness.

topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
topics.summary:
Web protocols command and control describes adversary use of HTTP and HTTPS to carry instructions and exfiltrated data between an implant and its controller. The traffic is designed to resemble ordinary web browsing: it uses standard ports, valid transport encryption, conventional request methods and headers, and often a legitimate-looking hostname or a domain fronted by a content delivery network. Because the channel is encrypted and rides on the same infrastructure the business depends on, network inspection cannot rely on payload signatures, and detection shifts toward metadata, timing, and behavioural consistency.

Observable artefacts are concentrated in proxy, DNS, TLS, and endpoint data. Proxy logs capture the requested host, full URL path, method, user agent, response size, and byte counts in each direction, and beaconing appears as a strikingly regular interval between requests to the same endpoint from a single internal host, often continuing outside working hours. TLS metadata may reveal a self-signed or unusual certificate, a mismatch between the certificate subject and the requested hostname, or a client that fails to perform expected revocation checks. DNS logs show resolution of the controller domain, sometimes to hosting ranges rather than content networks. On the endpoint, the responsible process is frequently an unexpected binary or a legitimate one with no reason to make network connections, and its command line and file origin provide additional context.

Benign web traffic is the largest data source in any environment and includes software updates, telemetry, and cloud applications, several of which also beacon on fixed intervals. Investigations therefore combine multiple weak signals: an unusual process making regular requests, to a domain with a short registration history, with a consistent user agent that matches no deployed software, and either a long-lived connection or a request pattern that persists through nights and weekends.
objectives: Explain how adversaries shape HTTP and HTTPS traffic to resemble legitimate browsing and why payload inspection fails.
Identify beaconing through interval regularity, byte-size consistency, and persistence outside business hours in proxy logs.
Analyse TLS metadata such as certificate subject, issuer, and validity to surface infrastructure that does not match its hostname.
Correlate endpoint process telemetry with proxy and DNS records to attribute a network connection to a specific binary.
Build baselined detection logic that suppresses known update and cloud application beaconing without losing coverage.
Map web protocol command and control to ATT&CK and describe the value and limits of each mitigation available.

topics.title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
topics.summary: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution covers persistence achieved by configuring code to run automatically when a system starts, when a user logs on, or when a session state changes. Rather than one mechanism, the parent technique collects the many autostart surfaces an operating system offers: registry keys and startup folders on Windows, launch agents, launch daemons and login items on macOS, init scripts, systemd units, cron entries and shell profiles on Linux, plus vendor extension points such as print monitors, authentication packages, security support providers and browser helper components. Adversaries favour these locations because they are legitimate features, they execute early or in a privileged context, and they are frequently ignored by users and asset owners alike. The evidence is largely static and configuration-based: registry values pointing at unusual binaries, new or modified service and unit definitions, changes to shell startup files, scheduled tasks with logon triggers, and file creation in autostart directories. Because thousands of such entries are legitimately present on any mature endpoint, the useful question is not whether autostart entries exist but whether one changed recently, points to an unsigned or user-writable location, runs with higher privilege than the account that created it, or coincides with other incident activity on the same host. Baselines built from known-good images, combined with change tracking on autostart locations and file integrity monitoring, reduce an unmanageable list to a small set of reviewable differences. That same baseline supports recovery, because persistence removal during containment has to be complete without breaking the legitimate startup software an organisation depends on.
objectives: Enumerate the principal autostart locations on Windows, Linux and macOS and the privilege each confers on the executed code.
Use baselining and change tracking to reduce autostart review to a manageable set of differences.
Interpret endpoint telemetry for processes launched at boot, logon or session state change.
Judge suspicious autostart entries by path writability, signature state, parent privilege and recency.
Plan persistence removal during containment without breaking legitimate startup software.
Write detection logic for new autostart entries that reference user-writable or unsigned binaries.

topics.title: Brute Force
topics.summary: Brute force is a credential access technique in which an adversary makes repeated authentication attempts, systematically varying one or more credential components, until a logon succeeds. The mechanism is simple: the attacker obtains a valid account identifier, then submits candidate secrets such as passwords from a word list, mutated variations, default vendor credentials, PINs or short numeric codes against whichever authentication interface is reachable, including VPN gateways, webmail portals, SSH, remote desktop services, database listeners and application programming interfaces. Modern variants avoid hammering a single account. Password spraying submits one weak candidate across many accounts to stay below per-account lockout thresholds, while credential stuffing replays username and password pairs harvested from unrelated breaches, betting on password reuse. The technique appears on every platform: Windows domain services such as Kerberos and NTLM, Linux and Unix authentication stacks reachable over SSH, network device management planes, cloud identity providers and consumer facing applications. The telemetry that matters most is authentication logging. On Windows this means records of failed and successful logons, account lockouts and Kerberos pre-authentication failures; on Linux it means authentication daemon, sudo and pluggable authentication module messages; identity providers expose sign-in logs with failure reason, source address, client application and risk score, and VPN concentrators record the source address and assigned session. Investigators distinguish brute force from ordinary user error by looking at volume and shape: many failures against few accounts from few sources, or few failures against many accounts from distributed sources, unusually uniform request timing, impossible travel between successes, and a success that immediately follows a burst of failures. Benign causes include stale saved credentials on a mobile client, a service account whose password was rotated without updating configuration, and an automation script that never received the new secret, so a finding usually needs corroboration before it is treated as malicious.
objectives: Explain how brute force, password spraying and credential stuffing differ in request volume, account targeting and detection signature.
Identify the authentication telemetry sources that record guessing attempts across Windows, Linux, network devices and cloud identity providers.
Write SIEM-style queries that surface distributed low-volume spraying which per-account lockout thresholds never trigger.
Distinguish malicious guessing from stale saved credentials, misconfigured service accounts and password rotation drift.
Prioritise authentication alerts by exposure, separating internet facing services from internal systems behind segmentation.

topics.title: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
topics.summary:
Credential stuffing is an automated credential access technique in which the adversary replays username and password pairs obtained from a breach of one service against authentication endpoints of other services, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords across systems. Because each attempt uses a valid credential for some unrelated site, failure rates are low enough that modest volumes of traffic produce a meaningful number of successful logins, and per-account lockout counters are rarely triggered since each account typically sees one attempt. Attacks are usually executed from distributed residential proxy networks or botnets so that source reputation and address-based throttling do not stop the campaign.

Artefacts appear in authentication and web telemetry. Identity provider or application logs show a large number of logins from many distinct addresses that share a narrow fingerprint: identical client or user agent strings, identical header ordering, uniform inter-request timing, and no preceding session or page views. The ratio of successful to failed logins is often unusually high compared with normal user behaviour, and the first action after a successful login frequently differs from that account's historical pattern, such as immediately creating access tokens, changing registered authentication methods, or reading mailbox rules. Account recovery and password reset events may cluster afterwards if the legitimate user is displaced.

Benign lookalikes include shared network address translation egress, corporate proxy pools, and users travelling. What separates stuffing is the breadth of accounts touched, the uniformity of the client fingerprint, the absence of normal session establishment, and the correlation of the username set with a known third-party breach. Detection therefore depends on joining authentication outcomes with network-level fingerprinting rather than on any single log source.
objectives: Explain how password reuse and third-party breach data make stuffing viable, and why per-account lockout does not stop it.
Identify the client fingerprint characteristics that distinguish automated replay from genuine interactive login.
Correlate successful authentications with post-login behaviour to determine whether an account was actually taken over.
Analyse source address distribution and proxy patterns to differentiate stuffing infrastructure from corporate egress.
Prioritise accounts for forced reset and session revocation based on observed post-authentication activity.
Map credential stuffing to ATT&CK and describe the controls that reduce impact when passwords are already compromised.

topics.title: Brute Force: Password Spraying
topics.summary:
Password spraying is a credential access technique in which an adversary attempts a small number of commonly chosen passwords against a large number of accounts, inverting the traditional brute force pattern of many attempts against one account. The objective is to stay below per-account lockout thresholds and below anomaly thresholds that trigger on repeated failures for a single identity, while still finding the few accounts in any population that use a weak or seasonal password. Spraying is frequently directed at externally exposed authentication surfaces such as webmail, remote access portals, virtual desktop gateways, and identity provider endpoints, and it is often distributed across many source addresses to avoid source-based rate limits.

The distinguishing telemetry is a burst of failed authentications that is broad but shallow: many distinct usernames, few attempts each, a short time window, and a small set of repeated password-derived failure patterns. Domain controller and identity provider logs record the authentication package, the client address, the user agent or client string, and the exact failure reason, which separates a wrong password from a disabled account or a logon outside permitted hours. Successful authentication following the spray, particularly from a new address or an unusual client, is the pivot point that converts reconnaissance into an account compromise. Where multifactor authentication is enforced, the spray may still succeed against legacy protocols that do not support it, which is why protocol-level breakdown matters.

Legitimate causes of distributed failure bursts include stale credentials in a scheduled job, a misconfigured service account, or a user with an outdated cached password. The reliable discriminators are the ratio of distinct accounts to attempts, the synchronisation of retry timing, the absence of an interactive client fingerprint, and whether the source addresses belong to hosting or proxy ranges rather than corporate networks.
objectives: Explain why low-and-slow spraying evades per-account lockout thresholds and how distributed source addresses defeat source-based rate limiting.
Construct SIEM queries that surface broad shallow failure bursts and distinguish them from single-account noise.
Interpret authentication failure reasons and client fields to separate wrong-password events from policy or account-state events.
Identify which legacy or non-interactive authentication protocols bypass multifactor enforcement in a given environment.
Prioritise a spray investigation when a success occurs, and describe the immediate containment and reset sequence.
Map spraying behaviour to ATT&CK and mitigation coverage, and state where detection depends on external-facing service logging.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
topics.summary: Command and Scripting Interpreter describes the abuse of native command interpreters and scripting runtimes to execute code on a target host, chain further actions, and stage additional payloads without necessarily writing a conventional executable to disk. The parent technique covers interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell, Unix shells, Python, JavaScript engines and platform-specific automation hosts, and it appears on Windows, Linux, macOS, network appliances and inside container and cloud execution contexts wherever a shell or runtime is reachable. At a mechanism level the adversary runs an interpreter interactively, passes commands as arguments, or loads script content from a local file, a remote share, or an encoded blob that is decoded into memory at execution time. The telemetry this produces is rich but noisy: process creation records showing interpreter binaries with unusual parent processes, command lines containing encoded or obfuscated arguments, script block and module logging on Windows, process accounting and execve audit records on Linux, shell history files, and the child processes the interpreter subsequently spawns. Investigators separate malicious from benign use by examining the parent-child relationship, the user and session context, the working directory and destination of any download, whether the interpreter was launched by a service or scheduled task, whether logging captured the full script content, and whether the same interpreter and argument pattern recurs across hosts at a rate that matches an automated campaign rather than an administrator. Change windows, software deployment tooling and signed management agents explain a large share of legitimate interpreter invocations, so the bar for escalation should be unusual lineage, unusual content or unusual timing rather than the mere presence of the interpreter.
objectives: Describe how interpreters such as PowerShell, the Windows command shell and Unix shells are invoked and how their command lines differ from routine administrative use.
Identify the process-creation, script-block, module and shell-history telemetry that records interpreter execution across Windows and Linux estates.
Explain how encoded or obfuscated interpreter arguments are surfaced in logging and where visibility gaps typically appear.
Distinguish adversary interpreter abuse from legitimate automation, configuration management and software deployment activity.
Design detection logic that keys on process lineage, argument content and cross-host recurrence rather than on interpreter presence alone.
Assess how interpreter logging configuration and constrained language modes change both visibility and attacker cost.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
topics.summary:
PowerShell is a task automation and configuration management framework from Microsoft, consisting of a command-line shell and an associated scripting language built on the .NET runtime. It is a first-class execution mechanism on Windows and is also available on Linux and macOS, which makes it attractive to adversaries because it ships with the operating system, is signed by Microsoft, and gives direct access to the .NET framework, WMI, Active Directory, and the registry without dropping a compiled binary to disk. Execution ranges from a simple encoded command passed to powershell.exe, to in-memory assembly loading through reflection, to full script blocks delivered over a remote session.

The telemetry footprint is unusually rich compared with most interpreters. Process creation records the full command line, which frequently exposes switches such as -enc, -nop, -w hidden, or -exec bypass. Script Block Logging writes the de-obfuscated script text to the event log, and Module Logging captures cmdlet invocations even when the script itself is heavily encoded. PowerShell transcription can record console input and output to files, and the Antimalware Scan Interface reports suspicious script content to the registered antivirus engine. Network-enabled cmdlets produce connections associated with the responsible process, and constrained language mode changes appear in the runtime's own logging.

Benign administrative use is pervasive in most enterprises, so volume alone proves nothing. Investigations distinguish malicious from routine activity by correlating parent process and user context, looking for scripting that originates from Office applications, web browsers, or service accounts that should never run interactive shells, and by comparing the target hosts against software deployment and configuration management baselines. Scripts arriving from temporary directories, download URLs appearing inside command lines, and execution outside change-management windows are stronger signals than the presence of PowerShell itself.
objectives: Explain how the PowerShell host resolves execution policy, what that policy actually constrains, and why it is not a security boundary in production.
Identify the specific process creation fields and log sources that expose encoded, obfuscated, or in-memory script execution.
Interpret Script Block Logging and Module Logging output and reconstruct a script's behaviour from the de-obfuscated text.
Correlate suspicious PowerShell process ancestry, such as Office or browser parents, with subsequent network and file activity.
Distinguish delegated administrative automation from adversary tradecraft using user context, host baseline, and change windows.
Map observed PowerShell behaviour to the relevant ATT&CK technique and describe the residual detection gaps in the environment.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
topics.summary:
A Unix shell is a command interpreter such as sh, bash, zsh, ksh, or dash that provides an interactive interface and a scripting language for Unix-like operating systems, including Linux, macOS, and the BSD family. It exposes pipelines, redirection, job control, variable and command substitution, and access to the full set of system utilities, which together make it a complete execution environment. Adversaries use it to run reconnaissance, download and stage payloads, establish persistence through cron or shell profile files, and pivot to remote hosts using the same credentials. Because the shell is the primary administrative interface on these systems, its presence is normal and only behaviour inside it differentiates intent.

Telemetry comes from several layers. Process execution auditing via the kernel audit subsystem, EDR process telemetry, or container runtime logs captures the argv of each spawned process, and the parent-child tree shows whether a shell was launched by a web server, database service, or container entrypoint. Shell history files record interactive commands but are trivially edited and often disabled. Scripts written to disk leave file creation and permission change events, and interactive shells frequently write to /tmp, /var/tmp, or the home directory, which may appear in file integrity monitoring. Audit records for executed syscalls supplement process data where the agent does not capture full argument vectors.

Legitimate shells are everywhere: package installers, container entrypoints, health checks, and administrator sessions. Investigations therefore anchor on context rather than on the interpreter. Shells spawned by internet-facing daemons, execution under an account whose normal role is non-interactive, odd execution paths, base64 decoding pipelines, and outbound connections immediately following shell creation are the reliable signals. Building a baseline of which service accounts execute shells on which hosts converts a very noisy dataset into a workable detection surface.
objectives: Explain how shell features such as pipelines, substitution, and redirection shape both behaviour and the arguments visible in telemetry.
Interpret process execution audit records and reconstruct a shell command sequence from parent-child lineage.
Assess how shell history, container logs, and file integrity monitoring each contribute to or mislead an investigation.
Distinguish shells spawned by internet-facing services from routine administrative or automation-driven execution.
Design a service account and host baseline that reduces false positives for shell execution detections at scale.
Map observed Unix shell behaviour to ATT&CK and identify which residual gaps require additional instrumentation.

topics.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
topics.summary:
The Windows Command Shell, implemented by cmd.exe, is the legacy interpreter for batch files and interactive command execution on Windows. It provides built-in commands for file manipulation, process and service control, network configuration, and scheduled task creation, and it acts as a launcher for other utilities. Adversaries favour it because it is universally present, is not typically removed by hardening, and blends with a very high volume of legitimate administrative and installer traffic. Typical abuse patterns involve chaining built-in commands together with shell redirection and the command separator to perform discovery, staging, and cleanup within a single short-lived process.

The artefacts left behind are concentrated in process creation telemetry. The parent process is often more informative than cmd.exe itself, because the shell is frequently spawned by a document reader, a script host, a service, or a webshell. Command lines containing long chains of separators, repeated directory traversal toward temporary or public directories, and redirection into executable file types are notable. Script Block Logging does not cover cmd.exe, so visibility depends on command line auditing, the process creation event source used by the endpoint agent, and file and registry events generated by whatever the shell touched. Batch files executed from user-writable paths leave a file creation record that may be deleted immediately afterwards.

Routine use includes login scripts, software deployment wrappers, backup jobs, and diagnostic commands run by administrators. The distinguishing factors are context and sequence: an unusual parent, a service account running console utilities interactively, network share access immediately preceding shell execution, and command content that maps to discovery or staging rather than to a scheduled maintenance task. Comparing the observed command line against the standard image of the host and against known automation accounts resolves most apparent positives.
objectives: Describe how cmd.exe parses command separators, redirection, and quoting, and why that parsing shapes what appears in log records.
Extract and interpret parent-child process relationships that indicate a shell spawned by an unexpected host application.
Build SIEM-style queries that surface anomalous command shell usage while suppressing known installer and login script noise.
Reconstruct a short shell session from command line auditing, file creation, and registry events when no script logging is available.
Explain the visibility limitations of resource kit tooling historically used to log console activity and how it fails on modern systems.
Map observed shell behaviour to ATT&CK and document the specific telemetry gaps that remain in the environment.

topics.title: Create Account
topics.summary: Create Account describes adversary creation of new accounts to maintain access after an initial foothold is lost or remediated. The accounts involved can be local or domain user accounts, accounts holding administrative rights, cloud and SaaS identities, service principals, or machine accounts created through directory APIs, and they can be created on a single host, in the enterprise directory, or in a hosted tenant the organisation only partially monitors. The technique is favoured because a fresh account survives the password resets that remediation applies to compromised existing accounts, blends into the constant background churn of real onboarding, and can be granted additional rights quietly if the adversary already holds privilege. The mechanism usually involves ordinary administrative interfaces rather than exploits: command-line account management utilities, remote management protocols, directory and cloud identity APIs, and application-specific user administration consoles. The artefacts are concentrated in directory and audit telemetry, including account creation events, group membership additions, privilege role assignments, cloud provider audit records, and the authentication activity of the new identity afterwards. Benign account creation is continuous in most environments, driven by hiring, contractor onboarding, automation and service deployment, so an investigation should weigh the identity of the creator, the interval between creation and first use, the privileges requested or assigned, how naming and description conventions compare with organisational standards, and whether the creating identity was itself recently established or recently elevated. Accounts created and then used immediately, added straight into a privileged group, or authenticating from unexpected infrastructure are the cases that warrant escalation, and reviewing them against a documented joiner process is usually what separates a real incident from a noisy one.
objectives: Identify the account types an adversary can create and the visibility each provides to the defender.
Interpret directory, local and cloud audit records to reconstruct who created an account and when.
Detect create-and-use patterns by comparing account creation with subsequent authentication activity.
Evaluate naming, privilege and approval controls that make rogue accounts distinguishable from legitimate ones.
Explain how identity governance and periodic access review limit the lifetime of adversary accounts.
Write detection logic for privileged account creation and for sensitive group membership changes.
