topics.title: Data Encrypted for Impact
topics.summary: Data encrypted for impact is the technique of rendering data unusable to its owner by encrypting it in place, typically to extort payment or to degrade an organisation's ability to operate. The mechanism relies on the same cryptographic primitives that protect data legitimately: a symmetric cipher such as AES with a randomly generated key for bulk file content, and asymmetric or hybrid wrapping of that key so the victim cannot recover it without the adversary's secret. Implementations vary. Some call operating system cryptographic interfaces, some ship a self-contained binary, and some abuse legitimate administration and backup tooling already trusted in the environment. Targets are chosen for operational value: user documents on workstations, file shares, database files, virtual machine disks and datastores, cloud object storage, and increasingly the backup repositories that would otherwise permit recovery. The technique appears on Windows, Linux, macOS, hypervisor platforms and cloud infrastructure, and it is frequently preceded by credential access, discovery and defence evasion, then accompanied or followed by inhibition of system recovery. Telemetry is distinctive at scale even when individual operations look ordinary. Investigators look for a single process touching thousands of files in a short window, bulk renames or extension changes, mass modification of file timestamps, sudden entropy shifts in stored content, note files written across many directories, deletion or truncation of shadow copies and snapshots, and storage performance anomalies. Endpoint detection platforms surface the responsible process tree, its parent, the account it runs under and the command line that launched it; file server and storage logs show the fan-out; backup and hypervisor audit logs show snapshot removal. Distinguishing this from benign encryption is a matter of scope and context. Full disk encryption tools, archive utilities, backup agents, synchronisation clients and mass deployment scripts all write many files, but they run on a known schedule, under known service accounts, with change records, and without note files or recovery tampering. Correlation of encryption activity with recovery inhibition, unusual account use and concurrent exfiltration is what turns a performance problem into a confirmed impact event.
objectives: Explain how hybrid encryption makes bulk data unrecoverable while keeping the decryption key outside the victim environment.
Recognise the file system, storage and backup telemetry that indicates mass encryption rather than normal archival or synchronisation.
Correlate encryption activity with recovery inhibition, credential access and exfiltration to confirm an impact event.
Separate legitimate full disk encryption, backup and deployment tooling from malicious encryption using scope, account and change records.
Prioritise response steps that preserve evidence and protect remaining recovery capability before containment.
Design detection coverage for hypervisor, cloud object storage and backup platforms rather than endpoint file systems alone.

topics.title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a command and control channel is the transfer of collected data out of a victim environment using the same communication path the adversary already uses to task and control implanted tooling. The mechanism matters because it removes a separate, conspicuous egress channel from the operation: the implant beacons to its controller, receives instructions, and returns results inside the same session, often over HTTPS to blend with ordinary web traffic but also over DNS, mail protocols, or a custom binary protocol on a non-standard port. Data is typically staged first, compressed and sometimes encrypted or encoded, then split into chunks that fit the profile of the carrier protocol, with the encoded bytes placed in request bodies, headers, URI parameters or DNS query names. Because command and control traffic is already expected to be periodic, exfiltration rides inside a pattern defenders must baseline before they can spot the change. The technique appears on endpoints, servers and cloud workloads alike, and the observable artefacts differ by vantage point. Network flow records show asymmetric byte counts, with outbound volume far exceeding inbound, across long lived sessions to the same destination. Web proxies and inspection logs show repeated uploads, unusual content types, large request bodies and consistent request sizes or timing. Name resolution logs show elevated query volume, long or high entropy subdomains and repeated queries to a single authoritative server. Endpoint telemetry captures the preceding collection and staging: archive creation, bulk file reads, access to database exports, clipboard or screen capture. Distinguishing malicious transfer from benign uploads requires context. Cloud synchronisation, update reporting, telemetry agents, backup replication and video conferencing all produce sustained outbound flows. Investigators therefore weigh destination reputation and age, whether the destination appears on any approved list, which process owns the connection, whether timing is machine regular, and whether the transfer coincides with staging activity on the same host.
objectives: Explain how an implant multiplexes command, control and data transfer over a single channel and why that complicates egress monitoring.
Interpret network flow asymmetries, long lived sessions and repeated upload patterns as candidate exfiltration rather than routine traffic.
Correlate endpoint staging artefacts such as archive creation and bulk file reads with outbound network volume on the same host.
Analyse name resolution carried transfer patterns using query volume, label entropy and authoritative server concentration.
Tune proxy, network detection and data loss prevention rules to reduce false positives from synchronisation, patch delivery and telemetry reporting.
Describe containment choices that stop the transfer without destroying evidence of the channel or the staged data.

topics.title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a web service moves data out of an environment through legitimate, publicly available or tenant sanctioned online services rather than through adversary controlled infrastructure. The mechanism sidesteps the assumption that egress to unknown destinations is the thing worth blocking. Instead, the transfer goes to a code repository, object storage bucket, file sharing site, paste service, webmail account, messaging platform or collaboration tool that either already appears on an allow list or is indistinguishable in a proxy log from ordinary collaboration. Two patterns dominate. The first uses the provider's public interface or web front end from an endpoint or server, uploading data with an authenticated or anonymous session over an encrypted channel. The second abuses services already provisioned inside the organisation, where the adversary has obtained an account and moves data into a personal folder, shares it externally, or grants a third party application permission to read it. Telemetry sits at three layers. Network and proxy logs show upload volume, session duration and destination service, but the payload is encrypted, so detection depends on comparing volume and frequency against the user's or host's baseline. Cloud and software as a service audit logs are richer: file creation, download, external sharing, permission changes, mailbox rule creation and third party application consent grants are recorded with actor, time and client application. Endpoint telemetry captures the preceding collection and staging steps, such as archiving directories, exporting mailboxes, reading databases or capturing screen content. The challenge is baseline noise. Synchronisation clients, build pipelines, backup products, log shippers and ordinary document collaboration generate large uploads continuously. Investigators distinguish malicious use by whose account is acting, whether the destination or sharing scope is new for that user, whether volume departs sharply from history, whether activity occurs outside working hours or from an unusual client, whether a new application consent appeared shortly before, and whether staging activity is visible on the source host at the same time. Sanctioned service visibility is only useful if the organisation has inventoried which services it actually uses.
objectives: Explain how legitimate web services and tenant sanctioned applications can serve as exfiltration channels.
Use cloud and software as a service audit logs to identify uploads, external sharing and permission changes by actor and client.
Baseline per user and per host upload volumes to detect transfers that hide inside encrypted traffic.
Detect malicious third party application consent as a precursor to data access and transfer.
Correlate endpoint collection and staging artefacts with service side upload activity.
Prioritise sanctioned service abuse over generic egress alerts using data classification and account context.

topics.title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
topics.summary: Exploit Public-Facing Application covers adversary exploitation of weaknesses in internet-reachable software to obtain code execution, data access or a foothold inside a network. The targets are the services an organisation deliberately exposes: web applications and their frameworks, remote access and virtual private network gateways, file transfer and mail servers, content management systems, and the APIs behind them. The mechanism is usually a flaw in input handling, authentication or deserialisation that lets an attacker influence server-side behaviour, but the category also includes misconfiguration such as an exposed administrative interface, a default credential on an appliance, or a debug endpoint left reachable, as well as exploitation of a dependency the application implicitly trusts. Time matters a great deal, because exploitation commonly follows public vulnerability disclosure closely and internet-wide scanning means exposed hosts are probed continuously, so telemetry often shows attempts against many assets rather than one carefully chosen request. The evidence lives in web and reverse proxy access logs, web application firewall and intrusion detection alerts, application error logs, process creation on the host running the service, and network flow records. An investigation must separate attempted exploitation from successful compromise, which requires correlating an anomalous request with a subsequent child process, a new file, an outbound connection or a configuration change on the same asset within a coherent time window. Heavy legitimate traffic, commercial vulnerability scanners and benign crawlers generate enormous volumes of superficially malicious requests, so triage should weight requests that returned a success status, that plausibly reached the vulnerable code path, and that were followed by follow-on activity on the affected host.
objectives: Identify which internet-facing assets and software versions carry exploitation risk and how exposure is verified rather than assumed.
Read web, proxy and application logs to distinguish probing from a request that reached vulnerable code.
Correlate a suspicious request with post-exploitation evidence such as child processes, new files or outbound connections.
Explain how virtual patching, web application firewall rules and rapid patching differ in coverage and operational cost.
Build a prioritisation method that combines exploit availability, exposure and asset criticality.
Write detection logic that keys on exploitation behaviour rather than on attacker-controlled request strings alone.

topics.title: External Remote Services
topics.summary: External Remote Services describes adversary use of legitimate remote access services to gain an initial foothold or to re-enter an environment from outside the perimeter. The services involved are ones the organisation exposes deliberately for business reasons: virtual private network concentrators, remote desktop gateways, remote shell and file transfer services, and hosted remote management or desktop-as-a-service platforms. Because the service is expected to be reachable and the protocol itself is legitimate, the technique sits on the boundary between initial access and persistence, and identical session types appear in both contexts. At a mechanism level an adversary authenticates with credentials obtained elsewhere, uses a valid account issued to a contractor or third party, exploits or misconfigures the gateway itself, or registers an account with a cloud-hosted remote access platform that the organisation cannot see at all. The telemetry lives mainly in the gateway and identity layers: authentication records with source address, client and device attributes, session start and duration, concurrent session anomalies, and configuration changes to the service, after which endpoint records show what the session did once established. Investigations separate legitimate remote work from abuse by examining the source network and its reputation, whether the account was expected to use that client and that geography, whether the session coincided with password spraying or credential stuffing activity, and whether the same account performed administrative actions outside its normal pattern. Strong controls tie every exposed service to multifactor authentication and device posture rather than treating network reachability as sufficient proof of identity, and they log enough session context to reconstruct who connected from where and when.
objectives: Inventory externally reachable remote access services and identify which are business-essential.
Read gateway authentication and session logs to establish source, client and duration for a session.
Correlate a remote session with identity anomalies and with post-authentication endpoint activity.
Evaluate multifactor, device posture and session recording controls for each remote access path.
Explain how third-party and hosted remote management platforms complicate visibility and attribution.
Write detection logic for remote sessions from unexpected geographies or concurrent with credential attacks.

topics.title: Impair Defenses
topics.summary: Impairing defenses is the deliberate degradation, misconfiguration or removal of security controls so that subsequent activity is neither observed nor blocked. The mechanism exploits the fact that defenders administer their own tools through the same operating system, directory and cloud control planes the adversary is trying to reach. On endpoints this can mean stopping or disabling antivirus and endpoint detection services, altering their configuration to add exclusions, unloading security drivers, tampering with logging agents, or editing firewall rules to permit traffic that policy would otherwise deny. In the identity and cloud control plane it can mean weakening audit configuration, disabling conditional access or log export, removing alerting integrations, or using a legitimate administrative role to change a policy that protects many accounts at once. A quieter variant disables nothing outright but blinds a specific sensor by reducing event verbosity, excluding a directory from scanning, or reconfiguring a collection rule so the activity of interest stops generating records. The artefacts are unusually valuable because they look administrative. Service state transitions, configuration and registry changes to security products, termination of protected processes, audit policy modifications, unexpected gaps in log ingestion and control plane change records all appear in the same places legitimate administration appears. Investigators therefore treat timing, actor and authorisation as the discriminators. A change made during a maintenance window by a known engineering account, with a change record and a plausible scope, is routine. The same change made outside any window by a newly created or compromised account, scoped narrowly to the hosts or accounts currently under investigation, and immediately followed by unusual authentication or execution activity, is a strong indicator. Gaps in telemetry matter as much as explicit disablement: a host that stops reporting, a sensor that no longer emits an expected event class, or a retention setting quietly shortened can serve the same objective with far less noise.
objectives: Explain how endpoint, directory and cloud control planes can each be used to degrade or disable security controls.
Recognise the administrative looking artefacts that indicate tampering, including service state changes and security product configuration edits.
Use telemetry gaps and unexpected changes in log volume as evidence in their own right.
Differentiate sanctioned maintenance from malicious impairment using change records, actor identity, scope and timing.
Correlate impairment events with the authentication, discovery or execution activity that follows them.
Recommend monitoring and hardening that keeps tamper attempts visible even when a control has been successfully disabled.

topics.title: Inhibit System Recovery
topics.summary: Inhibiting system recovery is the removal or disablement of the mechanisms that would let an organisation restore systems and data after destructive activity. It is the step that converts a recoverable outage into an existential one, and it is usually executed shortly before or alongside mass encryption or wiping activity. The mechanism targets every layer of resilience. On endpoints and file servers, native utilities that manage volume shadow copies and system restore points can delete recovery data, and boot configuration or recovery partitions can be modified so that built in repair options no longer work. Backup catalogues, backup files and backup agents can be deleted, stopped or reconfigured to point at storage that has been wiped, and backup infrastructure is often attacked directly because it holds credentials and trust relationships for everything else. In virtualised environments, hypervisor snapshots and datastores are removed. In cloud environments, snapshot deletion, backup vault tampering, retention policy changes and lifecycle rule manipulation achieve the same result through authenticated control plane calls. The telemetry is administrative and therefore easy to overlook. Endpoint and file server logs show shadow copy, restore point and backup service operations, often with the calling process, account and command line. Backup product audit logs record job deletion, catalogue changes and retention edits, and a sudden drop in successful backup jobs is itself a signal. Hypervisor and cloud audit logs record snapshot and vault operations together with the caller principal. Investigators distinguish malicious recovery inhibition from routine operations by correlating it with encryption, credential access and defence evasion in the same window, by checking whether the operation was scoped far more broadly than normal, by examining the account that performed it and whether that account was recently created or compromised, and by confirming the absence of a change record. Legitimate backup rotation and storage reclamation follow schedules and retain older copies, whereas malicious removal tends to be comprehensive and immediate. Monitoring that treats backup and snapshot deletion as high severity events in their own right is the most reliable control.
objectives: Explain how recovery inhibition targets endpoint, backup, hypervisor and cloud layers of resilience.
Identify the administrative artefacts that reveal shadow copy, snapshot, backup job and retention policy tampering.
Treat sudden degradation in backup success rates and catalogue integrity as a detection signal.
Differentiate scheduled backup rotation and storage reclamation from comprehensive malicious removal.
Correlate recovery inhibition with concurrent encryption, credential access and defence evasion activity.
Recommend monitoring, immutability and out of band recovery design that keeps restoration possible during an incident.

topics.title: Phishing
topics.summary: Phishing is the delivery of a deceptive message to a person in order to obtain credentials, execution or access on a system the sender cannot reach directly. The parent technique spans three broad vectors: messages carrying a malicious attachment, messages carrying a link to adversary-controlled or compromised infrastructure, and messages sent through a third-party service such as a collaboration platform, social network or messaging application rather than through corporate mail. At a mechanism level the adversary convinces the recipient to open a file that executes or exploits a client application, to follow a link that harvests credentials or serves a browser exploit, or to act on social pressure alone and hand over a token, a code or a decision. The artefacts an investigation relies on are spread across the mail path and the endpoint: message headers and authentication results, attachment names, types and hashes, rewritten or proxied URL records, gateway verdicts, web proxy and DNS logs for the destination, identity provider sign-in records for any captured credential, and process creation on the endpoint if something executed. Benign mail that resembles phishing is extremely common, since bulk marketing, file-sharing notifications, e-signature requests and internal awareness campaigns all share the same shape, so triage should weigh sender reputation and authentication failures, the age and hosting of the destination domain, whether other recipients in the same tenant received an identical message, and whether any recipient actually interacted rather than merely received it. Containment decisions follow the same evidence: resetting credentials, blocking a domain and removing a message are cheap, while quarantining a mailbox or rebuilding a host demands proof of interaction.
objectives: Describe how attachment, link and service-based phishing differ in delivery path and in the telemetry each produces.
Read message headers, authentication results and gateway verdicts to decide whether a reported message is genuinely malicious.
Correlate mail, proxy, DNS and identity logs to determine whether a recipient interacted with a phishing message.
Explain how URL rewriting, sandbox detonation and attachment detonation change the evidence available during triage.
Separate high-volume legitimate mail from phishing by evaluating sender reputation, domain age and tenant-wide recipient patterns.
Write detection logic for newly registered domains, display-name mismatch and authentication failure without flooding the queue.
Choose proportionate containment for a confirmed delivery, a confirmed click and a confirmed execution.

topics.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
topics.summary:
Spearphishing attachment is a targeted social engineering technique in which an adversary sends an email containing a malicious or weaponised file to a specific individual or small group, relying on the recipient to open it and trigger execution. The attachment is usually a document format that supports embedded macros or scripting, an archive that conceals the true file type, a shortcut or container file that resolves to a remote resource, or a disk image that bypasses attachment filtering. Delivery is often preceded by reconnaissance to select a plausible sender identity and a pretext matching the recipient's role, and the message body typically supplies a reason to enable content or to ignore a warning.

Artefacts span the mail gateway, the endpoint, and the network. The gateway logs record sender infrastructure, authentication results for the sending domain, attachment names, and hashes, which support correlation across recipients. On the endpoint, the file write event is followed by the spawning of a document reader or archive handler and then by an unexpected child process such as a script interpreter, a shell, or a system utility. Office applications may record the document's origin and protected view behaviour, and the mark-of-the-web alternative data stream indicates the file arrived from an untrusted source. Where the attachment fetches remote content, proxy records show the retrieval.

Benign business attachments are constant, so triage is driven by the relationship between the file and what it caused. A document that triggered a script interpreter, a shortcut pointing at a remote host, or an archived executable whose extraction coincides with an outbound connection are high-confidence signals. Investigations that begin from a user report should confirm whether other recipients received the same message hash and whether any of them produced the same child process pattern.
objectives: Explain how attachment formats such as macro-enabled documents, archives, shortcut files, and disk images each reach an execution point.
Identify gateway, endpoint, and file system artefacts that link a delivered message to an observed process on a host.
Interpret parent-child process relationships that indicate a document reader or archive handler triggered execution.
Correlate attachment hashes across mail logs and endpoint telemetry to determine the true scope of a campaign.
Distinguish user-initiated benign macro use from adversarial weaponised documents using trust, origin, and behavioural context.
Map attachment tradecraft to ATT&CK and describe the detection coverage gaps left by email filtering alone.

topics.title: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
topics.summary:
Spearphishing link is a targeted technique in which the adversary sends a message containing a hyperlink and relies on the recipient to click it, after which the browser is directed to infrastructure controlled by the attacker. The destination may host a credential harvesting page that mimics a legitimate login portal, a page that serves a malicious download, a redirect chain that filters out automated analysis, or a consent screen for an identity provider that grants persistent access. Links are frequently wrapped behind legitimate marketing or file-sharing domains, and the visible anchor text rarely matches the underlying destination, which defeats naive keyword inspection.

The evidence trail is split between mail, identity, proxy, and endpoint sources. Mail gateway and message trace records capture the URL and its rewriting service, giving a campaign-wide view when the same link is sent to multiple recipients. Secure web gateway and proxy logs show the click, the redirect chain, the user agent, and any subsequent file download, while DNS records expose resolution of first-stage domains. If credentials were entered, identity provider sign-in logs show the authentication together with contextual signals such as geography, device, and whether multifactor authentication was satisfied or bypassed. Browser and endpoint telemetry capture the download and the process that followed it.

Benign newsletters, password reset messages, and vendor notifications all generate clicks to external links, so prevalence alone is not actionable. Investigations focus on destination reputation and age, the mismatch between sender identity and link domain, the authentication outcome for the affected account, and whether a download or an unusual OAuth consent followed. Any credential submission must be treated as a potential account compromise rather than a simple click event, because the response differs substantially.
objectives: Explain how redirect chains, URL rewriting services, and hosted landing pages shape the evidence available after a click.
Correlate mail trace data with proxy and DNS records to reconstruct the full path from message to destination.
Analyse identity provider sign-in logs to determine whether a click resulted in credential or token compromise.
Identify contextual authentication anomalies such as impossible travel, new device, or unexpected consent grants.
Distinguish routine marketing-link clicks from adversary traffic using domain age, reputation, and post-click behaviour.
Map link-based phishing to ATT&CK and state which telemetry sources must be retained for retrospective hunting.

topics.title: Phishing: Spearphishing via Service
topics.summary:
Spearphishing via service is a targeted technique in which the adversary delivers a lure through a third-party platform rather than through corporate email. The channel may be a social network direct message, a professional networking site, a personal webmail account, a collaboration tool, a code hosting platform, or a voice and video service. Because these platforms sit outside the organisation's mail gateway, messages bypass attachment and URL filtering entirely, and the conversation often establishes rapport over several exchanges before any link or file is sent. The adversary may also impersonate a recruiter, vendor, or technical support contact to make the request plausible.

Detection is genuinely harder here because the primary evidence lives with a third party that the organisation does not control. What remains observable is the endpoint and identity side: the browser process for the service, the file download that follows a chat-based transfer, the executable that runs from a downloads or temporary directory, and the subsequent authentication or command activity. Where the organisation operates an enterprise tier of the platform, its audit and eDiscovery interfaces can provide message and file transfer records, and data loss prevention or secure web gateway logs may capture uploads and downloads. On the identity side, device registration and sign-in records show whether a lure led to credential capture or consent grant.

Routine use of these platforms for legitimate business communication is heavy, which makes behavioural baselines essential. Investigations look for downloads from collaboration or social domains that immediately precede process execution, files arriving through chat from external tenants, and users interacting with newly created or unverified accounts. Because the initial message may not be recoverable, endpoint evidence often carries the entire investigation, so retention and process telemetry quality determine whether scope can be established.
objectives: Explain why third-party delivery channels bypass mail gateway controls and what compensating telemetry exists.
Identify endpoint artefacts that reveal a file delivered through a collaboration or social platform rather than email.
Use platform audit interfaces and eDiscovery tooling where available to reconstruct external message delivery.
Correlate chat-based file transfers with subsequent process execution, authentication, or file system changes.
Distinguish routine business use of collaboration tools from adversary rapport-building and payload delivery.
Map service-based phishing to ATT&CK and communicate the investigative limitations created by third-party data custody.

topics.title: Process Injection
topics.summary: Process Injection covers techniques that place adversary code or data inside the address space of another running process so that execution appears to originate from a trusted binary. The parent technique spans several distinct mechanisms, including remote thread creation, memory allocation and writing followed by execution, section and file mapping abuse, asynchronous procedure calls, and manipulation of existing process or thread contexts, and its descendants differ mainly in which operating system interface they use to achieve the same result. Adversaries value injection because the code inherits the target process identity, token and reputation, can evade allow-listing that keys on the original image path, and can hide from tools that enumerate only top-level processes. The behaviour is most commonly described on Windows, but comparable approaches exist on Linux and macOS through debugging interfaces, dynamic loader features and memory mapping, and it appears in cloud and container workloads where a shared kernel makes cross-process visibility weaker. Telemetry is deliberately subtle: memory allocation and protection changes inside another process, thread creation in a process that should not create threads, cross-process handle acquisition, image loads from unusual paths, and instrumentation callbacks reported by endpoint agents. Because debuggers, crash reporters, backup agents, accessibility software, anti-cheat components and security products all legitimately manipulate other processes, an investigation hinges on establishing a benign parent, a signed and expected tool, and a plausible operational reason for the cross-process operation. When no such explanation exists, the combination of allocation, write, protection change and execution in one target process within a short window is far more meaningful than any single isolated event, and sequencing those events is what makes the detection defensible.
objectives: Describe the main injection mechanisms and the distinct API or system-call patterns each produces.
Interpret endpoint telemetry for cross-process memory allocation, protection changes and remote thread creation.
Explain which legitimate tools manipulate other processes and how to rule them out during triage.
Correlate injection indicators with subsequent credential access, network beaconing or defence impairment.
Assess how endpoint protection configuration affects both the visibility and the blocking of injection behaviour.
Write detection logic that sequences related events rather than alerting on isolated ones.

topics.title: Remote Services
topics.summary: Remote services is the use of legitimate remote access protocols and their native authentication to log on to another host and act there, rather than exploiting a vulnerability to gain a foothold. The technique exploits trust that already exists: domain credentials, SSH keys, administrative shares or a management plane that accepts connections from an internal network segment. Common carriers include Remote Desktop Protocol, Server Message Block and administrative shares, SSH, Windows Remote Management, and virtual network computing, with the same pattern appearing against cloud instances through their management interfaces. Mechanism level distinctions matter for detection. Interactive desktop protocols create session records and generate logon events with a network logon type on the destination. File sharing protocols leave share access records and service creation artefacts when tooling is copied and executed. Remote shell protocols produce authentication records, session start and end entries, and process trees whose parent is a remote service rather than a local shell. The consistent thread is that the destination sees an inbound authenticated session from an internal address that is not part of its normal peer set. Investigators reconstruct the movement path from source and destination pairs: which account authenticated, from which workstation, at what time, using which protocol, and whether that pair appears anywhere in historical baselines. Jump hosts, patch management, configuration management agents, helpdesk remote support, backup software and monitoring systems all legitimately connect to many hosts, so volume alone proves nothing. Discrimination comes from the account used, the protocol chosen relative to the destination role, the presence of default administrative share access or new service registration, off hours timing, whether the source is itself a workstation rather than a hardened management host, and whether discovery or credential access activity immediately precedes the connection. Sequence and context convert a common administrative event into evidence of lateral movement.
objectives: Explain how remote desktop, file sharing, SSH and remote management protocols differ in the logon and session artefacts they create.
Identify the authentication, service creation and session records that let investigators reconstruct a lateral movement path.
Build baselines of legitimate source to destination pairs for jump hosts, patch management and helpdesk tooling.
Recognise default administrative share access and new remote service registration as higher confidence indicators than connection volume alone.
Rank candidate lateral movement alerts by destination role, account privilege and proximity to discovery or credential access activity.
Select containment actions that terminate remote sessions while preserving destination side evidence.

topics.title: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
topics.summary:
Remote Desktop Protocol is a Microsoft protocol that provides graphical remote access to a Windows session, and it is one of the most common lateral movement mechanisms because it is enabled by default on many server builds and requires only valid credentials and reachable network access. An adversary who has obtained credentials or a session token can authenticate to a target host, interact with the desktop as the compromised identity, and from that host repeat the process toward further systems. The same protocol is used for legitimate administration and remote work, which is why detection depends on context, direction of travel, and authentication characteristics rather than on the protocol itself.

Events are recorded on both ends. The source host shows a client process and outbound connection to the destination port, while the destination host records the logon with a network logon type, the source address, and often a dedicated operational log for connection and session events that captures the connecting account, address, and session identifiers. Where a gateway or jump host mediates access, gateway logs supply the external source address and may reveal whether the connection was brokered by a known administrative path. Additional artefacts include the creation of user profile directories on first logon, drive and clipboard redirection activity, and any process spawned from the session.

Benign remote desktop traffic is extremely heavy in most estates, frequently originating from administrative subnets and management platforms. Investigations look at whether the destination host is one this account or this source normally reaches, whether the connection occurred outside a change window, whether the authentication used a local or domain account that should not be used interactively on that host, and what happened immediately after the session began. Compromised sessions frequently exhibit short dwell time, tool execution, and a rapid sequence of connections to additional hosts using the same credentials.
objectives: Explain how network logon types, session identifiers, and connection logs combine to identify remote desktop access to a host.
Correlate source-side client process telemetry with destination-side authentication records to confirm a session.
Distinguish bastion and administrative remote desktop use from adversary lateral movement using baseline direction and account norms.
Analyse authentication anomalies such as local account usage, unusual logon hours, and first-seen source to destination pairs.
Describe the evidence available when a session is brokered through a gateway or jump host and how it changes scoping.
Map remote desktop lateral movement to ATT&CK and specify the mitigation controls that constrain it most effectively.

topics.title: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
topics.summary:
SMB and Windows administrative shares provide file and named pipe access over the Server Message Block protocol, and the administrative shares that exist on Windows systems by default can be used both to move files to a remote host and to request remote execution of a service or scheduled task. An adversary with administrative credentials can copy a payload to a target, then trigger execution through a remote service control or task scheduling interface, and finally clean up the staged file. Because the underlying protocol is the same one used for ordinary file sharing, the traffic does not look unusual at the network layer, and command-line administrative tools are also entirely normal on managed systems.

The reliable evidence is a combination of authentication, share access, and service or task state changes. Destination hosts log network logons and, where detailed file share auditing is enabled, the specific share and path accessed together with the accessing account. Service creation and task registration events on the target record the moment execution was requested, including the binary path referenced, which frequently points at an administrative share path or a temporary directory. Process creation on the target shows what actually ran and under which account, and named pipe access may appear in telemetry from security tooling or from the endpoint agent. On the source side, administrative command execution produces process events that name remote hosts and share paths.

Legitimate configuration management, patching, and backup products use exactly these mechanisms, often at high volume. Effective triage requires knowing which accounts and hosts are authorised to perform remote administration and at what times. Signals that raise confidence include a single account authenticating to many hosts in rapid succession, service creation referencing binaries in user-writable locations, administration activity outside deployment windows, and correlation with an earlier credential access alert.
objectives: Explain how administrative shares, remote service creation, and scheduled task registration combine to produce remote execution.
Interpret share access auditing and service or task creation records on the destination host to confirm execution.
Build a baseline of authorised administrative accounts and hosts to reduce false positives from management tooling.
Detect anomalous fan-out patterns where one account authenticates to many hosts in a short interval.
Explain what evidence survives on the source host and what must be recovered from the target or network capture.
Map SMB-based lateral movement to ATT&CK and evaluate segmentation and credential-tiering controls against it.

topics.title: Remote Services: SSH
topics.summary:
Secure Shell is the standard encrypted remote login and command execution protocol on Unix-like systems, and it is also widely enabled on network devices, hypervisors, and appliances. It supports interactive sessions, single command execution, port forwarding, and agent-based authentication, all of which an adversary can use after obtaining valid credentials or private keys. Lateral movement commonly begins from a host the adversary already controls, using either a stolen key or a replayed password, and then proceeds host to host along the paths that trust relationships and automation accounts permit. Because SSH traffic is encrypted and the daemon runs on nearly every server, network inspection alone yields little.

Useful artefacts are on the endpoints. The SSH daemon logs accepted and failed authentications together with the source address, the account, and the authentication method used, which distinguishes public key acceptance from password acceptance. The client host records the execution of the SSH client process with its full argument vector, exposing destination hosts and any remote command string, and shell history may show the same. Where the client host retains user key material, file access to private keys appears in file integrity monitoring or process telemetry. Host-based session recording, if deployed, captures the interactive commands themselves, and the target's process accounting shows what executed inside the session.

Legitimate SSH use is continuous in most environments, especially for automation, deployment, and monitoring. The distinguishing features are direction and account fit: administrative hosts connecting outward is normal, application servers connecting to unrelated database or domain infrastructure is not, and interactive sessions by service accounts that normally only run automation are strong indicators. Failed authentication bursts followed by a success, connection attempts to many hosts from one source, and use of keys that belong to a different host all warrant escalation.
objectives: Explain how accepted key and password authentication records differ and what each proves about adversary access.
Reconstruct an SSH movement path from client process arguments, daemon logs, and session recordings on multiple hosts.
Identify automation accounts and trust relationships that create silent, credential-driven movement paths.
Correlate failed authentication bursts with subsequent successful logins to detect credential-driven approaches.
Distinguish legitimate deployment and monitoring traffic from interactive adversary sessions using timing and target fit.
Map SSH lateral movement to ATT&CK and rank key management, bastion, and segmentation controls by effectiveness.

topics.title: Remote System Discovery
topics.summary: Remote system discovery is the mapping of hosts, addresses and services reachable from a compromised position, producing the target list that later lateral movement and exploitation depend on. The mechanism varies with access level. From an endpoint, an adversary can use address resolution and name resolution traffic, broadcast name service queries, connection attempts to common ports, and management interfaces that enumerate peers. From a domain joined host, directory and network browsing interfaces reveal computer objects, trusts and shares, frequently returning far more than a single address sweep would. From cloud or virtualisation control planes, inventory interfaces list running instances, network interfaces, security group rules and storage endpoints, so discovery happens entirely through authenticated interface calls with no scanning traffic at all. The observable artefacts are therefore both network and host based. Flow records show one internal host attempting connections to many distinct destinations or ports in a short window, with a high proportion of rejects or resets. Firewalls and intrusion detection systems record denied connection attempts and scan like patterns. Name resolution logs show bursts of reverse lookups or queries that follow a host naming convention. Endpoint logs capture the scanning or enumeration process with its command line, parent process and execution path. Cloud audit logs show bursts of describe and list operations across regions or accounts. The main investigative problem is that authorised vulnerability scanners, asset inventory platforms, network monitoring and deployment tools do exactly the same things. Analysts distinguish them by source identity, scheduling regularity, whether the source appears on an approved scanner list, whether the scan is credentialed and authenticated, the breadth relative to the source host's normal role, and the absence of any change management context. Discovery that originates from an ordinary workstation or a server that has never scanned before, especially shortly after a new foothold or credential access event, carries far more weight than identical traffic from a known appliance. Sequence remains the strongest signal, because discovery is meaningful mainly for what follows it.
objectives: Explain how host, service and cloud inventory discovery mechanisms produce different network and host artefacts.
Interpret flow, firewall and name resolution data to distinguish scanning from normal peer communication.
Whitelist and profile authorised scanners, inventory agents and monitoring platforms so their activity is not repeatedly triaged.
Detect cloud and virtualisation inventory enumeration through control plane audit logs rather than network traffic.
Correlate discovery bursts with the credential access, lateral movement or exploitation that follows.
Rank discovery alerts using source host role, breadth of targeting and deviation from historical behaviour.

topics.title: User Execution
topics.summary: User Execution describes adversary reliance on a person to take an action that results in code running or a security decision being made in the attacker interest. It is the human step that completes many delivery chains: opening an attachment, enabling macros or add-ins, clicking through a security warning, running a downloaded installer, mounting a disk image, pasting and executing a copied command, or approving a fraudulent push notification. The technique appears wherever an adversary cannot reach a system directly and must borrow a legitimate user session and its privileges, which makes it relevant on Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile platforms and cloud consoles alike. The artefacts are a mixture of endpoint and identity telemetry: process creation showing a document reader, archive tool or installer spawning a shell or a scripting host, file creation in download and temporary directories, mark-of-the-web and quarantine attributes, macro and add-in events in productivity suites, click-through records for protected-view prompts, and authentication logs for push-notification or help-desk style social engineering. Investigators distinguish malicious from benign execution by examining the parent process, the file origin and zone information, whether the resulting process made outbound network connections, whether the same lure reached other users, and whether the account later exhibited behaviour inconsistent with its history. Because the triggering action is legitimate and user-driven, prevention leans on policy and interface friction rather than detection alone, and the honest measure of a control is how many prompts an ordinary employee must evaluate during a normal working day before the prompts themselves become the vulnerability.
objectives: Explain how user-initiated execution differs from remote exploitation and why that shapes the defensive response.
Trace a document, archive or installer parent process to the child processes and network activity it produced.
Read mark-of-the-web, quarantine and macro telemetry to establish how a file was obtained and opened.
Evaluate user-facing controls such as attachment policy, macro restriction and prompt design against real user behaviour.
Write detection logic for productivity and reader applications that spawn interpreters or shells.
Rank response urgency when a user action is confirmed versus merely suspected.

topics.title: Valid Accounts
topics.summary: Valid Accounts describes adversary use of legitimate credentials or existing accounts to gain and keep access rather than exploiting a software flaw. The accounts involved may be default or built-in accounts shipped with an operating system, application or appliance, local or domain accounts whose passwords were obtained earlier in an intrusion, or cloud, SaaS and federated identities issued to real users or service principals. The technique is attractive precisely because the resulting activity is authenticated and therefore blends into the very large volume of normal sign-in and administration traffic. Mechanism varies by target: an interactive logon at a console or over remote desktop, a remote service session over SSH or server message block, an API call authenticated with a stolen token, or a service account used to run scheduled work. The artefacts that make investigation possible are concentrated in identity and access telemetry, including authentication logs, sign-in records carrying location, device and client application, token issuance and refresh events, Kerberos ticket requests, privilege role assignments and group membership changes, alongside the endpoint and network records of what the authenticated session then did. Distinguishing misuse from normal work depends on context: impossible travel, sign-ins from hosting or anonymising infrastructure, first-time combinations of device and application, dormant accounts that suddenly become active, service accounts authenticating interactively, and privilege use far outside an established baseline. Because the credentials are genuine, the decisive question in an investigation is rarely whether authentication succeeded but whether the account, the source and the behaviour are consistent with how that identity is normally used, and whether the same session also produced actions that no business process explains.
objectives: Explain how default, local, domain and federated accounts differ as footholds and what each leaves in identity telemetry.
Interpret sign-in, token and Kerberos records to identify authentication that is valid but inconsistent with an identity baseline.
Recognise the behavioural signatures of dormant, service and shared account misuse.
Correlate identity evidence with endpoint and network activity to confirm what an authenticated session actually did.
Prioritise credential hygiene controls such as multifactor authentication, just-in-time access and privileged access management against observed gaps.
Document a valid-account incident timeline from first anomalous sign-in through credential rotation and containment.
